report.framework: The eight principal passions ("thoughts", logismoi): Evagrius's list, John Cassian's eight principal faults, and Gregory the Great's reworking into pride as root plus seven principal vices (Moralia XXXI.45). Also covered: the stages of a temptation (Gregory, Climacus, Mark).
report.verdict_reason: The public-domain texts are rich, specific and verified. Cassian gives each fault its kinds, everyday signs, excuses, offspring and remedy. Gregory gives each vice its "daughters" and the reasonable-sounding speech it makes to the heart. Cassian also states outright that each person has a "besetting sin" to find and fight first. That is enough to carry a "Start here / how it argues with you" layer. It stops short of "strong" for four reasons. (1) The sources describe passions that attack everyone and shift with a person's situation and progress. They are not temperaments, so the layer cannot work as a fixed type. (2) Six of Cassian's eight overlap with the live seven deadly sins quiz. (3) Most of the signs are set in a monastery and need careful translation into ordinary life. (4) The fullest treatment of lust (Institutes VI) is missing from the public-domain English.
report.sorts_people:
Partly. The sources treat these as states and struggles, not as kinds of people. But they do say which one leads differs from person to person.

For sorting: Cassian, Conference 5.13 says the eight "do not attack them all in the same way. For in one man the spirit of fornication holds the chief place: wrath rides rough shod over another". Conference 5.14 says "every one should discover his besetting sin, and direct his main attack against it". Conference 5.27 says the order of battle differs by person: one starts with the third fault on the list, another with the fourth or fifth. Gregory, Moralia XXXI.87 says "all faults do not occupy the heart with equal access". Pastoral Rule III.38 says to treat first the vice "through which there is the more rapid tendency to death". Evagrius, Praktikos 43 and 50 (paraphrase) tell the monk to observe which thoughts come to him, how often, how strongly, at what times and in what order.

Against sorting: the same passage (Conference 5.13) says "we are all attacked by all of them". The ruling fault changes as you win: after one fault is beaten, "single out the worst fault which he can see among those still there" (Conference 5.14). Some faults depend on stage or situation, not character. Vainglory and pride strike "when we have proved victorious" (Conference 5.10). Covetousness attacks only the lukewarm (Conference 5.8). Spiritual pride attacks only the nearly perfect, and carnal pride attacks beginners (Institutes XII.24). Acedia besets solitaries at midday (Institutes X.1). Anger shows itself in company (Institutes VIII.18-19). Gregory himself separates a lasting "constitution" from a passion that suddenly arises (Pastoral Rule III.37).

Plainly: this can say "the fault leading in you now, the one to fight first". It cannot say "your type".
report.summary:
The eight "thoughts" come from the Egyptian desert. Evagrius listed them about 380: gluttony, lust, love of money, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride. John Cassian brought them west about 420. He swapped sadness and anger, and gave each fault a whole book (Institutes V to XII). He also set out the whole scheme in one dialogue, Conference 5. Gregory the Great reshaped the list in the Moralia (XXXI.45). Pride became the root, outside the list. Vainglory became the first of seven. Envy was added, and acedia was folded into melancholy. That list, adjusted later, is the one the site's live seven deadly sins quiz uses.

The sources are concrete. For each fault Cassian names its kinds and its everyday signs. He gives the excuses it makes, what it breeds, and its cure. Gregory adds each vice's "daughters". Best of all, he gives the reasonable-sounding speech each vice makes to the heart. Anger says that bearing wrongs patiently "is a sin". Avarice says you only fear being in want. Cassian and Gregory each give a chain in which one fault feeds the next. Cassian also names the virtue that takes each fault's place. The Eastern writers add stages of a temptation: a first suggestion, then conversing with it, consent, captivity, and finally a settled habit.

Do they sort people? Partly. Cassian says plainly that all eight attack everyone. But in each person one "holds the chief place", and each must find his "besetting sin" and fight it first. Gregory says to treat first the vice with "the more rapid tendency to death". Yet the sources also tie faults to situation and progress. Vainglory and pride strike after victories. Covetousness strikes the lukewarm. Spiritual pride strikes the nearly perfect. So this is not a temperament. It is "where the fight is for you now".

That makes it a good second layer for the Gregory personality quiz: start here, how it talks to you, what feeds it, what takes its place. It is not a type system. It also overlaps heavily with the live deadly sins quiz, so it needs a different frame.

elements.name: Gluttony (gastrimargia; Gregory: gula)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's first fault: the pleasures of the palate. It is natural to us and can never be fully rooted out, only held down (Conference 5.19-21, the simile of the eagle). It comes in three kinds: eating before the set time, filling the belly, and looking for dainties. Gregory counts five ways it tempts (too early; daintier food; food prepared more carefully; too much; baser food wanted with burning desire). He says the fault lies in the desire, not the food.
everyday_signs: Eating or drinking outside meal times, or taking a morsel after the meal is over (Institutes V.20)
As a guest, asking the host to add something to the dish he offered (Conference 5.11)
Wanting variety: Evagrius prescribes bread and water when the soul longs for many foods (Praktikos 16, paraphrase)
Severe fasts followed by relaxation, rather than steady daily moderation (Institutes V.9)
A heavy, dulled mind after eating (Institutes V.6)
elements.disguise: The plea of bodily weakness: people eat more than they need 'on the plea of weakness' (Institutes V.7). Evagrius: the thought paints stomach trouble, long illness and no doctors, and recalls brothers who fell ill from fasting (Praktikos 7, paraphrase). Gregory's version of its speech: 'God has created all things clean, in order to be eaten', so refusing food gainsays the gift (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.hidden_side: The thing to watch is the desire, not the food (Moralia XXX.60). Gluttony 'opened the door to other passions' (Conference 5.26). Someone who cannot master small open appetites will not master hidden ones (Institutes V.11, V.20).
elements.counsel: Wait for the set hour. Do not gorge. Be content with common food (Institutes V.23). Daily moderation is better than long fasts at intervals (V.9). Keep your fasting hidden. Break your own fast for a guest's sake, because hospitality is a command and a fast is a free offering (V.23-24). Gregory: give nature what it needs and refuse what gluttony adds (Moralia XXX.61, paraphrase).
elements.links: Gluttony leads to fornication (Conference 5.10; Moralia XXXI.89). Its three kinds lead in turn to dislike of the monastery, to lust, and to covetousness (Conference 5.11). Gregory, Pastoral Rule III.38: unchecked gluttony brings on lechery, and fighting it by abstinence brings on vainglory. Offspring: surfeiting and drunkenness (Conference 5.16). Gregory's daughters: foolish mirth, scurrility, uncleanness, babbling, dulness of sense (Moralia XXXI.88).

elements.name: Fornication / lust (porneia; Gregory: luxuria)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's second fault. It is natural and is completed through the body. It comes in three kinds: the act itself; uncleanness without a woman; and lust conceived in the heart, citing Matthew 5:28 (Conference 5.11). Because it lives in body and mind together, it needs a double remedy (Conference 5.4). Cassian's full book on it (Institutes VI) was left out of the NPNF edition and is not on New Advent. It was not checked here.
everyday_signs: What the mind does with a look: the look only brings to the surface a sickness already hidden inside (Institutes IX.6)
Evagrius: it drives a desire for different bodies. It makes the soul speak and hear words as if the thing were present (Praktikos 8, paraphrase)
Offspring in speech: filthy conversation, scurrility, buffoonery, foolish talking (Conference 5.16)
elements.disguise: Gregory's version of its speech: enjoy it now, since life is short, and God made them male and female (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.hidden_side: The fall is never sudden. The occasion only shows what was already stored in the heart (Institutes IX.6). Gregory's daughters describe the hidden cost: blindness of mind, inconsiderateness, inconstancy, precipitation, self-love, affection for this present world (Moralia XXXI.88).
elements.counsel: Fasting, vigils and contrition, with a change of scene. Put the material that feeds it out of reach. Meditate on Scripture, keep watch, and withdraw (Conference 5.4). Evagrius: burning desire is quenched by hunger, toil and withdrawal (Praktikos 15, paraphrase). Three sources note that vainglory can hold lust back for a while (Conference 5.12; Praktikos 58; Pastoral Rule III.38). Cassian warns that vainglory is then harder to escape.
elements.links: Lust comes from gluttony and leads to covetousness (Conference 5.10; 'a special tie' with gluttony). It pulls against vainglory: Praktikos 58 (paraphrase), Conference 5.12, Pastoral Rule III.38. Evagrius: vainglory can hand a man over to lust (Praktikos 13, paraphrase).

elements.name: Covetousness / love of money (philargyria; Gregory: avaritia)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's third fault. It is 'a foreign warfare, and one outside of our nature' (Institutes VII.1). It is not inborn. It attacks only those whose foundation is lukewarm (Conference 5.8). It comes in three kinds: refusing to give things up; taking back what was given away; and wanting what you never had (Conference 5.11; Institutes VII.14, with Ananias and Sapphira, Judas and Gehazi as the three examples).
everyday_signs: Keeping a private reserve 'just in case' of illness or old age (Institutes VII.7)
A secret side-earning, then worry over where to keep it and how to double it (VII.7)
It grows with every gain (VII.7) and is never satisfied (VII.24)
Complaining that the provision is too little, murmuring, finding fault with everything (VII.8-9)
Looking for chances to be offended, to justify leaving (VII.9)
Covetous in wish without owning anything (VII.22)
elements.disguise: It gives 'excellent and almost reasonable excuses' (Institutes VII.7): prudence about sickness, old age and not being a burden. People misread 'It is more blessed to give than to receive' to keep their wealth (VII.16). Evagrius: it suggests a long old age, weak hands, famine, disease, and the shame of taking from others (Praktikos 9, paraphrase). Gregory's version of its speech: you seek not increase but only fear want, and you would spend it better than others do (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.hidden_side: Owning little does not free you if the desire is there (VII.21-22). The Apostle calls it idolatry, because it loves 'images stamped on gold instead of God' (VII.7).
elements.counsel: Cut the desire, not only the possession (VII.21). Keep not even the smallest coin (VII.28). Stay in community and be content with food and clothing (VII.29). Patience, which springs from humility, keeps you there (VII.31). Evagrius: love cannot live alongside wealth (Praktikos 18, paraphrase).
elements.links: It comes from fornication and leads to anger (Conference 5.10). Gluttony's search for dainties feeds it (Conference 5.11). Gregory: melancholy 'runs down into avarice' because a heart without joy seeks comfort outside (Moralia XXXI.89). Offspring: lying, deceit, theft, perjury, false witness, violence, inhumanity (Conference 5.16). Gregory's daughters: treachery, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, hardness of heart against compassion (Moralia XXXI.88).

elements.name: Anger (orge / thumos; Gregory: ira)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's fourth fault. Its seed is in us (Conference 5.8) but outside things set it off (Conference 5.3). It comes in three kinds: rage within (thumos); rage breaking out in word and deed (orge); and anger that lasts for days (menis) (Conference 5.11). Cassian's line is strict: the aim is 'not being angry at all' (Institutes VIII.21). The only right anger is anger at your own sinful stirrings (VIII.7-9).
everyday_signs: Sulking: saying you are not angry while withholding ordinary warmth and civility for days (Institutes VIII.11)
Holding back only because there is no chance for revenge (VIII.12)
Irritation at objects: the pen, the penknife, the flint (VIII.19)
Blaming others and wishing for solitude where nobody provokes you (VIII.16)
Evagrius: all day the soul turns savage, and in prayer the offender's face appears before the mind (Praktikos 11, paraphrase)
elements.disguise: Righteous anger: 'God Himself is said to be angry', so anger at wrongdoers must be fine (VIII.2). The added words 'without a cause' in Matthew 5:22 were put in to excuse just anger (VIII.21). Gregory's version of its speech: to bear such things patiently would itself be a sin (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.hidden_side: A man seems patient only while nobody tests him (VIII.18). The trouble comes from our own stored faults, not from other people (IX.5). Anger nursed in silence shuts out the Spirit as much as anger shown openly (VIII.12).
elements.counsel: Decide never to be angry, whether for good reasons or bad. Do not pray while angry. Remember you will soon die (VIII.22). Be reconciled first, even when it is the other who holds the grudge (VIII.13-14). Your peace depends on your own patience, not on others being perfect (VIII.17). Do not run to solitude to fix it (VIII.18). Evagrius: anger is calmed by psalmody, patience and mercy (Praktikos 15, paraphrase).
elements.links: It comes from covetousness and leads to dejection (Conference 5.10). Gregory: envy leads to anger, and anger to melancholy (Moralia XXXI.89). Evagrius: sadness can follow anger (Praktikos 10), and pride brings anger after it (Praktikos 14) (paraphrase). Offspring: clamour, indignation, even murder (Conference 5.16). Gregory's daughters: strifes, swelling of mind, insults, clamour, indignation, blasphemies (Moralia XXXI.88). The sources disagree here. Gregory allows right zeal but watches for 'anger from zeal' (Moralia XXXI.86; compare Pastoral Rule III.16 in the personality README). Cassian allows no anger at others at all.

It makes the soul savage all day, and above all in prayer it seizes the mind with the image of the one who hurt us. If it lingers it turns into rancour. elements.name: Dejection / sadness (lupe; Gregory: tristitia, 'melancholy' in the 1844-50 translation)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's fifth fault. Evagrius puts sadness fourth, before anger. It comes in two kinds: sorrow after anger, a loss or a thwarted plan; and sorrow from unreasonable anxiety or despair (Conference 5.11). It rises from within and harasses people who are alone (Conference 5.3, 5.9). Cassian keeps one sorrow as good: sorrow for sin, longing for perfection, or longing for the life to come (Institutes IX.10-12).
everyday_signs: You cannot receive people you love with ordinary warmth, and whatever they talk about seems ill-timed (Institutes IX.4)
No gladness in prayer or reading; impatient and rough at work (IX.1)
It can come after anger or disappointment, or with no apparent reason (IX.4)
Evagrius: thoughts of home, family and your former life, then gloom that they are gone (Praktikos 10, paraphrase)
elements.disguise: It passes for the reasonable response to being wronged. Gregory's version of its speech: 'What ground hast thou to rejoice, when thou endurest so many wrongs from thy neighbours?' (Moralia XXXI.90). It also imitates godly sorrow. The test: godly sorrow is 'obedient, civil, humble, kindly, gentle, and patient', while the worldly kind is 'rough, impatient, hard' (Institutes IX.11).
elements.hidden_side: The cause lies in our own stored faults, not in others (IX.5). Its worst form is despair that produces no amendment, as with Cain and Judas (IX.9).
elements.counsel: Keep the mind on the hope of what is to come. Be neither crushed by present troubles nor lifted up by good fortune, since both will pass (IX.13). Do not run from other people; perfection comes through patience, not separation (IX.7).
elements.links: It comes from anger and leads to acedia (Conference 5.10). It is paired with acedia (Conference 5.10). Gregory: it comes from anger and runs into avarice (Moralia XXXI.89). Gregory's daughters: malice, rancour, cowardice, despair, slothfulness in fulfilling the commands, and a wandering of the mind on unlawful objects (Moralia XXXI.88). Cassian's offspring: rancor, cowardice, bitterness, despair (Conference 5.16). Its place is taken by 'a godly sorrow and one full of joy' (Conference 5.23). Note that Gregory's seven have no separate acedia; its sluggishness sits among melancholy's daughters.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: Of dejection there are two kinds: one, that which springs up when anger has died down, or is the result of some loss we have incurred or of some purpose which has been hindered and interfered with; the other, that which comes from unreasonable anxiety of mind or from despair.

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: we are by the instigation of our crafty enemy suddenly depressed with so great a gloom that we cannot receive with ordinary civility the visits of those who are near and dear to us; and whatever subject of conversation is started by them, we regard it as ill-timed and out of place

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: But the other kind is rough, impatient, hard, full of rancour and useless grief and penal despair

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: we are not depressed by present accidents, or over-elated by prosperity, but look on each condition as uncertain and likely soon to pass away.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: What ground hast thou to rejoice, when thou endurest so many wrongs from thy neighbours?

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
sources.paraphrase: Sadness sometimes comes from frustrated desires and sometimes follows anger. With frustrated desire, thoughts first draw the soul back to home, parents and its former life. When the soul follows them into pleasant reverie, they plunge it into gloom that those things are gone.

elements.name: Acedia / accidie (akedia)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's sixth fault: 'weariness or distress of heart'. It is akin to dejection. It strikes those who live alone, especially around midday, and some elders called it the midday demon of Psalm 90 (91) (Institutes X.1). It comes in two kinds: one sends you to sleep, the other makes you run away (Conference 5.11). Evagrius calls it the heaviest of the demons (Praktikos 12).
everyday_signs: Dislike of where you are. Contempt for your companions as careless or unspiritual (Institutes X.2)
Praising far-off places and communities as better (X.2)
Midday weariness and hunger. Going in and out, watching the sun, hoping someone will visit (X.2)
Relief sought in sleep or in visiting (X.3)
Idleness turning into restlessness, gossip and meddling in others' affairs (X.7, X.13)
Evagrius: the day seems fifty hours long. Hatred of the place, the life and the work; the thought that love has left the brethren (Praktikos 12, paraphrase)
elements.disguise: Pious duties. It suggests visiting the sick and one's relatives, or 'that it would be a real work of piety to go more frequently to visit that religious woman' (Institutes X.2). It gets you to leave 'under some pious excuse or pretext' (X.5). Evagrius: it adds that God can be worshipped anywhere, so why stay here (Praktikos 12, paraphrase).
elements.hidden_side: The remedy it offers (a visit, a nap) leaves you weaker and invites a fiercer attack (X.3; X.25). The Egyptian saying: a working monk faces one devil, an idle one countless spirits (X.23).
elements.counsel: Work with your hands (X.14). Abbot Paul burned a year's handiwork every year simply to stay put and defeat acedia (X.24). Resist it; do not run from it (X.25). Evagrius: no other demon follows straight after this one; after the struggle come peace and unspeakable joy (Praktikos 12, paraphrase).
elements.links: It comes from dejection (Conference 5.10) and is paired with it (Conference 5.10). Offspring: laziness, sleepiness, rudeness, restlessness, wandering about, instability of mind and body, chattering, inquisitiveness (Conference 5.16). Its place is taken by courage (Conference 5.23). It is absent from Gregory's seven.

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
sources.paraphrase: The demon of acedia, also called the noonday demon, is the heaviest of all. It besets the monk from about the fourth to the eighth hour. It makes the sun seem to stand still. It makes him keep looking out and leaving his cell to see if a brother is coming. It stirs hatred of the place, the life and the work of his hands, and a longing for other places, adding that God can be worshipped anywhere. No other demon follows directly after it; after the struggle come peace and unspeakable joy.

elements.name: Vainglory (kenodoxia; Gregory: inanis gloria, the first of his seven)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's seventh fault. It 'takes many shapes, and is changeable and subtle' (Institutes XI.1). It attacks through the flesh and through spiritual progress alike (XI.2). It comes in two kinds: pride in visible things, and hunger for praise for spiritual things (Conference 5.11). For Gregory it is the first offspring of pride and the first of the seven (Moralia XXXI.87, 89).
everyday_signs: It works through dress, manner, walk, voice, work, fasting, prayer, reading, knowledge, silence, obedience and humility (Institutes XI.3)
In beginners: pride in a good singing voice, looks, a thin ascetic body, rich or noble relatives, or a career given up (XI.13)
Imagining you would have had honours and riches if you had stayed in the world (XI.13)
Daydreams of preaching and converting crowds; one brother was overheard delivering an imaginary sermon in his cell (XI.14-16)
Evagrius: wanting to make one's efforts known; fantasies of healing people, crowds touching one's clothes, being sought out for the priesthood (Praktikos 13, paraphrase)
elements.disguise: It works only through the virtues (XI.6, XI.9). If neat dress will not serve, shabby dress will; hiding a fast feeds it as much as showing one (XI.4). Gregory's version of its speech: aim at greater things so you can do more good for more people (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.hidden_side: It is like an onion: strip one layer and another is underneath (XI.5). It rises again stronger after being beaten (XI.7). Neither solitude nor age cures it (XI.8). It strikes after victories (Conference 5.10). Evagrius: after lifting a man up with empty hopes it drops him into pride, gloom or lust (Praktikos 13, paraphrase).
elements.counsel: Do nothing for the sake of vainglory. Keep up with the same care whatever you began well. Avoid whatever would make you stand out as the only one who could do it (XI.19). Remember that God 'has scattered the bones of those who please men' (XI.19).
elements.links: It leads to pride (Conference 5.10, 'closely allied'). Gregory: it comes from pride and begets envy (Moralia XXXI.89). It pulls against lust (Conference 5.12; Praktikos 58; Pastoral Rule III.38). Cassian's offspring: contention, heresies, boasting, confidence in novelties (Conference 5.16). Gregory's daughters: disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contentions, obstinacies, discords, and the presumptions of novelties (Moralia XXXI.88).

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: For it tries to injure the soldier of Christ in his dress, in his manner, his walk, his voice, his work, his vigils, his fasts, his prayers, when he withdraws, when he reads, in his knowledge, his silence, his obedience, his humility, his patience

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: For where the devil cannot create vainglory in a man by means of his well-fitting and neat dress, he tries to introduce it by means of a dirty, cheap, and uncared-for style.

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: Nor does this malady endeavour to wound a man except through his virtues

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: Sometimes too it persuades a man that if he had remained in the world he would easily have obtained honours and riches

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: It makes a man, even when alone and sitting in his cell, to go round in mind and imagination to the dwellings and monasteries of others, and to make many conversions under the inducements of imaginary exultation.

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: whatever would render us remarkable among the others, and for which credit would be gained among men, as if we were the only people who could do it, this should be shunned by us.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Thou oughtest to aim at greater things, that, as thou hast been able to surpass many in power, thou mayest be able to benefit many also.

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
sources.paraphrase: The thought of vainglory is very subtle and slips in among those whose lives are going well. It makes them want to publicise their efforts and hunt for human glory. It pictures demons crying out, women healed, crowds touching his clothes, and people at his door wanting to make him a priest. Then it leaves him to the demon of pride or of gloom, and sometimes of fornication.
sources.translation: Checked in Dysinger's modern translation; paraphrase only

elements.name: Pride (hyperephania; Gregory: superbia, the root outside the seven)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's eighth fault. It is last in the order of battle but first in origin (Institutes XII.1, XII.6). It comes in two kinds: spiritual pride, which attacks the advanced, and carnal pride, which attacks beginners and the lukewarm (XII.2, XII.24). Other faults each ruin one opposite virtue; pride ruins them all (XII.3). Its root is Lucifer's belief that his gifts came from his own nature, not from God (XII.4). For Gregory, pride is 'the queen of sins' and the root of the seven (Moralia XXXI.87).
everyday_signs: Loud in talk, bitter in silence, noisy in laughter, gloomy when serious (Institutes XII.29)
Quick to insult others, faint-hearted when insulted (XII.29)
Obedient only when the duty matches your wishes. Cannot take correction. Prefers your own opinion to the elders' (XII.29)
Thinks any serious talk is aimed at you, and fidgets through it (XII.27)
Refuses an apology, and grows angrier when the other apologises first (XII.27)
Wants to leave and teach or lead others instead of being taught (XII.30)
Evagrius: not acknowledging God's help, thinking yourself the cause of your successes, looking down on others as foolish (Praktikos 14, paraphrase)
elements.disguise: A proud silence looks like compunction (XII.27). The wish to found a community and teach looks like zeal, 'as if he would do good to many more people' (XII.30).
elements.hidden_side: It attacks hardest those who have almost reached the top (XII.1, XII.24). Everything else can be in order while this undoes it all (XII.3).
elements.counsel: Lay the foundation of fear of God and humility, 'proceeding from kindness and simplicity of heart' (XII.31). Do not grieve or hurt your brothers. Bear injuries by remembering 'the passion of our Lord and of all His Saints' (XII.33). Believe that even understanding this is God's gift (XII.33).
elements.links: It comes from vainglory (Conference 5.10). It is the root and 'queen' of the seven (Moralia XXXI.87). Offspring: contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, backbiting (Conference 5.16). Evagrius: anger and gloom follow it (Praktikos 14, paraphrase). Its place is taken by humility (Conference 5.23).

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: although it is the latest in our conflict with our faults and stands last on the list, yet in beginning and in the order of time is the first

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: impudent in offering insults to others, faint-hearted in bearing them himself

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos

sources.translation: Checked in Dysinger's modern translation; paraphrase only

elements.name: Envy (Gregory's addition; not one of Cassian's or Evagrius's eight)
elements.what_it_is: Gregory puts envy second among his seven, as vainglory's child (Moralia XXXI.87, 89). Cassian does not count it among the eight. He lists it among pride's offspring (Conference 5.16) and calls it a 'food of the mind' (Institutes V.21). It is included here because the site's live quiz has it and any Gregory-based layer would too.
everyday_signs: Misery at another's success (Institutes V.21)
Gregory's daughters: hatred, whispering, detraction, glee at a neighbour's misfortune, distress at his prosperity (Moralia XXXI.88)
elements.disguise: Gregory's version of its speech: why are you not equal or superior to them, when you can do things they cannot? (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.hidden_side: Envy admits that the other person is greater: 'while he envies another he shows that the one at whose prosperity he is vexed, is greater than he' (Institutes V.22, commenting on Job 5:2).
elements.counsel: These sources say little. For the envious hearer, see Gregory's Pastoral Rule III.10 (kindly/envious), already in the personality README. That was not re-checked in this pass.
elements.links: Gregory: it comes from vainglory and leads to anger (Moralia XXXI.89). Cassian: it comes from pride (Conference 5.16).

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: Envy is a food of the mind, corrupting it with its poisonous juices and never ceasing to make it wretched and miserable at the prosperity and success of another.

sources.work: John Cassian, Institutes
sources.quote: while he envies another he shows that the one at whose prosperity he is vexed, is greater than he.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: In what art thou inferior to this or that person? why then art thou not either equal or superior to them?

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences
key_passages.quote: Although then these eight faults trouble all sorts of men, yet they do not attack them all in the same way. For in one man the spirit of fornication holds the chief place: wrath rides rough shod over another: over another vainglory claims dominion: in an other pride holds the field: and though it is clear that we are all attacked by all of them, yet the difficulties come to each of us in very different ways and manners.
key_passages.paraphrase: Everyone is attacked by all eight, but a different one leads in each person.
key_passages.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF2 vol. 11 (1894)

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences
key_passages.quote: Wherefore we must enter the lists against these faults in such a way that every one should discover his besetting sin, and direct his main attack against it
key_passages.paraphrase: Fight the chief fault first. Once it is beaten, 'single out the worst fault which he can see among those still there'. Each victory makes the next easier. Fighting one fault does not leave you careless of the others. The victory is God's, not our own strength.

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences
key_passages.quote: each one of us ought also to begin the battle with due regard to the character of the attack which is especially made on him so that one man will have to fight his first battle against the fault which stands third on the list, another against that which is fourth or fifth.
key_passages.paraphrase: The order of the fight is personal, not the order of the list.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Book of Pastoral Rule
key_passages.quote: it is undoubtedly right to haste to the succour of that through which there is the more rapid tendency to death.
key_passages.paraphrase: When two vices press on someone, treat first the one that is more deadly. You may even let a lesser one (vainglory in fasting) stand for a while to hold back a worse one (lust from gluttony).

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Book of Pastoral Rule
key_passages.quote: For it is commonly the case that some one is of too joyous a constitution, and yet sadness suddenly arising immoderately depresses him.
key_passages.paraphrase: Gregory separates a lasting constitution (temperament) from a passion that suddenly arises. This is the clearest source for keeping a temperament layer and a passion layer apart.

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences
key_passages.quote: have a sort of connection with each other, and are, so to speak, linked together in a chain, so that any excess of the one forms a starting point for the next. For from superfluity of gluttony fornication is sure to spring, and from fornication covetousness, from covetousness anger, from anger, dejection, and from dejection, accidie.
key_passages.paraphrase: The first six form a chain: to overcome one, overcome the one before it. Vainglory and pride form a separate pair. They arise after victories: 'into these two we are in danger of falling when we have proved victorious, and above all after some splendid triumph.' They also fall into four couples: gluttony with fornication, covetousness with anger, dejection with accidie, vainglory with pride.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: But seven principal vices, as its first progeny, spring doubtless from this poisonous root, namely, vain glory, envy, anger, melancholy, avarice, gluttony, lust.
key_passages.paraphrase: Pride is the root; the seven are its generals. Gregory's order and chain (section 89): pride, vainglory, envy, anger, melancholy, avarice; then gluttony leads to lust. 'Of these seven, five namely are spiritual, and two are carnal' (section 88).
key_passages.translation: Library of the Fathers, Oxford: Parker, 1844-1850 (transcribed at Lectionary Central)

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.locus: Book XXXI, ch. xlv, section 88 (the daughters, exactly)
key_passages.quote: For from vain glory there arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contentions, obstinacies, discords, and the presumptions of novelties. From envy there spring hatred, whispering, detraction, exultation at the misfortunes of a neighbour, and affliction at his prosperity. From anger are produced strifes, swelling of mind, insults, clamour, indignation, blasphemies. From melancholy there arise malice, rancour, cowardice, despair, slothfulness in fulfilling the commands, and a wandering of the mind on unlawful objects. From avarice there spring treachery, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardnesses of heart against compassion. From gluttony are propagated foolish mirth, scurrility, uncleanness, babbling, dulness of sense in understanding. From lust are generated blindness of mind, inconsiderateness, inconstancy, precipitation, self-love, hatred of God, affection for this present world, but dread or despair of that which is to come.
key_passages.paraphrase: The full list of daughters, verbatim.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: because the first vices force themselves into the deluded mind as if under a kind of reason
key_passages.paraphrase: Each of the seven speaks to the heart 'as if with reason'. Gregory writes out each speech: vainglory (aim higher to benefit many), envy (why are they above you?), anger (patience here is a sin), melancholy (what have you to rejoice at?), avarice (you only fear want), gluttony (God made all food clean), lust (life is short). This is the richest 'disguise' material in any source.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: how arrogance rises from learning, cruelty from justice, carelessness from tenderness, anger from zeal, sloth from gentleness.
key_passages.paraphrase: Vices grow out of good qualities. This gives a strength-to-shadow map from Gregory himself.

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences
key_passages.quote: then at once the place in our heart which the spirit of concupiscence and fornication had occupied, will be filled by chastity. That which wrath had held, will be claimed by patience. That which had been occupied by a sorrow that works death, will be taken by a godly sorrow and one full of joy. That which had been wasted by accidie, will at once be tilled by courage. That which pride had trodden down will be ennobled by humility
key_passages.paraphrase: The opposite virtue takes each fault's place. Cassian names five pairs here. Institutes XII.3 adds gluttony against temperance, lust against purity, anger against patience.

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Institutes
key_passages.quote: so that sometimes a man who is in bondage to some one sin is not altogether wanting in other virtues
key_passages.paraphrase: A ruling fault attacks mainly its own opposite virtue, so a person can keep his other virtues. Pride is the exception. Contrast Institutes V.11: 'he is proved to possess no virtue perfectly, who is known to have broken down in some part of them.'

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Institutes
key_passages.quote: Christ is at the present time divided, member by member, among all of the saints.
key_passages.paraphrase: Virtues are spread among different people: knowledge, discretion, patience, humility, continence, simplicity. So we learn each virtue from the one who has it. This is the best source found here for 'who you are in the Body of Christ'. It concerns virtues, not vices.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Book of Pastoral Rule
key_passages.quote: Thus by suggestion we have knowledge of sin, by delight we are vanquished, by consent we are also bound.
key_passages.paraphrase: There are three stages: suggestion (from the enemy), delight (in the flesh), consent (of the spirit), as in Eden. The same chapter lists the soothing excuses: others did worse, it was nothing, God is merciful, there is time later. It also counsels being 'alarmed in such wise that they still be by no means broken down.'

key_passages.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
key_passages.locus: Step 15, paragraph 74 in the Greek (Migne PG 88, col. 896-897); paragraph 62 in the online English text of unidentified edition
key_passages.quote: Ἄλλο προσβολὴ, καὶ ἄλλο συνδυασμὸς, καὶ ἄλλο συγκατάθεσις, καὶ ἄλλο αἰχμαλωσία, καὶ ἕτερον πάλη, καὶ ἄλλο τὸ λεγόμενον πάθος ἐπὶ τῆς ψυχῆς
key_passages.paraphrase: The discerning Fathers distinguish six things. Provocation: a bare word or image newly appearing in the heart. Coupling: conversing with it, with or without passion. Consent: the soul's pleasurable nod toward it. Captivity: the heart carried off by force, or a lasting intimacy with it that ruins our best state. Struggle: a force equal to the attacker, which wins or loses by choice. Passion: what has nested in the soul for a long time until it becomes a habit the soul runs to of its own will. The first is sinless, the second not wholly so, and the third depends on the state of the one struggling. Whoever meets the first without passion cuts off all the rest at once.
key_passages.translation: Greek (ancient text) verified; English is this report's paraphrase. Modern English: Moore 1959 and Luibheid/Russell 1982, not checked.

key_passages.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
key_passages.paraphrase: Ch. 6: there are eight most general thoughts: gluttony, fornication, love of money, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory, pride. Whether they trouble the soul is not up to us. Whether they linger and stir the passions is. Ch. 43: learn the differences between the demons and their times, and which are rare and heavy or frequent and light. Then you can name the one present before it drives you far from your proper state. Ch. 50: whoever wants to know them should watch his thoughts. Note their intensity and slackening, how they interweave, their timing, which comes after which, and ask Christ for the reasons.
key_passages.translation: Checked in Luke Dysinger OSB's modern translation with the Greek; paraphrase only

key_passages.work: Mark the Ascetic, On Those Who Think That They Are Made Righteous by Works
key_passages.paraphrase: The devil tempts by provocations (prosbolai) of evil thoughts. He does not force; he only suggests the beginning. The person, through love of pleasure and vainglory, responds gladly: though he did not want it on reflection, in practice he took pleasure and accepted it.
key_passages.translation: Checked only in a modern Greek rendering (onisimos.gr). The English Philokalia vol. 1 (Palmer, Sherrard, Ware, 1979) was not checked. Mark's further terms, such as 'prepossession', were NOT verified and should not be used without checking.

report.measurement_notes:
What the sources themselves treat as evidence of a passion. These are not quiz items.

1. What a person does AFTER an event, more than in the moment. Anger shows in days of withheld civility while denying anger (Institutes VIII.11), or in holding back only for lack of opportunity (VIII.12). Dejection shows when you cannot greet loved ones warmly (IX.4). Pride shows in refusing an apology and growing angrier when the other apologises first (XII.27).

2. The excuse a person finds reasonable. Gregory says each vice enters 'as if under a kind of reason' and writes out each one's argument (Moralia XXXI.90). Cassian lists the 'almost reasonable excuses' of covetousness (VII.7) and the pious pretexts of acedia (X.2, X.5). Which rationale sounds most sensible to someone is, per these sources, a direct sign of the passion speaking.

3. Timing and triggers. Acedia comes at midday (Institutes X.1; Praktikos 12). Anger appears in prayer (Praktikos 11). Vainglory and pride come after success (Conference 5.10; Institutes XI.6-7). Covetousness and anger are set off from outside, dejection and acedia from within (Conference 5.3). Anger is exposed in company and hides in solitude (VIII.18-19).

4. Daydreams. Vainglory rehearses sermons and imagined honours (Institutes XI.13-16; Praktikos 13). Acedia praises distant places (X.2). Dejection replays the former life (Praktikos 10).

5. Small signs. Asking a host for extra (Conference 5.11). Anger at a pen or a knife (VIII.19). Watching the clock and hoping for visitors (X.2). Fidgeting through serious talk and thinking it aimed at you (XII.27).

6. The Fathers' own method is observation over time. Evagrius tells the monk to note which thoughts come, how strongly, how often, in what order and at what times (Praktikos 43, 50, paraphrase). This supports repeat-taking and tracking in the profile. It argues against a one-shot verdict.

Cautions for measurement. The sources place every sign in a monastery (cell, abbot, fasts, brethren), so any everyday version is an adaptation and should be flagged as such. The sources say the leading passion changes with stage. Carnal pride strikes beginners and spiritual pride the advanced (XII.24). Covetousness strikes the lukewarm (Conference 5.8). So situational items will measure the present state, not a fixed trait. Because of the chains (Conference 5.10; Moralia XXXI.89), high scores on neighbouring faults are expected to go together: gluttony with lust, anger with dejection, vainglory with pride. That is a feature to report, not noise.
report.orthodox_standing:
From general knowledge, not from the fetched texts.

- John Cassian: venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church (St John Cassian the Roman). The English Philokalia vol. 1 carries two works under his name drawn from the Institutes and Conferences: 'On the Eight Vices' and 'On the Holy Fathers of Sketis and on Discrimination'. Some Western writers suspected his Conference 13 on grace; that dispute is Western, and the Orthodox Church receives him fully. He is the safest foundation for this layer.
- Evagrius Ponticus: the originator of the eight 'thoughts'. His speculative, Origenist teaching was condemned in the sixth century, and his name is tied to that condemnation. He is not venerated as a saint. His practical chapters survived and are in the Philokalia, some under the name of St Nilus. Use him as a witness through Cassian, not as the foundation. None of his English is public domain; paraphrase only.
- Gregory the Great: St Gregory the Dialogist in the Orthodox Church. He was a pre-schism pope. The Moralia and the Pastoral Rule are pre-schism works.
- John Climacus: a major Orthodox saint. The Ladder is read in Great Lent, and a Lenten Sunday is dedicated to him. Public-domain English is doubtful: an 1858 paraphrase exists but was not located. The Greek (PG 88) was checked directly.
- Mark the Ascetic: an Orthodox saint whose works open the Philokalia's first volume. Only a modern Greek rendering was checked here.
- Post-schism Western (not a foundation): Aquinas carried Gregory's list and the five ways of gluttony into the Summa. The seven deadly sins as the site's live quiz states them are that later Western form. It replaced Gregory's melancholy with sloth and folded vainglory into pride.
