report.report_layer_ideas:
Ideas only, no copy.

1. 'Start here' (one leading passion, now). Grounded in Conference 5.13-14 and 5.27 and in Pastoral Rule III.38. Frame it as the fight to begin with at present, which will change (Conference 5.14), not as an identity. It fits the README's existing 'Start here' slot and can be fed by Gregory's own pair links (sad leads to anger; joyful to lust; meek to sloth; abstinent to pride; gluttonous to much talk).

2. 'How it talks to you' (the disguise). One field per passion. Source it from Gregory's speeches 'as if with reason' (Moralia XXXI.90), backed by Cassian's excuses: pious visits for acedia (X.2), 'almost reasonable excuses' for covetousness (VII.7), 'God is angry too' for anger (VIII.2), shabby dress for vainglory (XI.4). This is the strongest 'aha' material in the sources.

3. 'What feeds it, and what it feeds' (the chain). Two authorities, drawn as two chains: Cassian's (gluttony, fornication, covetousness, anger, dejection, acedia; then vainglory and pride) and Gregory's (pride, vainglory, envy, anger, melancholy, avarice; gluttony and lust). They disagree, and both should be named. The practical point is Cassian's: to weaken a fault, weaken the one before it (Conference 5.10).

4. 'What it breeds' (daughters). Gregory's exact list (Moralia XXXI.88) and Cassian's offspring (Conference 5.16). These are recognisable behaviours such as whispering, detraction, murmuring, inquisitiveness and restlessness. They suit a 'you may have noticed' line.

5. 'Your strength's shadow'. Moralia XXXI.86: arrogance from learning, cruelty from justice, carelessness from tenderness, anger from zeal, sloth from gentleness. This links naturally to the Gregory pairs layer and to Pastoral Rule II.9, already in the README.

6. 'What takes its place' (the antidote virtue). Conference 5.23 gives chastity, patience, joyful godly sorrow, courage and humility. Institutes XII.3 gives temperance, purity and patience. Gaps (covetousness, vainglory) should be left as gaps or filled only from Cassian's remedies, not invented.

7. 'When it strikes' (timing). Midday for acedia; in prayer for anger; after success for vainglory and pride; in company for anger; alone for dejection and acedia.

8. 'Catch it early' (the stages). Gregory's suggestion, delight, consent (III.29); Climacus's six stages (Step 15); Evagrius, Praktikos 6: whether a thought comes is not in our power, whether it stays is. A short, teachable, actionable section.

9. 'Hope' framing. Institutes XII.3: one ruling fault does not cancel your other virtues (except pride). Conference 5.14: each victory strengthens you. Pastoral Rule III.29: be alarmed but never broken. Institutes IX.9-11: the two sorrows. This guards against despair.

10. 'In the Body of Christ'. Institutes V.4 (Antony): virtues are spread member by member among the saints, so each person carries some part of Christ, and one learns each virtue from the person who has it. This fits a virtues or gifts layer and a 'people to learn from' section better than the passions layer. It may connect to the spiritual gifts quiz and to the early Christians quiz.

11. Profile feature. Praktikos 43 and 50 recommend watching one's thoughts over time. That justifies retakes and a 'how your leading passion has moved' view in the account profile. It also fits the owner's cross-quiz profile idea.

12. Relationship to the live quiz. Either make this the deeper 'second step' of the seven deadly sins quiz, or make the personality report link to it. Do not ship a second 'which sin are you weakest to'.
risks: These are passions that attack everyone, not temperaments (Conference 5.13: 'we are all attacked by all of them'). A result that says 'you are a vainglory type' misreads the source. Frame it as the leading fight now, which changes over time (Conference 5.14).

The sources tie several passions to stage and situation, not character. Covetousness strikes the lukewarm (Conference 5.8). Spiritual pride strikes the advanced and carnal pride beginners (Institutes XII.24). Vainglory and pride strike after victories (Conference 5.10). Acedia strikes those alone at midday (X.1). Items built on present circumstances will measure circumstances.

Heavy overlap with the live seven deadly sins quiz (site/src/lib/quizzes/seven-deadly-sins.ts: pride, envy, wrath, sloth, greed, gluttony, lust; 14 items, category strategy, 'weakest to'). Six of Cassian's eight map directly: gluttony, lust, greed, wrath, sloth and pride. Cassian adds dejection and vainglory as separate faults and lacks envy. A 'ruling passion' layer would largely repeat that quiz's headline result unless it is reframed around disguise, chain, timing and antidote. The owner has already seen that quiz; duplicating it risks the 'shallow, same shape' verdict he gave the scrapped list.

The existing quiz's source claims were spot-checked against these texts and hold. (a) Gregory set pride outside the seven as their root and named vainglory first (Moralia XXXI.87). (b) The five ways of gluttony are at Moralia XXX, section 60; the quiz paraphrases them loosely as too soon, too finely, too much, too eagerly, too fussily, and the text reads: anticipates the time, seeks daintier food, wants it prepared more carefully, exceeds the quantity, and wants even baser food with burning desire. (c) The noonday demon is at Praktikos 12, and Cassian, Institutes X.1 says the same. One nuance: Gregory's own seven had melancholy, not sloth.

The sources disagree on anger. Cassian forbids all anger at others, even for good reasons (Institutes VIII.21-22). Gregory allows right zeal but warns that anger rises from zeal (Moralia XXXI.86; Pastoral Rule III.16). Do not flatten this into one voice.

The two chains differ. Cassian: gluttony, fornication, covetousness, anger, dejection, acedia; then vainglory and pride. Gregory: pride, vainglory, envy, anger, melancholy, avarice; and gluttony, lust. Evagrius's list order puts sadness before anger. Pick one per statement and name it.
The monastic setting. Signs involve cells, abbots, fasts, brethren and ordination. Any everyday rendering is an adaptation and must be written as one, not presented as the Father's words.

Lust. Cassian's full book on it (Institutes VI) is missing from NPNF and was not checked. The topic is sensitive on a shareable result card. The live quiz already handles it through attention, not acts.
Evagrius was condemned for his speculative theology. Cite the eight through Cassian, and use Evagrius only as paraphrased supporting detail.

Translations. The Moralia text is a Lectionary Central transcription of the 1844-50 Library of the Fathers. Verify against a scan before printing long quotations. The Ladder English online is of unidentified edition and was not quoted. No public-domain English was found for Evagrius or Mark. Their facts here are paraphrases checked in modern translations.

Despair and scrupulosity. A report naming someone's chief sin can wound. The sources themselves guard against this: Pastoral Rule III.29 says to be alarmed but 'by no means broken down', and Institutes IX.9 warns against destructive despair. Build that in.

The Enneagram comparison. The owner's frame calls these the 'ancestor of the Enneagram's passions'. The modern Enneagram is a 20th-century system, and none of these sources supports a nine-type personality scheme. Say the eight thoughts are older and different; do not imply continuity or endorsement.

Do not use Mark the Ascetic's other stage terms, such as 'prepossession', or exact Climacus paragraph numbers from English editions, without checking them. Only the Greek of Ladder Step 15 paragraph 74 and Mark's text 224 (in modern Greek) were checked.

report.framework: The powers (parts) of the soul in the Fathers: the rational (logistikon), the incensive or spirited (thymikon), the desiring (epithymetikon), and the virtues of each. Also covered: the cardinal virtues guarding each other (Ambrose; Gregory's Moralia), the seven gifts in guarding pairs (Moralia), vices passing as virtues (Pastoral Rule II.9), and what the Fathers say about natural temperament.
report.verdict_reason: The anatomy is solid and well attested. Cassian, Evagrius, Maximus, John of Damascus and the Philokalia text "On the Virtues and the Vices" each give vices, virtues and remedies for each of the three powers. But it is anatomy that every soul has. It is not a typology. I found no Father who sorts people into rational-led, incensive-led or desiring-led types. Gregory of Nyssa goes further: he refuses Plato's chariot as a guide and says anger and desire are not the soul's essence. What the sources CAN honestly carry: (1) a reading of which power is most troubled in you now (Cassian Conference 24.15-16 names vices by the power they wound; Conference 5.13-14 says each person has a "besetting sin" and should fight it first); (2) a reading of each strength and the partner virtue it needs (Moralia I.32.45 and XXII.1.2); (3) one real temperament grid, Gregory's four sorts of anger (Moralia V.45.80): quick or slow to catch fire, quick or slow to let go. So it is usable as a supporting layer. It cannot carry a "you are type X" headline on its own.
report.sorts_people: Mostly no. The three powers are described as parts that every person has (Damascene II.12; Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection; Maximus III.32; Evagrius Praktikos 86 and 89). No text I read types people by which power leads them. The Platonic idea that different people are ruled by different parts (Republic IX) is not taken over. Nyssa sets aside "the Platonic chariot" in so many words. What the Fathers DO say about differences between people: (a) Different vices dominate different people. Cassian, Conference 5.13: "these eight faults trouble all sorts of men, yet they do not attack them all in the same way". 5.14: "every one should discover his besetting sin". 5.27: people start the fight at different places on the list. Combined with Conference 24.15 (vices named by the power they affect), this supports a "most troubled power" reading. Cassian presents it as a present illness, not a fixed nature. In 24.16 Abbot Abraham tells one monk that his rational part is the corrupt one. That is diagnosis of one person, not a type. (b) Gregory, Moralia V.45.80, gives a true four-way sorting of people by how anger behaves in them. It is the only real temperament typology I found on this topic. (c) Several Fathers admit inborn temperament. Pastoral Rule III.3: "some are not made joyful or sad by circumstances, but are so by temperament". Damascene II.7: the air produces "different temperaments, and habits, and dispositions", but habits are in our hands. Ambrose, Duties I.21.93: not being roused at all is "an effect of nature", while calming anger is an act of will. Climacus, Ladder Step 26.28 (Moore, paraphrase): some are by nature inclined to temperance, silence, purity, modesty, meekness or contrition. Those who force themselves against their nature rank higher. The end of Step 8 says the same of meekness. (d) There are moral or stage sortings, not temperament ones. Nyssa, Making of Man VIII.6, gives carnal, natural and spiritual "dispositions" (from 1 Cor 2-3). Maximus III.26 divides all people into godly and ungodly. Nyssa, Making of Man XIII, says the wanton and the continent, the liberal and the avaricious, dream differently. These describe states a person moves through, not types.
report.summary:
The Fathers teach that every soul has three powers. The rational power thinks, judges and should rule. The incensive power is roused and fights. The desiring power longs and reaches out. The scheme comes from Greek philosophy. Christian writers use it as a map for diagnosis, not as doctrine. Evagrius (Praktikos 89, paraphrase) gives each power its virtues. The rational has prudence, understanding and wisdom. The desiring has temperance, love and self-control. The incensive has courage and patience. Justice belongs to the whole soul and makes its parts agree. Maximus (Four Centuries on Love, paraphrase) and Cassian (Conference 24.15, quoted) list the vices of each power and its remedy. Cassian's list: pride and vainglory in the rational, rage and sulkiness in the incensive, gluttony and avarice in the desiring. Maximus's remedies: prayer and reading for the mind, almsgiving and love for the incensive, fasting and self-control for desire. Gregory of Nyssa is cautious. He sets aside Plato's chariot and says anger and desire are not the soul's essence. But he keeps them as good seed. Ruled by reason, anger becomes courage and desire becomes love of true beauty. "If love is taken from us, how shall we be united to God?"

The key finding: this is anatomy every soul has, not a sorting of people into types. The honest ways it can speak to a person are these. First, which power is most troubled in you now: Cassian's "besetting sin", named by the power it wounds. Second, which strength you have and which partner virtue it lacks. Ambrose and Gregory both teach that the virtues cannot stand alone. Gregory pairs the gifts: counsel without fortitude never acts, and fortitude without counsel rushes to ruin. Third, Gregory's real four-way anger temperament from the Moralia: quick or slow to catch fire, quick or slow to let go. The Fathers also admit inborn temperament. They warn that a natural gift is not yet a virtue (Climacus Step 26, paraphrase; Ambrose Duties I.21).

elements.name: The rational power (logistikon: reason, intelligence, the ruling part)
elements.what_it_is: The part that thinks, weighs, judges and contemplates, and is meant to rule the other two. Damascene: it naturally bears rule over what lacks reason. Evagrius (Praktikos 86, paraphrase): it works as it should when it gives itself to the contemplation of created things. Maximus II.83 (paraphrase): human intelligence is meant to be subject to God's and to rule the non-rational in us. Nyssa: reason alone bears the stamp of the Divine character. Its virtues, per Evagrius Praktikos 89 (paraphrase): prudence, understanding, wisdom. Maximus III.3 (paraphrase): its right use gives spiritual knowledge and moral judgment.
everyday_signs: A wandering mind that will not settle (Evagrius, Praktikos 15, paraphrase)
When this part is sick: vainglory, conceit, envy, pride, presumption, strife, heresy (Cassian, Conference 24.15)
Fancying you can already teach others while you still need a teacher (Cassian, Conference 24.16)
Ignorance and stupidity from its misuse (Maximus, Love III.3, paraphrase)
Unbelief, folly, ingratitude, and assenting to sins that start in the other powers ('On the Virtues and the Vices', Philokalia, paraphrase)
Understanding that climbs into high mysteries without wisdom and falls the harder (Moralia I.32.45)
Thinking a thing through but never carrying it out: counsel without fortitude (Moralia I.32.45)
elements.hidden_side: The mind is darkened by what happens in the other two powers. 'On the Virtues and the Vices' (paraphrase): when the incensive power is ruled by dislike of people and desire is dissolute, the intelligence is in darkness. Maximus III.20 (paraphrase): every impassioned thought stirs desire, disturbs the incensive power or darkens the intelligence. Nyssa (Making of Man XVIII.3-4): reason can become the servant of passion and multiply it. Anger grows into malignity, envy, deceit and hypocrisy by 'the evil husbandry of the mind'.
elements.disguise: Cassian, Conference 24.16: the sense of being 'capable and sufficient to instruct others' is vainglory in the rational part. Moralia II.49.78: the mind that prides itself on seeing high things is suddenly dulled in low ones. The sources do not assign Gregory's counterfeit virtues (Pastoral Rule II.9) to this power. Pairing 'tardiness passing as deliberation' with the mind would be our mapping, not his.
elements.counsel: Evagrius, Praktikos 15 (paraphrase): reading, vigils and prayer steady the wandering mind. Maximus IV.44 (paraphrase): give the intelligence spiritual reading, contemplation and prayer. Love I.80: humility frees the intellect from conceit. IV.80: give it wings with prayer. Cassian, Conference 24.16: heal it with discretion and humility. Admit with sorrow how hard it is to save one's soul, and that you still need a teacher.
elements.links: Cassian 24.15: all faults have one source, and each is named after the part it wounds. Maximus I.67 (paraphrase): forgetfulness and ignorance affect one power, but listlessness (acedia) seizes all three at once, which makes it the most serious. Gregory, Moralia I.32.45: understanding needs wisdom, and counsel needs fortitude.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences, Conference 24 (Abbot Abraham)
sources.quote: For if the plague of sin has infested its rational parts, it will produce the sins of vainglory, conceit, envy, pride, presumption, strife, heresy. If it has wounded the irascible feelings, it will give birth to rage, impatience, sulkiness, accidie, pusillanimity and cruelty. If it has affected that part which is subject to desire, it will be the parent of gluttony, fornication, covetousness, avarice, and noxious and earthly desires.
sources.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF2 vol. 11 (1894)

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences, Conference 24
sources.quote: you must recognize that the rational part of your mind and soul is corrupt, that part namely from which the faults of presumption and vainglory for the most part spring.

sources.work: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
sources.quote: The reasoning part, it should be understood, naturally bears rule over that which is void of reason.
sources.translation: S. D. F. Salmond, NPNF2 vol. 9 (1899)

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
sources.paraphrase: Ch. 86: the rational part acts according to nature when it applies itself to contemplating created things. Ch. 89: virtue in the rational part is called prudence, understanding and wisdom. Prudence plans the fight against opposing powers, defends the virtues and manages neutral things as the times require. Understanding orders everything toward the goal. Wisdom contemplates the inner reasons of things. Ch. 15: reading, vigils and prayer steady a wandering mind.
sources.translation: Checked against Luke Dysinger's online English with the Greek (modern, copyrighted). Greek terms confirmed: phronesis, synesis, sophia.

sources.work: Maximus the Confessor, Four Centuries on Love
sources.paraphrase: Misusing the intelligence gives ignorance and stupidity; its right use gives spiritual knowledge and moral judgment (III.3). Assign to it spiritual reading, contemplation and prayer (IV.44). Humility frees the intellect from conceit (I.80). Give it wings with prayer (IV.80). Impassioned thoughts darken it (III.20).
sources.translation: Checked against Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, The Philokalia vol. 2 (1981), copyrighted

sources.work: 'On the Virtues and the Vices', attributed to John of Damascus (Philokalia vol. 2)
sources.locus: the section on the tripartite soul
sources.paraphrase: The sins of the intelligent aspect are unbelief, heresy, folly, blasphemy, ingratitude and assent to sins from the passible aspect. They are cured by unwavering faith, study of Scripture, pure and ceaseless prayer and giving thanks. The intelligence is lit when the incensive power is imbued with love and desire with purity. It is darkened when dislike of others and dissolute desire rule.
sources.translation: Checked against Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, Philokalia vol. 2 (1981), copyrighted. The attribution to Damascene is traditional. I did not verify its authenticity in this session.

elements.name: The incensive power (thymikon: the spirited, irascible part)
elements.what_it_is: The power to be roused, to resist and to fight. Damascene II.12: together with desire, it is the part of the non-rational soul that can listen to reason. II.16: 'the satellite of reason, the vindicator of desire'. II.22: the notion of something bad produces anger. Evagrius, Praktikos 86 (paraphrase): by nature it fights for virtue. Praktikos 24 (paraphrase): it is meant to fight demons, not people. Nyssa: ruled by reason, anger becomes courage. Courage and contempt are its strong phase; cowardice and fear are its weakening. So this power has two failure directions, too much and too little. Its virtues, per Evagrius 89 (paraphrase): courage and patience. Maximus III.3 and IV.15 (paraphrase): rightly used, it becomes love.
everyday_signs: Rage, impatience, sulkiness, accidie, pusillanimity (faint-heartedness), cruelty (Cassian, Conference 24.15)
Heartlessness, hatred, lack of compassion, rancour, envy ('On the Virtues and the Vices', paraphrase)
Three stages (Damascene II.16): rage as it first rises; wrath, where the memory of the wrong abides; rancour, which watches for a moment to take revenge
In the body: the heart beats fast, the body trembles, the tongue stammers, the face burns, friends go unrecognised (Moralia V.45.79, paraphrase)
When it grows strong, dreams of things that cause fear; when it is stirred constantly, a man ends up cowardly (Maximus, Love II.69-70, paraphrase)
Anxiety, 'fear of failure' (Damascene II.15), and cowardice and fear, which Nyssa calls a weakening of this same impulse
Too little of it: Eli, lukewarm toward the wrongs of those in his charge (Moralia V.45.82); Ambrose I.21.96 (paraphrase): never being roused by base things is not virtue but apathy and neglect
elements.hidden_side: It is harder to fight than desire. Maximus I.66 (paraphrase): so the Lord gave the stronger remedy, the commandment of love. Evagrius, Praktikos 38 (paraphrase): indignation needs more remedies than desire. By itself anger would be a short-lived bubble. It is thought that feeds it into malignity, envy, deceit, conspiracy and hypocrisy (Nyssa, Making of Man XVIII.4). Its root may be a thwarted desire: anger is 'the vindicator of desire' (Damascene II.16). Even rightful zeal troubles the mind's eye: 'anger that comes of zeal disturbs it' (Moralia V.45.82).
elements.disguise: Pastoral Rule II.9: 'unbridled wrath is accounted the virtue of spiritual zeal'. The same sentence names the opposite counterfeit: 'inordinate laxity is believed to be loving-kindness'. Moralia V.45.83: excess anger 'takes the evil of a hot temper for a good quality'. Nyssa, Making of Man XVIII.4: 'the high spirit of the horse becomes the origin of pride'.
elements.counsel: Evagrius, Praktikos 15 (paraphrase): psalmody, long-suffering and mercy calm a churning temper. Maximus (paraphrase): almsgiving heals it (I.79); gentleness keeps it calm (I.80); kindness, compassion, love and mercy cure it (II.70); give it spiritual love, the opposite of hatred (IV.44); bridle it with love (IV.80). Gregory, Moralia V.45.81 (paraphrase), gives two ways. Before acting, foresee the insults you may meet, thinking of the Redeemer's. And when others offend, remember your own offences. V.45.83: anger must follow 'in the rear of reason' like a handmaid. Ambrose, Duties I.21.92 (paraphrase): first calm the mind; if you cannot, check the tongue; then seek reconciliation. I.21.97: prepare the mind beforehand by reflection.
elements.links: Damascene II.16: this power defends desire. 'On the Virtues and the Vices' (paraphrase): a desiring soul deprived of what it wants is overcome by wrath and rancour. Pastoral Rule III.3: the sad temperament has wrath close at hand. The owner's Book III layer (III.9 impatient/patient, III.16 meek/passionate) sits on this power.

sources.work: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
sources.quote: Anger further is the satellite of reason, the vindicator of desire.

sources.work: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
sources.quote: Wrath again implies that the bile endures, that is to say, that the memory of the wrong abides

sources.work: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
sources.quote: Rancour, on the other hand, implies watching for a suitable moment for revenge

sources.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
sources.locus: the dialogue with Macrina, on anger and desire
sources.quote: Courage and contempt, for instance, exhibit a certain phase of the irascible impulse; the dispositions arising from cowardice and fear exhibit on the other hand a diminution and weakening of that same impulse.
sources.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF2 vol. 5 (1893)

sources.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Making of Man
sources.quote: if reason instead assumes sway over such emotions, each of them is transmuted to a form of virtue; for anger produces courage, terror caution, fear obedience, hatred aversion from vice, the power of love the desire for what is truly beautiful

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule
sources.quote: Often inordinate laxity is believed to be loving-kindness, and unbridled wrath is accounted the virtue of spiritual zeal.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For anger that comes of evil blinds the eye of the mind, but anger that comes of zeal disturbs it.
sources.translation: Library of the Fathers, Oxford: Parker, 1844-1850

sources.work: Maximus the Confessor, Four Centuries on Love
sources.paraphrase: Passions of the incensive power are harder to combat than those of desire, so the Lord gave the stronger remedy of love (I.66). Almsgiving heals it and gentleness keeps it calm (I.79-80). When it is constantly stimulated it ends cowardly and unmanly; kindness, compassion, love and mercy cure it (II.70). Give it spiritual love (IV.44).
sources.translation: Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, Philokalia vol. 2 (1981), copyrighted

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
sources.paraphrase: Its natural work is to fight for virtue (86). It is meant to fight demons, but demons turn it against people (24). Psalmody, long-suffering and mercy calm it (15). It needs more remedies than desire, which is why love is called great (38). Its virtues are courage and patience: not to fear the enemy and to endure hardship readily (89).
sources.translation: Dysinger online translation with Greek (modern, copyrighted). Greek terms confirmed: andreia, hypomone, psalmodia, makrothymia, eleos.

elements.name: The desiring power (epithymetikon: appetite, the part that longs)
elements.what_it_is: The power to long for and reach toward what seems good. Damascene II.12: a good in anticipation is desire; a good realised is pleasure. II.22: the notion of something good produces desire. Evagrius, Praktikos 86 (paraphrase): by nature it longs for virtue. Nyssa: ruled by reason, 'the instinct of desire will procure for us the delight that is Divine and perfect'. Its virtues, per Evagrius 89 (paraphrase): temperance, love (agape) and self-control. Maximus II.48 (paraphrase): in one whose mind stays with God, desire grows into intense longing for God.
everyday_signs: Gluttony, fornication, covetousness, avarice, earthly desires (Cassian, Conference 24.15)
Gluttony, greed, drunkenness, unchastity, love of material things, and desire for empty glory ('On the Virtues and the Vices', paraphrase)
Desire is drawn to three things: pleasure of the flesh, vain self-glory and material wealth ('On the Virtues and the Vices', paraphrase)
A habit of self-indulgence that is hard to break when desire is often stirred (Maximus, Love II.70, paraphrase)
When desire grows strong, dreams of sensual pleasure (Maximus II.69, paraphrase)
Damascene II.13 (paraphrase) gives a test of good pleasures. They bring no pain or regret, do no harm, keep to moderation, do not draw us from serious work, and do not enslave us.
elements.hidden_side: A thwarted desire turns into anger. Damascene II.16 calls anger desire's 'vindicator'. 'On the Virtues and the Vices' (paraphrase) says the man deprived of what he wants is overcome by wrath and rancour. The same text says the love of possessions is more culpable than bodily lust because its drive is less natural. It uses the image of a charioteer who cannot even control a gentle horse. Nyssa (paraphrase): misdirected, 'the power of loving' leaves its true objects for immoderate pleasures of sense.
elements.disguise: Pastoral Rule II.9: 'niggardliness palliates itself under the name of frugality', and 'prodigality hides itself under the appellation of liberality'. Gregory does not tie these to a power. 'On the Virtues and the Vices' puts avarice under desire, so the link is fair, but the pairing is ours.
elements.counsel: Evagrius, Praktikos 15 (paraphrase): hunger, toil and withdrawal quench burning desire. These are monastic remedies. Maximus (paraphrase): fasting withers desire (I.79); long practice of fasting, vigils and prayer cures self-indulgence (II.70); give it moderation and self-control (IV.44); quench it with self-control (IV.80). 'On the Virtues and the Vices' (paraphrase): fasting, self-control, hardship, giving possessions to the poor, and longing for the kingdom and for divine sonship. Damascene II.13 (paraphrase): follow natural and necessary pleasures, take the natural but unnecessary ones in season and measure, and renounce the rest.
elements.links: Damascene II.16: desire and anger are linked, because anger defends desire. Pastoral Rule III.3: the joyful temperament has lust close at hand. Nyssa: the same power, rightly aimed, is how we are united to God ('If love is taken from us, how shall we be united to God?').

sources.work: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
sources.quote: For the notion of something good results in desire, and the notion of something bad results in anger.

sources.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
sources.locus: the dialogue with Macrina, on the passions
sources.quote: and anger fortitude, and cowardice caution; and the instinct of desire will procure for us the delight that is Divine and perfect.

sources.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
sources.locus: the parable of the wheat and tares
sources.quote: If love is taken from us, how shall we be united to God? If anger is to be extinguished, what arms shall we possess against the adversary?

sources.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
sources.locus: the parable of the wheat and tares
sources.quote: whenever their impulse is towards what is noble, then they become matter for praise, as his desire did to Daniel, and his anger to Phineas, and their grief to those who nobly mourn.

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
sources.paraphrase: Desire acts according to nature when it longs for virtue (86). Its virtues are temperance, love and self-control. Temperance looks without passion on things that stir irrational fantasies. Love treats every image of God almost as it would the Prototype. Self-control gladly declines the pleasures of the palate (89). Hunger, toil and withdrawal quench it (15).
sources.translation: Dysinger online translation with Greek (modern, copyrighted). Greek confirmed: sophrosyne, agape, enkrateia.

sources.work: Maximus the Confessor, Four Centuries on Love
sources.paraphrase: Fasting withers desire (I.79). Frequent excitement of desire makes a habit of self-indulgence, cured by fasting, vigils and prayer (II.70). Misused desire gives licentiousness; well used, self-restraint (III.3). A soul is rightly ordered when desire is subject to self-control (IV.15). In one whose mind stays with God, desire becomes longing for God (II.48).
sources.translation: Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, Philokalia vol. 2 (1981), copyrighted

elements.name: Justice: the harmony of the whole soul
elements.what_it_is: Not a fourth power but the right order among the three. Evagrius, Praktikos 89 (paraphrase): justice belongs to the whole soul. It brings about a symphony and harmony among the soul's parts. Maximus, Love IV.44 (paraphrase): to be just, give each aspect of yourself what fits it: prayer and reading to the intelligence, love to the incensive, self-control to desire, and only food and clothing to the body. Ambrose, Duties I.24.115, defines justice as the virtue that 'assigns each man his own'.
everyday_signs: A rightly ordered soul: desire under self-control, the incensive power refusing hatred and holding to love, the intelligence moving toward God by prayer (Maximus, Love IV.15, paraphrase)
Its failure: 'some in appearance just, but trusting in themselves rather than in the Lord' (Moralia XXII.1.2)
elements.hidden_side: Self-love. Moralia II.49.76: 'self-love invades the mind, makes it swerve by a secret declension from the straight line of justice'.
elements.disguise: Moralia XXII.1.2: righteousness that trusts in itself 'overturns to himself the order of the highest justice' (paraphrase of the sentence around quote M1).
elements.counsel: Maximus IV.44 (paraphrase): give each part its due. Ambrose I.27.127 (paraphrase): justice is first owed to God, then to country, then to parents, then to all.
elements.links: Ambrose I.27: prudence and justice cannot exist without each other. Moralia XXII.1.2: justice is not genuine without prudence, fortitude and temperance.

sources.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
sources.paraphrase: Justice is the virtue of the whole soul. Its work is to make a symphony and harmony among the soul's parts.

sources.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
sources.quote: In the first place they showed prudence, which is exercised in the search of the truth, and which imparts a desire for full knowledge; next, justice, which assigns each man his own, does not claim another's, and disregards its own advantage, so as to guard the rights of all; thirdly, fortitude, which both in warfare and at home is conspicuous in greatness of mind and distinguishes itself in the strength of the body; fourthly, temperance, which preserves the right method and order in all things that we think should either be done or said.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: And sometimes self-love invades the mind, makes it swerve by a secret declension from the straight line of justice

sources.work: Maximus the Confessor, Four Centuries on Love
sources.paraphrase: To be just, assign to each aspect of yourself what accords with it (IV.44). The soul is rightly ordered when each power is turned to its proper end (IV.15).

elements.name: Gregory's four sorts of anger (a real temperament grid)
elements.what_it_is: The one genuine typology of people on this topic. Gregory the Great, Moralia V.45.80, sorts people by two things: how fast anger catches in them, and how long it holds. (1) Quick to catch, quick to leave: 'like kindled reeds'. (2) Slow to catch, long to hold: like 'the heavier and harder kinds of wood'. (3) Quick to catch and slow to let go: 'their conduct is the worst'. (4) Slow to catch, quick to let go: nearest to 'the excellence of peace of mind'. He ranks them himself: the fourth is best, the third worst, and the second is less bad than the third.
everyday_signs: Reeds: they 'clamour with their voices' and 'give out something like a crackle at their kindling', flare up, then cool to ashes
Hard wood: slow to heat, 'with difficulty put out', keeps 'the longer the fire of their rage'
The bodily signs of anger in V.45.79 (paraphrase): quick heartbeat, trembling, stammering, burning face, fierce eyes
elements.hidden_side: Gregory separates anger stirred by 'hastiness of temper' from anger that comes from zeal (V.45.82). The first is born of evil, the second of good. Phinehas had the good kind. Eli lacked it and brought judgement on himself. Even zeal-anger clouds contemplation for a time.
elements.disguise: V.45.83: excess anger 'takes the evil of a hot temper for a good quality'. Pastoral Rule II.9 makes the same point: wrath passing as zeal.
elements.counsel: V.45.81 (paraphrase) gives two ways to break anger. Before acting, foresee every insult you may meet, thinking of the Redeemer's, so it cannot catch you asleep. When others offend, recall your own offences, 'as if fire were extinguished by water'. V.45.83: let anger serve as a handmaid behind reason, never lead as mistress.
elements.links: Ambrose, Duties I.21.93, is a parallel, not a source Gregory cites. Boys quarrel quickly and are quickly calmed, and Ambrose holds them up as the model ('never to keep an injury in mind'). He also says not being roused at all is 'an effect of nature', while calming anger is an act of will. Damascene II.16's 'wrath that abides' (mēnis) and rancour describe the 'long to hold' side. That is a thematic parallel only. The owner's Book III layer (III.9 impatient/patient, III.16 meek/passionate) touches the same power. CAUTION: Gregory does not tie these four to the four humours. Do not map them to choleric, sanguine and the rest.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: But we are to know that there be some, whom anger is somewhat prompt in inflaming, but quickly leaves them; while there are others whom it is slow in exciting, but the longer in retaining possession of.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Others again, and their conduct is the worst, are both quick in catching the flames of anger, and slow in letting them go; and others both catch them slowly, and part with them quickly.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: In which same four sorts, the reader sees clearly that the last rather than the first approaches to the excellence of peace of mind, and in evil the third is worse than the second.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For some, like kindled reeds, while they clamour with their voices, give out something like a crackle at their kindling

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: the anger, which hastiness of temper stirs is one thing, and that which zeal gives its character to is another.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: that same anger, which we adopt as an instrument of virtue, never gain dominion over the mind, nor take the lead as mistress, but like a handmaid, prompt to render service, never depart from following in the rear of reason.

sources.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
sources.quote: It is no light thing to calm one's anger. It is no less difficult a thing than it is not to be roused at all. The one is an act of our own will, the other is an effect of nature.

elements.name: The four virtues guard one another (prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice)
elements.what_it_is: The four 'cardinal' virtues cannot stand alone. Each is imperfect or false without the others. Ambrose, Duties I.27: prudence is the first source, and the others spring from it and cannot be torn apart. I.35.176: fortitude never stands alone, and without justice it becomes wickedness. Gregory, Moralia XXII.1.2: 'one virtue without another is either none at all or but imperfect'. He says real strength in one virtue means not being ruled by a vice somewhere else. Both men admit the fourfold list comes from outside Scripture. Gregory introduces it with 'as it has seemed best to some persons'. Ambrose says the worldly wise borrowed it and modelled his book on Cicero's De officiis, whom he names in Book I.
everyday_signs: Gregory's own portraits of lopsided virtue (Moralia XXII.1.2): 'some modest indeed but not humble, some seemingly humble but not pitiful, some seeming pitiful but not at all just, some in appearance just, but trusting in themselves rather than in the Lord'

What shakes each virtue (Moralia II.49.76, paraphrase): idleness makes prudence stop forecasting; delight in this life makes temperance decay; fear of losing what we love confounds fortitude; self-love bends justice
elements.hidden_side: A strength that others admire can be hollow if its partner is missing. Gregory's test: are you ruled by bad habits 'in another quarter'?
elements.disguise: Moralia XXII.1.2: humility without pity 'has no right to be called humility'. Mercy without justice is not true mercy. Chastity without humility is corrupted within by pride.
elements.counsel: Look for the partner virtue your strength lacks. Moralia II.49.76-77 (paraphrase): the Spirit forms the four virtues first, then tempers the mind with the seven gifts.
elements.links: Maximus, Love II.79 (paraphrase): stupidity, cowardice, licentiousness and injustice are the image of the earthy man; the four virtues are the image of the heavenly man. Evagrius 89 places the virtues in the three powers, with justice over the whole.

sources.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
sources.quote: The first source of duty is prudence, from whence spring three other virtues; and they cannot be separated or torn asunder, since they are mutually connected one with the other.
sources.translation: de Romestin, NPNF2 vol. 10. Note: the italic chapter summaries in NPNF may be the editor's, not Ambrose's. Para. 129 carries the same point in Ambrose's text.

sources.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
sources.quote: It is clear, then, that these and the remaining virtues are related to one another.

sources.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
sources.quote: fortitude without justice is the source of wickedness.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For very often it has happened to us to see some modest indeed but not humble, some seemingly humble but not pitiful, some seeming pitiful but not at all just, some in appearance just, but trusting in themselves rather than in the Lord.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For neither is it real prudence which has not justice, temperance, fortitude, nor perfect temperance which has not fortitude, justice, and prudence, nor complete fortitude which is not prudent, temperate, and just, nor genuine justice which has not prudence, fortitude, and temperance.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: he, who is supposed to be strong in any particular virtue is then really strong when he is not subject to evil habits in another quarter.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Sometimes fear works its way into the heart and confounds the powers of our fortitude

elements.name: The seven gifts in guarding pairs (Gregory)
elements.what_it_is: Gregory reads Job's seven sons as the seven gifts of the Spirit (Isaiah 11:2-3 in his Latin): wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear. Each gift answers an opposite (Moralia II.49.77): wisdom against folly, understanding against dulness, counsel against rashness, fortitude (courage) against fear, knowledge against ignorance, piety against hardness of heart, fear against pride. They must 'feed one another' (Moralia I.32.45). They come in pairs: wisdom with understanding, counsel with fortitude, knowledge with piety. Fear needs them all.
everyday_signs: Understanding without wisdom climbs into high things and falls harder (I.32.45)
Counsel without fortitude thinks a thing over and never gets it done (I.32.45)
Fortitude without counsel rushes headlong into ruin (I.32.45)
Knowledge without piety knows the good and neglects to do it; piety without knowledge 'knows not the way to shew mercy' (I.32.45)
Fear without the others is agitated about everything and does nothing good (I.32.45)
elements.hidden_side: Moralia II.49.78 (paraphrase): God sometimes withdraws a gift for a moment, for example a sudden rashness in one proud of always deliberating, so that we learn where our good qualities come from.
elements.counsel: Find your strong gift and ask what its partner is. Gregory: 'virtue is refreshed by virtue'.
elements.links: This mirrors the four virtues guarding each other (Moralia XXII.1.2). The pair structure fits the owner's two-sided Gregory design.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For each particular virtue is to the last degree destitute, unless one virtue lends its support to another.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Counsel is worthless, when the strength of fortitude is lacking thereto, since what it finds out by turning the thing over, from want of strength it never carries on so far as to the perfecting in deed; and fortitude is very much broken down, if it be not supported by counsel

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: so as against folly to bestow Wisdom, against dulness, Understanding, against rashness, Counsel, against fear, Courage, against ignorance, Knowledge, against hardness of heart, Piety, against pride, Fear.

elements.name: Vices that pass for virtues (Pastoral Rule II.9)
elements.what_it_is: Gregory warns that vices commonly disguise themselves as virtues. He gives six: niggardliness as frugality, prodigality as liberality, laxity as loving-kindness, wrath as zeal, haste as promptness, tardiness as serious deliberation. They come as three pairs of opposite errors, each wearing the mask of a virtue.
everyday_signs: Stinginess you call being careful with money
Waste you call generosity
Letting things slide that you call kindness
Anger you call standing up for what is right
Rushing you call being prompt; putting off you call thinking it through
elements.hidden_side: The person enjoys the virtue's name. Gregory: 'while he exults in seeming frugal', or 'glory in being as it were compassionately liberal' (paraphrase of the rest of II.9).
elements.disguise: The whole element is about disguise.
elements.counsel: Tell virtue and vice apart with vigilant care (II.9). A related note on nature and gift, in Climacus Step 26.28 and the end of Step 8 (paraphrase): a good trait you were born with is a gift, not yet a virtue won.
elements.links: Directly supports the 'disguise' field for the incensive power (wrath/zeal, laxity/kindness) and for desire (niggardliness/frugality, prodigality/liberality). Gregory does not assign them to powers himself.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule
sources.quote: The ruler also ought to understand how commonly vices pass themselves off as virtues.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule
sources.quote: Often inordinate laxity is believed to be loving-kindness, and unbridled wrath is accounted the virtue of spiritual zeal.

elements.name: Nature and struggle: what the Fathers say about inborn temperament
elements.what_it_is: Several Fathers admit that people differ by nature. They add at once that nature is not merit, and that habits can be changed. Pastoral Rule III.3: some are joyful or sad 'by temperament', not by circumstance, and 'certain defects are connected with certain temperaments'. Damascene II.7: the air produces different temperaments, but habits are in our hands, 'for it is reason that rules, and directs, and changes them'. Ambrose I.21.90 and 93: passion is 'implanted in our nature and character' and must be checked by reason; staying unroused is nature, calming yourself is will. Climacus, Ladder Step 26.28 (Moore, paraphrase): some are by nature inclined to temperance, silence, purity, modesty, meekness or contrition, and he does not pry into why. Those who force themselves against their nature, though they sometimes fail, stand higher. The end of Step 8 (paraphrase): whoever is meek by nature may win no other crown, but whoever wins meekness by sweat has conquered all eight passions. Damascene II.12 mentions the four humours, but only as what bodies are made of. He does not build a personality theory on them.
everyday_signs: Moods that are yours whatever the day brings (Pastoral Rule III.3)
A good trait that costs you nothing (Climacus 26.28, paraphrase)
elements.hidden_side: A natural gift can hide the fact that no virtue has yet been won (Climacus, paraphrase). The struggler may be further along than the naturally calm.
elements.counsel: Damascene II.7: habits are in our hands. Ambrose I.21.90: make tranquillity your disposition by constant practice.
elements.links: Grounds a report line such as 'this is your temperament, not your score'. It also fits the site rule to count knowledge, never devotion.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule
sources.quote: But some are not made joyful or sad by circumstances, but are so by temperament.

sources.work: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
sources.quote: the quality of the air which is produced by sun, and moon, and stars, produces in various ways different temperaments, and habits, and dispositions. But the habits are among the things that we have in our own hands, for it is reason that rules, and directs, and changes them.

sources.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
sources.quote: But since passion is to a large extent implanted in our nature and character, so that it cannot be uprooted and avoided, it must be checked by reason

sources.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
sources.paraphrase: Some people are by nature prone to temperance, silence, purity, modesty, meekness or contrition. Others force themselves against their own nature, and although they are sometimes defeated, they rank higher. Of meekness: whoever has it by nature may win no other crown, but whoever wins it by sweat has conquered all eight passions.
sources.translation: Checked against Archimandrite Lazarus Moore's translation (1959), copyrighted

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences, Conference 24 (Abbot Abraham)
key_passages.quote: Of all faults there is one source and origin, but different names are assigned to the passions and corruptions in accordance with the character of that part, or member, if I may so call it, which has been injuriously affected in the soul
key_passages.paraphrase: All faults have one root, but they are named by the power they wound: the rational, the irascible or the desiring. The same chapter lists the vices of each.

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences, Conference 5 (Abbot Serapion)
key_passages.quote: every one should discover his besetting sin, and direct his main attack against it
key_passages.paraphrase: Ch. 13: all eight faults trouble everyone, but not in the same way; in one man fornication rules, in another wrath, in another vainglory or pride. Ch. 14: find your besetting sin and fight it first. Ch. 27: people start the fight at different places on the list.

key_passages.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos
key_passages.paraphrase: 86: the soul acts according to nature when desire longs for virtue, the incensive part fights for it, and the rational part contemplates created things. 89 (crediting 'our wise teacher'): the rational part's virtues are prudence, understanding and wisdom; the desiring part's are temperance, love and self-control; the incensive part's are courage and patience; justice belongs to the whole soul and brings harmony among the parts.
key_passages.translation: Dysinger online English with Greek (modern, copyrighted). The 'wise teacher' is usually identified by editors as Gregory of Nazianzus. I did not verify that in this session.

key_passages.work: Maximus the Confessor, Four Centuries on Love
key_passages.paraphrase: A soul is rightly ordered when desire is subject to self-control, the incensive power rejects hatred and holds to love, and the intelligence moves toward God by prayer and contemplation (IV.15). Justice means giving each part its due: reading, contemplation and prayer to the intelligence; spiritual love to the incensive; moderation and self-control to desire; food and clothing to the body (IV.44). The commandments match the powers: almsgiving heals the incensive, fasting withers desire, prayer purifies the intellect (I.79).
key_passages.translation: Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, Philokalia vol. 2 (1981), copyrighted

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: Others again, and their conduct is the worst, are both quick in catching the flames of anger, and slow in letting them go; and others both catch them slowly, and part with them quickly.
key_passages.paraphrase: The four sorts of anger: quick to catch and quick to leave (reeds); slow to catch and long to hold (hard wood); quick and long (worst); slow and quick (best).

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: And so one virtue without another is either none at all or but imperfect.
key_passages.paraphrase: The four virtues are perfect only when joined together.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: For each particular virtue is to the last degree destitute, unless one virtue lends its support to another.
key_passages.paraphrase: The seven gifts guard each other in pairs: wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, with fear needing all of them.

key_passages.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
key_passages.locus: the dialogue with Macrina, on anger and desire
key_passages.quote: We must therefore neglect the Platonic chariot and the pair of horses of dissimilar forces yoked to it, and their driver, whereby the philosopher allegorizes these facts about the soul
key_passages.paraphrase: Nyssa refuses Plato's chariot as a guide. Anger and desire are common to people and animals, so they are not the soul's essence; Moses rose above both. Yet they are good seed. Ruled by reason they become virtue, as with Daniel's desire and Phinehas's anger.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule
key_passages.quote: But some are not made joyful or sad by circumstances, but are so by temperament.
key_passages.paraphrase: Temperament is real and separate from circumstance, and 'certain defects are connected with certain temperaments'.

key_passages.work: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
key_passages.quote: That which listens to and obeys reason, on the other hand is divided into anger and desire.
key_passages.paraphrase: The standard Orthodox summary of the soul's anatomy: reason rules, and anger and desire are the parts that can obey it.

key_passages.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
key_passages.paraphrase: Some are by nature inclined to certain virtues. Those who struggle against their own nature rank higher.

report.measurement_notes:
These are what the sources say shows up in ordinary life. They are not quiz items.
- Incensive power: this is the most measurable, because Gregory himself gives two dimensions. How fast does anger catch? How long does it stay (Moralia V.45.80)? Damascene II.16 adds three stages that can be observed separately: the first flare (rage), the lingering memory of the wrong (wrath), and waiting for a chance to get even (rancour). Nyssa gives the under-side: cowardice and fear are the same power weakened. So 'too little' is a real pole. Eli (Moralia V.45.82) and Ambrose I.21.96 treat never being roused as a fault too. Other observable points: whether anger lands on people or on wrongs (Evagrius Praktikos 24); what you do after it flares (Ambrose I.21.92: calm the mind, check the tongue, seek reconciliation); and Pastoral Rule II.9's test of whether you call your anger 'zeal'.
- Desiring power: what you reach for. 'On the Virtues and the Vices' names three objects: bodily pleasure, being thought well of, and possessions. Also whether a blocked want turns into irritation (Damascene II.16). Also Damascene II.13's test of a pleasure: does it bring regret, harm, excess, pull you from serious work, or enslave you? Habit strength (Maximus II.70).
- Rational power: a wandering mind (Evagrius 15); wanting to teach before you have learned (Cassian 24.16); ingratitude ('On the Virtues and the Vices').
- The guarding pairs give the clearest behavioural contrasts in the whole topic (Moralia I.32.45): thinking it over but never doing it, against doing it without thinking; knowing the good but not doing it, against meaning well but not knowing how to help. Moralia XXII.1.2 adds modest but not humble, humble but not merciful, merciful but not just, just but self-trusting. Moralia II.49.76 names what shakes each virtue: idleness, delight, fear of losing what you love, self-love.
- Most troubled power: Cassian's besetting sin (Conference 5.13-14), read through Conference 24.15's vice-to-power list. This is a current-state reading. Cassian treats it as an illness, not a fixed type.
- Temperament and struggle: Pastoral Rule III.3 separates mood by temperament from mood by circumstance. Climacus 26.28 separates a trait that comes easily from one that is fought for. Both could be asked about honestly, as 'is this effortless for you, or a fight?'.
- Answer scale: nothing in these sources bears on 5 versus 7 answer points.
report.orthodox_standing:
- John of Damascus: saint (feast 4 December). The Exact Exposition is received as a standard summary of Orthodox doctrine. Its chapters on man (II.12-22) are widely said to draw on Nemesius of Emesa's On the Nature of Man. I did not check that in this session.
- Gregory of Nyssa: saint, one of the Cappadocians. On the Soul and the Resurrection is fully received. Note his caution about the Platonic scheme.
- Maximus the Confessor: saint and Confessor. The Four Centuries on Love are in the Philokalia (vol. 2). This is the safest foundation for the three powers.
- John Cassian: venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church. Two of his works are in the Philokalia (vol. 1): On the Eight Vices, and On the Holy Fathers of Sketis and on Discrimination. Conference 24 itself is not in the Philokalia, but it is his.
- Evagrius Ponticus: NOT a saint. His speculative Origenist teaching was condemned in the sixth century, in anathemas associated with the Fifth Ecumenical Council of 553. His ascetic teaching passed into the tradition through Cassian, Climacus and Maximus. Some of his texts are in the Philokalia, one of them under the name of Nilus. Use him as the earliest detailed list, never as the foundation. Maximus and Cassian carry the same scheme.
- John Climacus: saint. The Ladder is read in Lent, and the fourth Sunday of Lent is his.
- 'On the Virtues and the Vices': printed in the Philokalia (vol. 2) under John of Damascus's name. The attribution is traditional, and I did not verify it.
- Gregory the Great (St Gregory the Dialogist): saint of the undivided Church, honoured in the East. The Moralia and the Pastoral Rule are Latin.
- Ambrose of Milan: saint (7 December), Latin, before the schism. Duties is modelled on Cicero, which Ambrose says himself.
- None of these is a post-schism Western-only author. Aquinas's treatment of the passions (irascible and concupiscible) was not used.
report.report_layer_ideas:
Ideas for sections and fields only, with no copy:
1. 'Your three powers': a balance readout showing which power is most troubled now. Cassian: vices named by the power they wound, and fight your besetting sin first. Give the Fathers' remedy for that power (Evagrius 15, Maximus I.79 / II.70 / IV.44). Present it as a state, not an identity. It fits the existing 'Start here' (Pastoral Rule III.38) well. Fields: power_most_troubled (rational / incensive / desiring), its vices named from the source, its remedy.
2. 'How your anger works': Gregory's own 2x2 grid (Moralia V.45.80), with fields anger_catch (quick/slow) and anger_hold (short/long). His own ranking can be shown honestly. Add the zeal-versus-temper line (V.45.82) and his two ways to cool (V.45.81). Nyssa's 'too little' pole (cowardice and fear) and Eli could be a separate note. This is the most 'type-like' honest layer on this topic.
3. 'Your strength and its partner': Gregory's pairs (Moralia I.32.45) and his lopsided virtues (XXII.1.2). Fields: strongest_gift, missing_partner. The hidden side is what the strength turns into without its partner. This matches the owner's two-sided Book III design.
4. 'What your strength may be passing for': the six counterfeit virtues of Pastoral Rule II.9, tied to the reader's own answers.
5. 'Gift or victory?': Climacus 26.28 and Ambrose I.21.93. A calm or temperate trait may be a gift of nature, not a virtue won, and struggle ranks higher. This is encouraging for people who score as strugglers, and it keeps the report from scoring holiness.
6. 'Who you are in Christ' angle: Nyssa's point that each power is good seed meant for God. Daniel's desire and Phinehas's anger (Nyssa's own examples). Maximus II.48: desire becomes longing for God and anger becomes divine love.
7. Possible cross-links to the site's deadly-sins quiz: Cassian's vice-to-power table ties the eight vices to the three powers.
risks: Overclaiming a typology. The Fathers do not sort people into rational, incensive or desiring types. A headline like 'You are a Thymic soul' would be invented. Use it as a current-state reading or as a balance of three.

Plato. The three-part scheme is Platonic. Nyssa explicitly sets aside Plato's chariot and says anger and desire are not the soul's essence. Present the scheme as the ascetic Fathers' map for diagnosis (Cassian, Maximus), not as dogma.

Evagrius's standing. He is not a saint, and his Origenist teaching was condemned. Quoting him as a foundation invites criticism from Orthodox readers. Carry the virtue list through Maximus and Cassian, and mention Evagrius only as the earliest detailed list.

Copyright. No public-domain English was found for the Praktikos, the Four Centuries on Love, the Ladder or 'On the Virtues and the Vices'. Paraphrase them only. The saved copies are for checking and must not be published.

Monastic context. Hunger, vigils, solitude, withdrawal and 'hermits versus communities' (Praktikos 5) are monastic remedies. Moving them to lay life honestly needs care. Anything practice-shaped should point readers to their priest.

Heavy vice lists. The lists include fornication, murder, heresy and blasphemy. This fits the owner's rule of putting the weakness part behind a tap. Choose vices from the lists, not invented softer ones.

The four humours. Gregory's four sorts of anger look tempting to map onto choleric, sanguine, melancholic and phlegmatic. Gregory makes no such link. Damascene mentions the humours only as what bodies are made of. Do not connect them.
Counting devotion. A 'health of your three powers' score could read as a holiness score. Climacus says a natural gift is not a virtue won. Keep it as knowledge of oneself, never merit.

Locus formats. The Moralia is cited by book, Roman-numeral chapter and paragraph, as the Oxford translation marks them. Damascene's chapter numbers follow NPNF; Greek editions number them differently. The NPNF chapter summaries for Ambrose may be the editor's words, not Ambrose's.

Attribution. 'On the Virtues and the Vices' is traditionally John of Damascus's, but I did not verify its authenticity. Evagrius's 'wise teacher' is usually taken to be Gregory of Nazianzus; that is also unverified here.
Pastoral Rule II.9 does not say which power each counterfeit virtue belongs to. Any such mapping is ours and must be labelled as ours.

report.framework: Why people do good: fear of punishment (the slave), hope of reward (the hireling), love (the son). With two companions the same Fathers name: the fear that belongs to love, and doing good to be seen.
report.verdict_reason: The sourcing is excellent. Basil, Cassian, Clement, Gregory (Pastoral Rule III.13 and Dialogues III.34), Chrysostom, Isaac, Dorotheos, Climacus and Gregory of Nyssa all teach the same three motives. That makes it one of the most widely shared patristic teachings there is, and 65 public-domain quotes pass the machine check. It also answers the owner's 'who you are in Christ' goal directly: slave or son is Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:7. And it gives a Christian answer to the Enneagram's 'core fear': what do you fear, punishment, missing out, or grieving the One you love? But it is a ladder, not a temperament. Every Father ranks love above fear and hope, and most describe one person climbing from one to the next. So it cannot be a two-sided pair like Gregory's Book III, where neither side is the good one. It can carry one report section, framed as 'what moves you now and your next step', never as a type or a grade. Handled carelessly, it becomes a holiness score, which breaks the 'count knowledge, never devotion' rule. Self-report will flatter, because everyone will say 'love'. The Fathers' own tests are indirect, and any items would have to use them.
report.sorts_people:
Mostly no. The Fathers treat these as stages on one road and as the motive that is strongest in you now. They do not treat them as a fixed temperament. The evidence, source by source:
- Cassian (Conf. 11.7, 11.12) says 'stage', 'step' and 'mount' throughout. He also says Scripture calls each mind 'in accordance with the condition and measure' of it, because 'all have not the same virtue, or purpose, or fervour'. So people really are found at different grades, but the grades are places on a climb. In 11.7 the prodigal son is carried 'through the two stages without delay'. In 11.7 goodness built on fear or hope also lapses when the soul relaxes.
- Basil (Longer Rules, Preface) is the closest to a typology. He speaks of 'three different dispositions' ('slavish', 'like hirelings', 'the disposition of sons'), and he honours all three: each keeps every commandment. But he says 'we' of all Christians, and he never sorts named people into them.
- Clement (Str. VII.11) calls those moved by fear, reward or glory 'children in faith; blessed indeed, but not yet become men'. That is a stage of growth, and 'crowns for men and for children' honours both.
- Gregory, Pastoral Rule III.13, does treat 'those who fear scourges, and on that account live innocently' as a class of hearer, to be spoken to in its own way. But the counsel is to leave the class: 'grow up by the nursing of charity to the grace of love'. In Dialogues III.34 fear comes 'first' and love 'afterward', in one soul.
- Dorotheos (Instr. 4.47-49, paraphrase) is explicitly developmental. You cannot reach the perfect fear except through the beginner's fear. He traces one person from slave to hireling to son.
- Isaac (Treatise LXII) says a man can tell 'to which degree he belongs' from his thoughts. Those are degrees, not types. But in Treatise L he does describe two kinds of people now: 'Some people are made humble by their fear, others by their joy in Him', and he gives each a visible manner.
- Climacus (Step 1.5, 1.13, paraphrase) treats the motive a person starts with as shaping the course that follows: incense, millstone or fire. It is still about beginnings.
Plain verdict: this can describe a person's present mixture and direction honestly. It cannot honestly be called their type.
report.summary:
The Fathers agree that people keep from wrong and do good for one of three reasons. The first is fear of punishment. The second is hope of reward. The third is love of the good and of God. Basil names them as the slave, the hireling and the son. Cassian, Dorotheos, Gregory of Nyssa and Climacus teach the same three. Clement, Gregory the Great, Chrysostom and Isaac add their own angles.

All of them rank love highest. Most describe one road: fear turns you from evil, you begin doing good and hoping for a reward, and in time you taste the good itself and cannot be parted from it. None of them despises the lower motives. Cassian calls fear and hope 'useful'. Basil says 'he is pronounced blessed who fears always with reverence'. Clement calls the fearful and the hopeful 'blessed indeed'. Dorotheos says no one reaches the perfect fear except through the first one.

The texts give concrete everyday signs, and this is their strength for the site:
- What you do when no one can see (Cassian 11.8; Clement IV.22).
- Whether you only avoid harm or also do good ('does not wrong, but does not show mercy', Dorotheos 4.50).
- Whether you quit a good work once it stops paying (Dorotheos 14.153).
- Whether others' sins make you a judge or move you to pity (Cassian 11.9-10).
- Whether doing right feels like a war or like rest (Cassian 11.8; Dorotheos 4.51; Climacus 1.16).
- Above all, what you fear: punishment, missing the reward, or grieving and losing the One you love (Cassian 11.13; Augustine; Isaac LXII; Chrysostom on Paul).

The fear that belongs to love is its own element. Augustine gives a clear everyday picture: two wives both say 'I fear my husband', one 'lest he should come', the other 'lest he depart'.

The limit is that this is a stage, not a temperament. It fits one honest report section on 'what moves you now, what it hides, and your next step'. It cannot be a type, a two-sided pair, or a score.

elements.name: Fear of punishment (the slave)
elements.what_it_is: Keeping from wrong, or doing right, because of what happens if you do not: hell, God's judgment, or present penalties such as the law or being found out. Basil calls it the 'slavish disposition'. Cassian calls it the first stage, 'servile' fear, and names both 'the fear of hell or of laws even now imposed'. Gregory's hearers 'fear scourges, and on that account live innocently'.
elements.disguise: It looks like innocence and strictness. Gregory's fearful 'live innocently'. Clement's dog 'may be said to be continent' because it dreads the stick. Basil says those who fear cannot 'neglect any of God's orders, or ... perform them carelessly', so it can look like the most careful obedience of all.
elements.hidden_side: The wish is still there. Gregory: the one who does good because he fears torments 'wishes that what he fears were not, that so he might commit what is unlawful boldly', and so 'innocence is thus lost before God'. Cassian: when fear is removed he 'will ... once more return to what he loves', and he is never at peace but always at war and wounded. Clement: take away the promise and the threat, and 'the disposition of such people will be revealed'. Gregory also finds the fearful prizing temporal goods and dreading present troubles. Isaac warns against the picture of God as 'the revenger', which 'denounces Him as destitute of bounty'.
everyday_signs: Behaves differently when no one is watching, or when there is no chance of being caught (Cassian 11.8; Clement IV.22, on Epicurus's wise man who does no wrong only because he cannot be sure of escaping detection)

Keeps from wrong but starts little good: does no one wrong but shows no mercy, does not hate but does not love (Dorotheos Instr. 4.50, paraphrase; Clement VII.12: 'fear works abstinence from what is evil')
Doing right feels like a constant fight, done with effort and grief (Cassian 11.8; Dorotheos 4.51 and Climacus 1.16, paraphrase)
Early zeal that fades, 'fragrance' that ends in 'smoke' (Climacus 1.13, paraphrase)
Only punishment really registers; losing closeness to Christ hardly does (Chrysostom, Matthew Hom. 23: 'many tremble only at hell')
Fears death most while careless, then the Judgment once drawing near to God (Isaac LXII)
A humility of restraint: 'limbs subdued and ordered senses and ... perpetual contrition of heart' (Isaac L)
Anxious to keep present goods and to escape present troubles (Gregory PR III.13)
Obeys every command out of dread of the penalty, and neglects none (Basil, Preface)
elements.counsel: Gregory PR III.13: tell the fearful not to prize temporal goods, since bad men have them too, and not to dread present evils, since good men suffer them too. If they fear, they should fear the eternal. But they must not stay in fear: 'grow up by the nursing of charity to the grace of love'. Dorotheos 4.49 (paraphrase): keep turning from evil, begin to do good, and hope and then love will grow. Cassian 11.12: fear is 'useful' and introduces people 'to the first beginning of blessedness'. Cassian 11.7: the Father may lift a person through both lower stages at once, as with the prodigal. Isaac: 'Hope in God elevates the heart. Fear of Hell breaks it.' Clement VII.12: such self-restraint is 'the basis of knowledge, and an approach to something better'.
elements.links: The sources' own links: Cassian 11.6 ties this fear to faith, which shuns sin from fear of judgment, and 11.13 sets penal fear against the fear that belongs to love. Isaac L ties fear to one of two kinds of humility. Isaac LXII ties fear of death to the 'bodily' state and fear of judgment to the 'psychic' state. Gregory, Dialogues III.34, ties fear to the first kind of compunction (tears for sins from fear of torments), which is followed by the compunction of love. Gregory PR III.13 ties it to overvaluing temporal goods. Dorotheos 4.52 (paraphrase) says the fear of God is gained by remembering death and the punishments, by examining oneself each evening and morning, by avoiding over-familiarity, and by living near someone who fears God.

elements.name: Hope of reward (the hireling)
elements.what_it_is: Doing good to gain what is promised: heaven, blessing, the reward. Basil: 'seeking to profit by the reward, we fulfil the commandments for the sake of our own benefit, and are accordingly like hirelings'. For Cassian it is the second stage, 'compared not to a slave but to a hireling, because it looks for the payment of its recompense'. Note that the Fathers praise hope as such. Cassian counts it among faith, hope and love (1 Cor 13:13), and Isaac writes 'Hope in God elevates the heart.' What they call the hireling's is mercenary hope, which wants the pay more than the Giver.
elements.disguise: It looks like real, even model, diligence. Basil: 'Nor indeed will the hireling choose to transgress any of the commandments', because he will not lose his pay. Clement: 'reward makes this one; or rather, makes him appear to be just.' Gregory of Nyssa (paraphrase) says it treats the virtuous life like a business deal. Cassian 11.7 says it seems free from care about its sins, 'conscious of its own good works'.
elements.hidden_side: What it is after is the reward, not the One who gives it. Cassian 11.9: 'a mercenary greed of hope, whereby there is sought not so much the good of the donor as the recompense of reward'. It cannot reach the son's confidence that all the father has is already his (Cassian 11.7). Isaac: working 'with a view to future reward' is 'easily led to deviation'. Dorotheos 14.153 (paraphrase): one who serves the sick only for a wage stops the moment something unpleasant happens.
everyday_signs: Treats good deeds as a trade and expects a return (Basil, Preface: 'for the sake of our own benefit'; Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses II, paraphrase: a business-like arrangement)
Drops a good work as soon as it turns unpleasant, or the person helped is difficult (Dorotheos Instr. 14.153, paraphrase)
A steady but unchanging round, 'like a millstone, that always moves in the same way' (Climacus 1.13, paraphrase)
Aware of their own good works and little troubled by their own sins (Cassian 11.7)
Keeps doing good with effort and grief, held up by hope of the wage (Dorotheos 4.51, paraphrase)
elements.counsel: Cassian 11.11-12: Scripture itself praises working 'for the reward' (David, and Moses who 'looked unto the reward'). Such hope is useful and leads to the beginning of blessedness, but love carries it further. Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15: because we lack desire for Him, God 'keeps putting various other things before us, so as to hold us to Himself'. In that homily Christ appeals first to gratitude, then to pity for His poverty, and only then to the Kingdom's rewards. Dorotheos 4.49 and 4.51 (paraphrase): keep doing good, and with God's help it becomes habit, then rest, then joy in the good itself. Clement VII.11: such people are 'blessed indeed, but not yet become men in love to God'.
elements.links: The sources' own links: Cassian 11.6 ties hope to withdrawing the mind from present things. Cassian 11.9 sets mercenary hope against adoption as sons. Dorotheos 4.51 (paraphrase) ties the hireling stage to doing good with struggle and grief, before peace comes. A Syriac desert saying (Budge, Paradise vol. 2, section 695) says 'the penitent are hirelings, but the humble are sons', linking the hireling to the penitent's labour.

sources.work: Basil the Great, The Longer Rules
sources.quote: And, in short, I perceive three different dispositions which by inevitable necessity lead us to obey. Either through fear of punishment we turn away from that which is evil, and so are of a slavish disposition; or, seeking to profit by the reward, we fulfil the commandments for the sake of our own benefit, and are accordingly like hirelings; or else we do good for the sake of the good itself and from love of Him Who gave us the law, rejoicing that we are thus thought worthy to serve the glorious and great God, and so we have the disposition of sons.
sources.translation: W. K. L. Clarke (SPCK 1925); typed from the page scan; US public domain only

sources.work: Basil the Great, The Longer Rules
sources.quote: Nor indeed will the hireling choose to transgress any of the commandments.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: which is compared not to a slave but to a hireling, because it looks for the payment of its recompense
sources.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894)

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: from a mercenary greed of hope, whereby there is sought not so much the good of the donor as the recompense of reward

sources.work: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata
sources.quote: For as fear makes that man just, so reward makes this one; or rather, makes him appear to be just.

sources.work: Isaac of Nineveh, Mystic Treatises
