sources.work: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans
sources.quote: For since we have not the right feeling of desire after Him, He keeps putting various other things before us, so as to hold us to Himself.
sources.translation: J. B. Morris and W. H. Simcox, rev. G. B. Stevens, NPNF 1st series vol. 11 (1889)

sources.work: Dorotheos of Gaza, Instructions
sources.locus: Instruction 14 (the house of the virtues), section 153
sources.paraphrase: Serving a sick person only to earn a wage is not done with understanding. If something unpleasant happens, that person stops at once and does not finish. The one who serves out of compassion bears everything calmly, even the patient's irritation, and believes the patient does him more good than he does the patient.
sources.translation: Checked in a modern Greek rendering; paraphrase only

sources.work: Gregory of Nyssa, The Life of Moses
sources.locus: Book II, closing paragraphs (numbered 320 in the Malherbe-Ferguson translation, pp. 131-132; confirm against the book)
sources.paraphrase: True perfection is not avoiding evil like slaves who fear punishment. Nor is it doing good for rewards, as if virtue were a business deal. It is dreading only one thing, falling from God's friendship, and prizing only one thing, becoming His friend.
sources.translation: No public-domain English. Checked only through secondary quotations of Malherbe and Ferguson (Paulist, 1978).

sources.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
sources.paraphrase: Someone who leaves the world in hope of reward is like a millstone that always turns the same way.

elements.name: Love of the good and of God (the son)
elements.what_it_is: Doing good for the good itself and out of love for God, as a grown son pleases a father he loves. Basil: 'we do good for the sake of the good itself and from love of Him Who gave us the law'. Cassian 11.6: 'a liking for goodness itself and the love of virtue', which 'belongs specially to God and to those who have received into themselves the image and likeness of God'. Dorotheos 4.48 (paraphrase): the son does his father's will not for fear of a beating nor for pay, but because he loves and honours him and is sure that all his father has is his. Chrysostom on Paul: 'For Christ he loved not for the things of Christ, but for His sake the things that were His'.
elements.disguise: Its counterfeit is presumption that calls itself love. Basil, right after the three dispositions: 'Let us not then know God by halves, nor make His kindness an occasion of sloth.' Dorotheos 4.52-53 (paraphrase) says over-familiarity (parrhesia) drives the fear of God out of the soul. He quotes Abba Agathon calling it the mother of all passions. The real son is more careful, not less: he will not 'grieve him in small matters' (Basil).
elements.hidden_side: The son is not without fear. He carries a new fear, of hurting or losing the one he loves (see the next element). Gregory, Dialogues III.34: love also weeps, now for the heavenly joys it still lacks. Isaac L: the humility born of joy knows no 'bashfulness'; such people 'do not know how to regulate or to order their limbs', and love has 'oblivion of measure'. That is a trait others may misread.
everyday_signs: The same person watched or alone: 'neither will regard for the presence of another add anything to his goodness nor will solitude take anything away from it' (Cassian 11.8)
Careful in small things so as not to grieve the Father (Basil, Preface)
Pity rather than anger at other people's sins; prays for enemies and persecutors (Cassian 11.9-10)
Serves the sick with compassion, bears their irritation, and feels helped by them (Dorotheos 14.153, paraphrase)
Doing good feels like peace and joy, not war (Cassian 11.8; Dorotheos 4.51 and Climacus 1.16, paraphrase)
Fervour that grows and spreads like fire set to fuel (Climacus 1.13, paraphrase)
A joyful, unselfconscious humility: 'full exuberance and ... an exulting heart' (Isaac L)
Longs for God's presence rather than dreading His coming (Augustine, Hom. 9 on 1 John; Isaac LXII: love 'longs after departure')
Does good spontaneously, not under pressure (Clement VII.12: love builds 'to the point of spontaneousness'; VII.12: righteous 'from free choice')
elements.counsel: Cassian 11.7: we reach it when, 'as He first loved us', we love Him for His love alone. Cassian 11.9 says it comes to one 'relying on the help of God and not on his own efforts'. Dorotheos 4.51 (paraphrase): it arrives by persevering in doing good until peace is tasted. Basil p. 149: 'Let us then either love Him for those, or fear Him for these', and not know God by halves. Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15: love of Christ is shown by giving Him bread, clothing and visits in the poor.
elements.links: The sources' own links: Cassian 11.9-10 says love brings patience, gentleness, compassion for sinners and prayer for enemies, while 'rigid censure of the judge' is the sign of a soul not yet purified. Cassian 11.13 says love brings a higher fear. Isaac L says love brings a joyful humility. Isaac LXII: 'love annihilates fear'. Clement VII.12 links love to doing good, where fear only abstains from evil. Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15, links love of Christ to mercy to the poor. Budge section 695: 'the humble are sons'.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: There are, said he, three things which enable men to control their faults; viz., either the fear of hell or of laws even now imposed; or the hope and desire of the kingdom of heaven; or a liking for goodness itself and the love of virtue.
sources.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894)

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: To such an one, I say, neither will regard for the presence of another add anything to his goodness nor will solitude take anything away from it

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: But it is a clear sign of a soul that is not yet thoroughly purged from the dregs of sin, not to sorrow with a feeling of pity at the offenses of others, but to keep to the rigid censure of the judge

sources.work: Basil the Great, The Longer Rules
sources.quote: The third service is that of love. What son, seeking to please his father, and satisfying him in great things, will choose to grieve him in small matters?

sources.work: Basil the Great, The Longer Rules
sources.quote: Let us then either love Him for those, or fear Him for these

sources.work: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata
sources.quote: Now fear works abstinence from what is evil; but love exhorts to the doing of good, by building up to the point of spontaneousness

sources.work: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans
sources.quote: For Christ he loved not for the things of Christ, but for His sake the things that were His, and to Him alone he looked, and one thing he feared, and that was falling from his love for Him. For this thing was in itself more dreadful than hell, as to abide in it was more desirable than the Kingdom.

sources.work: Isaac of Nineveh, Mystic Treatises
sources.locus: Treatise L ('Short sections containing various considerations...'), p. 232
sources.quote: There is a humility that has its origin in the fear of God and there is a humility that arises through the love of God. Some people are made humble by their fear, others by their joy in Him. The former live with limbs subdued and ordered senses and in perpetual contrition of heart; the latter in full exuberance and with an exulting heart which is never checked.
sources.translation: A. J. Wensinck (1923); checked against the page scan

sources.work: Dorotheos of Gaza, Instructions
sources.paraphrase: Citing Basil's three dispositions: a son who has come of age does his father's will not for fear of a beating nor for pay, but because he loves and honours him and is sure that all his father has is his. Dorotheos quotes Antony: he no longer fears God, but loves Him. The path runs like this: fear turns a person from evil, and little by little he starts doing good. Doing good, he begins to hope for a reward, like a hireling. Persevering by grace, he tastes God's presence and will not be parted from Him. Then he loves the good for its own sake, and he fears because he loves.
sources.translation: Checked in a modern Greek rendering; paraphrase only

elements.name: The fear that belongs to love (the son's fear)
elements.what_it_is: A fear that remains after love has cast out the fear of punishment. It is the fear of hurting or losing the one you love. Cassian 11.13 calls it 'that still more sublime fear belonging to love', the fear a son has of a kind father, a friend of a friend, a wife of her husband. Dorotheos 4.47-48 (paraphrase) calls it the 'perfect fear' of the saints: they fear to lose the sweetness of being with God, and to do anything against the will of the Beloved. Augustine's 'chaste fear' is the fear 'lest He forsake you'. Chrysostom says Paul feared one thing only, 'falling from his love for Him'. Gregory of Nyssa (paraphrase): falling from God's friendship is the only thing to dread.
elements.disguise: From outside it sounds exactly like the servile fear. Augustine: both wives, asked, say they fear their husband. 'The voice is one, the mind diverse.'
elements.hidden_side: The difference shows only in the 'why'. Augustine: 'I fear my husband, lest he should come' against 'lest he depart from me'. 'I fear to be condemned' against 'I fear to be forsaken'.
everyday_signs: Dreads letting the other down, or love cooling, more than any penalty: 'care taken by anxious affection lest the warmth of his love should cool' (Cassian 11.13)
Would rather be chastised and near the Father than at ease and apart from Him (Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15, on Paul)
Where it is missing: people unbothered at offending God will do anything to repair a trivial quarrel with a friend (Climacus 1.15, paraphrase)
elements.counsel: Dorotheos 4.47 and 4.49 (paraphrase): no one reaches this fear except through the beginner's fear. Cassian 11.13: this is the fear that 'filled' Christ (Isaiah 11:3), 'the treasure of wisdom and knowledge'.
elements.links: The sources' own links: Cassian 11.13 ties it to Isaiah 33:6 and 11:2-3, and separates it from the 'beginning of wisdom' fear. Augustine ties the servile fear to dreading the day of judgment. Isaac LXII: love 'longs after departure'.

The one who loves has tasted what it is to be with God, and fears to lose that sweetness. That perfect fear drives out the first. But no one reaches the perfect fear except through the first.

elements.name: Love of glory (doing good to be seen)
elements.what_it_is: Not a stage on the ladder but a motive the same Fathers name beside it. Clement lists it first among the motives of those who are 'children in faith'. Basil opens his three dispositions by setting aside good done 'that they may be seen of men', a zeal he calls 'fruitless'.
elements.disguise: Real good works, done in view of others.
elements.hidden_side: Basil, citing Matthew 6:5: they 'have received their reward'. The reward is already spent on the audience.
everyday_signs: Good works tied to being seen (Basil, Preface, citing Matt 6:5)
For the mature, praise may follow but is not the aim, and serves only 'the imitation and benefit of those who praise him' (Clement VII.12)
elements.counsel: Clement IV.22: do good 'neither for glory, nor ... for reputation, nor from reward either from men or God; but so as to pass life after the image and likeness of the Lord'.
elements.links: Clement VII.11 places love of glory alongside fear of punishment and hope of delights after death, as the motives of 'children in faith'.

key_passages.work: Basil the Great, The Longer Rules

key_passages.quote: And, in short, I perceive three different dispositions which by inevitable necessity lead us to obey. Either through fear of punishment we turn away from that which is evil, and so are of a slavish disposition; or, seeking to profit by the reward, we fulfil the commandments for the sake of our own benefit, and are accordingly like hirelings; or else we do good for the sake of the good itself and from love of Him Who gave us the law, rejoicing that we are thus thought worthy to serve the glorious and great God, and so we have the disposition of sons.
key_passages.paraphrase: The source text for slave, hireling and son. Basil then says each of the three keeps every commandment. He does not despise the first two.

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, The Book of Pastoral Rule
key_passages.quote: For good should be loved for itself, not pursued because of the compulsion of penalties. For he that does what is good for this reason, that he is afraid of the evil of torments, wishes that what he fears were not, that so he might commit what is unlawful boldly.

key_passages.work: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata
key_passages.quote: But let the predicted promise be taken away, and the threatened dread cancelled, and the impending danger removed, and the disposition of such people will be revealed.
key_passages.paraphrase: Clement's test: take away the threat and the promise, and see what remains.

key_passages.work: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans
key_passages.quote: For since we have not the right feeling of desire after Him, He keeps putting various other things before us, so as to hold us to Himself.
key_passages.paraphrase: God Himself meets people at the level of their motive. Rewards are His mercy to the not-yet-loving.

key_passages.work: Isaac of Nineveh, Mystic Treatises
key_passages.locus: Treatise LXII, 'That by the thoughts which stir in a man he knows to which degree he belongs', p. 288
key_passages.quote: But when he proceeds firmly, both kinds of fear are taken away.
key_passages.paraphrase: Isaac says a person can tell his own degree by what he fears. While careless he fears death. Drawing near to God, he fears the Judgment. Once firm, he is 'consumed by love'.
key_passages.translation: A. J. Wensinck (1923); checked against the page scan

key_passages.work: Dorotheos of Gaza, Instructions
key_passages.locus: Instruction 4, 'On the fear of God', sections 47-49
key_passages.paraphrase: Dorotheos cites Basil's three dispositions and joins them into one road. Fear of punishment turns you from evil. Doing good, you begin to hope for a reward. Persevering, you taste God and will not leave Him. Then you love the good for itself and fear only because you love. The perfect fear cannot be reached except through the first.
key_passages.translation: Modern Greek rendering checked; Wheeler's English (Cistercian 1977) is copyrighted; paraphrase only

key_passages.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
key_passages.paraphrase: People leave the world for one of three reasons: the future Kingdom, their many sins, or love of God. Leaving from fear is like incense that ends in smoke. Leaving for a reward is like a millstone that always turns the same way. Leaving for love of God is fire from the start, and it spreads.

key_passages.work: Gregory of Nyssa, The Life of Moses

key_passages.paraphrase: True perfection is not avoiding evil from servile fear, nor doing good for rewards as in a business deal. It is dreading only the loss of God's friendship and desiring only to be His friend.
key_passages.translation: No public-domain English; checked through secondary quotations of Malherbe and Ferguson (1978)

report.measurement_notes:
These are not quiz items. They are what the Fathers themselves say gives each motive away in daily life. Self-report on motive flatters, because almost everyone will say 'love'. So the Fathers' own tests are indirect, and each looks at a behaviour or an inner experience, not at a stated reason.
1. Unwatched conduct. Cassian 11.8 says love 'neither will regard for the presence of another add anything to his goodness nor will solitude take anything away from it'. Clement IV.22: take away the threat and the promise, and 'the disposition ... will be revealed'. Gregory III.13: the fearful man secretly wishes the penalty did not exist. A gap between public and private conduct points to fear, or to love of glory.
2. Avoiding versus doing. Dorotheos 4.50 (paraphrase): does no wrong but shows no mercy, does not hate but does not love. Clement VII.12: fear 'works abstinence from what is evil'; love 'exhorts to the doing of good'. A goodness made mostly of things one does not do points to fear.
3. Staying power when it stops paying. Dorotheos 14.153 (paraphrase): one who serves for a wage quits at the first unpleasantness. One with compassion bears even the patient's irritation. This is the hireling's clearest everyday sign.
4. What you fear. Isaac LXII: death, then the Judgment, then neither. Augustine: 'lest he should come' against 'lest he depart'. Cassian 11.13 and Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15: the only dread left is cooling or losing love. Chrysostom, Matthew Hom. 23: 'many tremble only at hell'. This maps to a 'core fear' slot.
5. How doing right feels. Cassian 11.8: war and wounds against 'the security of peace'. Dorotheos 4.51 and Climacus 1.16 (paraphrase): labour and grief first, then rest and joy.
6. Course over time. Climacus 1.13 (paraphrase): zeal that fades like incense smoke (fear); the same round like a millstone (reward); fire that spreads (love). Cassian 11.7: goodness built on fear or hope lapses when the soul relaxes into 'coldness or joy or delight'.
7. Reaction to other people's sins. Cassian 11.9-10: pity and prayer for them marks love. 'The rigid censure of the judge' marks a soul not yet purified.
8. Style of humility. Isaac L: fear-humility is restrained, ordered and contrite. Joy-humility is exuberant and unselfconscious.
9. Care in small things. Basil: the son will not 'grieve him in small matters'. Dread keeps the slave careful in everything too, so this sign separates the son from the careless, not from the slave.
10. Presumption. Basil p. 149: making 'His kindness an occasion of sloth'. Dorotheos 4.52-53 (paraphrase): over-familiarity in words, touch, looks and joking. This is the counterfeit of love. Someone who answers 'love' but shows these signs is not where they think.
The Fathers expect a mixture in each person, one motive leading. A result should report the leading motive and the next step, not a single label.
report.report_layer_ideas:
These are ideas for fields and sections, not copy.
- 'What moves you' section: the leading motive now (fear, reward, love), plus a second. Present it as a place on one road that every Christian walks, not as a type. The texts support the framing: Cassian 11.12 ('no uniform crown'), Clement VII.11 ('blessed indeed', 'crowns for men and for children'), and Basil's praise of all three.
- 'What you fear most' field. This is the patristic counterpart of the Enneagram's core fear: punishment, missing out, or grieving and losing the One you love (Isaac LXII; Augustine Hom. 9 on 1 John; Cassian 11.13; Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15). Augustine's two wives are a ready everyday illustration.
- 'What it hides' field, per motive. Fear: the wish that the rule did not exist (Gregory III.13), and a picture of God as avenger (Isaac XLV). Reward: goodness as a trade (Nyssa, paraphrase) that quits when unpaid (Dorotheos 14.153). Love's counterfeit: presumption, 'His kindness an occasion of sloth' (Basil).
- 'Your next step' field. Fear to doing good to hope to love (Dorotheos 4.49). 'Grow up by the nursing of charity' (Gregory III.13). The Father can carry you through both stages at once (Cassian 11.7). For the over-familiar, how the fear of God is gained (Dorotheos 4.52: remember death, examine each evening and morning, keep company with someone who fears God).
- 'How you are best spoken to' field. It fits the Book III design. Gregory III.13 for the fearful. Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15, for the reward-minded: God holds out gifts because we lack desire. Basil for everyone: know God 'not by halves'.
- 'In the Body of Christ' angle: love shows as pity for sinners and prayer for enemies (Cassian 11.9-10), and as bread and visits for Christ in the poor (Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 15). The Church holds every stage (Clement: crowns for children and for men).
- Possible joins to the Book III pairs. These are my suggestions, not the Fathers' own links, and need the main session's judgment. Ch. 35 (better in public or in private) with Cassian 11.8 and the love-of-glory motive. Ch. 17 (humble or haughty; fear passing as humility) with Isaac's two humilities. Ch. 34 (never begin or never finish) with Climacus's incense and Dorotheos 14.153. Ch. 33 (small faults) with Basil's son careful in small matters. Ch. 14 (judging in private) with Cassian 11.10. Ch. 7 (impudent) with Dorotheos on over-familiarity.
- Keep it one section, not the headline. It is not two-sided, and it must never read as a grade.
report.orthodox_standing:
Basil the Great: saint, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs. The Longer Rules are foundational for Orthodox monasticism. Strongest foundation here.
John Chrysostom: saint, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs. Foundation.
John Cassian: venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church (St John Cassian the Roman). His writings on the eight vices and on discernment are in the Philokalia. Conference 11 itself is not. The Western 'semi-Pelagian' suspicion attaches to his Conference 13, not to this one. Foundation.
Dorotheos of Gaza: venerated saint (Abba Dorotheos). His Instructions are standard reading in Orthodox monastic formation. Foundation, but paraphrase only in English.
John Climacus: saint. The Ladder is read in Great Lent, and the fourth Sunday of Lent bears his name. Foundation, paraphrase only.
Isaac the Syrian: venerated saint in the Orthodox Church. He was a bishop of the Church of the East, received through the Greek translation of his works. Foundation. Note that Wensinck's treatise numbers differ from the Greek 'Homily' numbers Orthodox readers know.
Gregory of Nyssa: saint, Cappadocian Father. Foundation, but no public-domain English for the Life of Moses.
Gregory the Great: saint in the Orthodox Church as St Gregory the Dialogist. Foundation.
Clement of Alexandria: an important early teacher, but not generally venerated as a saint in Orthodox calendars. His word 'Gnostic' (the mature Christian) is easily misread. Supporting witness only.
Augustine: pre-schism, honoured as 'Blessed Augustine' but received with reservations in Orthodoxy. The two-wives image is useful support, not a foundation.
Budge's Paradise, vol. 2: an anonymous Egyptian desert saying in a Syriac collection compiled by 'Anan-Isho of the Church of the East. A minor witness.
Post-schism Western writers carry the same scheme (Bernard of Clairvaux, On Loving God; Aquinas, Summa II-II q. 19 on servile, initial and filial fear). They were not checked in this pass, and they should not be used as a foundation.
risks: It is a ladder with a better end. That breaks the Personality Quiz rule that neither side of a pair is the good one. It must not be a pair, a type, or the headline.
Close to counting devotion. A 'spiritual maturity' score or a 'you are at stage 1 of 3' label breaks the owner's rule 'count knowledge, never devotion'. Report direction and next step, never a grade.

Self-report flattery. Nearly everyone will choose 'love'. Only the Fathers' indirect tests (unwatched conduct, quitting when unpaid, what you fear, pity or censure of sinners) can separate the motives. Even those can be gamed.
The Fathers see a mixture in every person, and the motives lapse and shift (Cassian 11.7). Calling someone 'a slave type' says more than any source says.
The words 'slave' and 'hireling' are harsh in modern English and carry the history of slavery. The main session will need care in naming them.
Chrysostom, Romans Hom. 14, applies slave and hireling to 'the Jews' under the Law against Christians under grace, and says hirelings 'never left murmuring'. Do not use that frame or that line.
Clement's 'Gnostic' will mislead readers, and Clement is not venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church. Use him as support only.

Paraphrase-only sources: Dorotheos (section numbers taken from a modern Greek rendering; confirm against Wheeler or SC 92), Climacus (Moore numbering; other translations number differently) and Gregory of Nyssa (paragraph 320 checked only through secondary quotations). Confirm the references against the printed books before publishing them.
Clarke's Basil (1925) is public domain in the US only. Clarke died in 1968, so it is still in copyright in the UK.

Isaac quotes come from Wensinck's 1923 English of the Syriac, with Bedjan's treatise order. The same passages carry other numbers, and read differently, in the Greek-based 'Ascetical Homilies' most Orthodox readers know.

Isaac praises love's 'frankness and oblivion of measure', while Dorotheos calls over-familiarity (parrhesia) the mother of passions. They are talking about different things (boldness with God, and over-familiarity with people). Do not flatten one into the other.

Hell and punishment language can frighten or alienate readers. The Fathers themselves insist fear is good and useful (Basil: 'blessed who fears always with reverence'; Cassian 11.12). A report that mocks the fear-motive would misrepresent them.
Basil's third group, 'those who transgress most of the commandments', and Gregory's hardened, who are not corrected even by scourges, fall outside the three. A quiz should not try to detect them.

report.framework: The active and the contemplative life (Martha and Mary) as a difference between people: Gregory the Great (Moralia VI.56-61; Pastoral Rule I.5-7, II.5, II.7; Homilies on Ezekiel I.3, II.2), John Cassian (Conferences 1, 14, 19, 24), Augustine (Sermons 103-104 Ben.; City of God XIX.19), Basil (Longer Rules 7; Letter 2), Chrysostom (On the Priesthood VI), Gregory Nazianzen (Oration 2), the Desert Fathers (Budge, Paradise vol. 2), John Climacus (Ladder, paraphrase only), Isaac the Syrian (paraphrase only)
report.verdict_reason: It gives one strong temperament axis in Gregory's own words (Moralia VI.57): some minds are quiet and crushed by business; some are restless and made worse by leisure. It names the hidden danger and the help for each side. It also gives a second layer, "your line in the Body" (Cassian Conference 14.4-7; Abba Nastir; Basil Longer Rules 7). Several other Fathers agree that not every life fits every person (Cassian 24.8, Climacus Step 1, Nazianzen Oration 2). But it is one axis, not a full system. The Fathers rank the two lives: contemplation is greater in merit, while action comes first and is required of everyone. And most of the material was written for monks and pastors.
report.sorts_people:
Mixed. Some texts sort people. Others describe lives or stages that everyone goes through.

These texts sort people (temperament or calling):
- Gregory, Moralia VI.57 is explicit. The "compositions" of souls differ (Latin conspersiones, literally "doughs" or "mixtures"). Some are "of such inactivity of mind" that business crushes them. Some are "so restless" that leisure makes their thoughts worse. So the quiet mind should not be loaded with work, and the restless mind should not shut itself away in contemplation. He adds: "if it were not that the contemplative life suited some minds more than the active life, the Lord would never say ... Be still". The Latin marginal summary "Alterutra cuique pro ingenio colenda" ("each should follow one or the other according to his natural bent") is an editor's heading in Migne. It is not Gregory's own sentence.
- Gregory, Pastoral Rule I.7: Isaiah volunteers "through an active life". Jeremiah shrinks back "through a contemplative life". Both come "from the same fountain of love". Here the disposition shows in how each answers a call.
- Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 2.6, describes his own lifelong bent toward "calm and retirement". Oration 2.114 says some come forward eagerly and others hold back, and neither is blamed.
- Cassian, Conference 14.4-7: the practical life "is distributed among many different professions and interests". Each should keep "the line which he has chosen as the grace which he has received". Conference 24.8: "all things cannot be fit for all men". The hermit's life is harmful for many, and hospitality costs some people their patience.
- Climacus (Moore translation, paraphrase only). Step 1.25: choose your way of life by your passions. Community life is not for everyone "on account of greed", and solitude is not for everyone "on account of anger". Step 4.119: only a few can live in solitude. Step 26 (Moore §28): some are by nature inclined to silence, temperance, meekness and the like.
- Abba Nastir (Budge, Paradise vol. 2, Appendix no. 605): "All rules of conduct are not alike". He names Abraham's hospitality, David's humility and Elijah's silence.

These texts do not sort people:
- Augustine, Sermons 103 and 104 (Ben.): the two lives are this life and the life to come. Everyone is Martha now, and "In so far as you do this, you are like Mary." City of God XIX.19 treats the three lives as a free choice with limits, not as temperaments.
- Cassian, Conference 1.8: contemplation is the chief good for everyone.
- Basil, Longer Rules 7: solitude is dangerous for all ascetics. It is a rule for everyone.
- Gregory, Homilies on Ezekiel I.3.10: the active life is necessary for all, the contemplative voluntary. Moralia VI.60: action comes first in time for everyone.

Net result: the make-up (quiet or restless) is a real temperament claim in Gregory, Nazianzen, Cassian and Climacus. The "active life" and the "contemplative life" themselves are ways of living that everyone should combine, with action first.
report.summary:
Yes. Some of the Fathers treat this as a difference between people, not only as two stages everyone passes through.

The clearest text is Gregory the Great, Moralia VI.57. He says souls are made differently. Some minds are so inactive that busy work crushes them from the start. Others are so restless that free time makes their thoughts worse. So the quiet mind should not be loaded with heavy business, and the restless mind should not shut itself up in contemplation. Each side has a named danger. The quiet mind, overloaded, falls. The restless mind, left idle, is "killed by the sword of their quiescence", or reaches past its powers in thought and ends in error.

Pastoral Rule I.7 shows the same split in two prophets. Isaiah volunteers. Jeremiah shrinks back. Both act "from the same fountain of love". Pastoral Rule II.7 shows what each side hides. The busy are "wearied all the more" by quiet. The quiet neglect outward needs, so no one listens to what they say.

Cassian (Conferences 14 and 24), Climacus (Steps 1, 4, 26 and 27) and the desert saying of Abba Nastir agree on two things. Not every life fits every person. Each should keep the line he was given.

Cassian 19, Basil (Longer Rules 7) and Chrysostom (On the Priesthood VI) name the solitary's danger. Solitude hides faults instead of healing them. Chrysostom calls his own seclusion "a veil" that others mistake for self-discipline.

Two cautions. First, the Fathers rank the two lives. Contemplation is greater in merit. Action comes first in time and is required of everyone (Moralia VI.60-61; Homilies on Ezekiel I.3.9-10). So this is not a pair where neither side is better in itself. What differs is which road is safer for which make-up. Second, Augustine's Martha and Mary sermons and Cassian's Conference 1 do not sort people. For them the two lives are this life and the next, or one goal for everyone.

This topic can carry one strong axis (quiet or restless make-up) and a layer on "your line in the Body". It cannot carry a whole framework.

elements.name: The quiet mind (Mary's bent; Jeremiah, Elijah, Arsenius)
elements.what_it_is: This is Gregory's "tranquil" or "inactive" mind (Latin otiosae mentis, quieta mens). It is a soul made for stillness, which busy work overwhelms from the start (Moralia VI.57). Gregory says contemplation suits some minds more than action. In Pastoral Rule I.7, Jeremiah shrinks from being sent because he longs for "silent contemplation". Nazianzen describes himself this way (Oration 2.6). In the desert sayings, Elijah "loved silence", and Arsenius "fleeth from the world" for God's sake.
everyday_signs: When a load of business falls on them, they give way at the very beginning (Moralia VI.57).
They love a secret place of quiet and long for a retreat (Pastoral Rule I.5).
Asked to lead or speak, they first plead unfitness, like Jeremiah and Moses (Pastoral Rule I.7; Nazianzen, Oration 2.114).
They want to be at leisure for their own spiritual concerns and not be occupied with outward things (Pastoral Rule II.7).
A visit, or a small delay by someone they are waiting for, makes them fretful. A request to borrow a book annoys them (Cassian, Conference 19.12, given as signs of hidden faults).
They seek rest that 'refreshes without toil' and shrink from other people's wants (Moralia VI.60).
elements.hidden_side: Their faults are asleep, not gone. In solitude 'it is only the opportunity and not the passion of sin of which we are deprived' (Cassian, Conference 19.12). Their patience is untested: 'the man who sits at the helm in harbor' proves nothing (Chrysostom, On the Priesthood VI.6-7). With no one to test them, they fall into self-pleasing and think they have 'reached perfection' (Basil, Longer Rules 7). A gift can be buried. The gifted who flee service 'deprive themselves of the very gifts' they had for others (Pastoral Rule I.5). Basil speaks of 'digging a hole for it in himself' (Longer Rules 7). Their words do not reach the needy, because 'the hand of compassion' is missing (Pastoral Rule II.7). Gregory also says some who rest outwardly keep turning over bad deeds in the mind (Homilies on Ezekiel I.12.19, paraphrase from the Latin). That passage is about anyone, not only this type.
elements.disguise: Seclusion passes for discipline. Chrysostom speaks of his own 'inactivity and negligence ... which others think to be a sort of self-discipline' but which is 'a veil' over his weakness (On the Priesthood VI.7). Refusal passes for humility. Gregory says humility is true only when it is 'not pertinacious' in refusing (Pastoral Rule I.6). Some imagine the solitary life consists in 'avoiding intercourse with the brethren' (Cassian, Conference 19.10). Climacus adds that the enemy tempts the solitary with visions of hospitality and service, to make him impatient (Step 4.118, paraphrase).
elements.counsel: Keep the quiet, but do not use it to escape your neighbour: 'No man has a right to lead such a life of contemplation as to forget in his own ease the service due to his neighbor' (Augustine, City of God XIX.19). Do not throw yourself into immoderate business (Moralia VI.57). Love is what moves 'inactive souls to work' (Moralia VI.58). Go in and out, like Moses at the tabernacle (Pastoral Rule II.5). When the call is real, flee in your heart 'but against [your] will to obey' (Pastoral Rule I.6). Test your peace with people, not only alone. Cassian gives a practice for this: picture wrongs done to you and rehearse meeting them gently (Conference 19.14, paraphrase). And Basil asks: 'Whose feet then wilt thou wash?' (Longer Rules 7).
elements.links: The sources link this side to hidden impatience, anger, avarice and pride in solitude (Cassian, Conference 19.12). Climacus says anger makes solitude dangerous (Step 1.25; Step 27.13, paraphrase). Basil links it to self-pleasing (Longer Rules 7). Gregory sets it beside the call to preach or rule (Pastoral Rule I.5-7). A possible link to Gregory's Book III pair 'listless and torpid' versus 'unquiet' (Pastoral Rule III.36): it shares the English word 'unquiet', and the Moralia Latin uses 'inquieti'. The Latin of III.36 was not checked, and Gregory does not make this link himself.

elements.name: The restless mind (Martha's bent; Isaiah, Abraham, Moses the Ethiopian)
elements.what_it_is: These are Gregory's 'restless' souls (Latin inquieti). Freed from work, they 'labour worse', because leisure gives their thoughts room (Moralia VI.57). They could live usefully in service. Left in quiet, they are instead 'killed by the sword of their quiescence'. Isaiah is the type who volunteers, 'eager to profit his neighbours through an active life' (Pastoral Rule I.7). In the desert sayings, Abraham 'was a lover of strangers', and Abba Moses 'receiveth and is gracious' for God's sake.
everyday_signs: Free time makes their thoughts worse, not better (Moralia VI.57).
'they count it pleasure to be tired by action: they esteem it labour not to labour' (Pastoral Rule II.7).
When there is nothing to do, they 'pant after' business 'night and day with seethings of turbid thought' (Pastoral Rule II.7).
When a task is offered, they volunteer: 'Here I am; send me' (Isaiah, Pastoral Rule I.7).
In study or prayer they 'hunt out more than their wits compass' (Moralia VI.57).
elements.hidden_side: The inner life starves. They become 'ignorant of the things that are within' (Pastoral Rule II.7, paraphrase of the passage). When they reach past their powers in contemplation, they go 'to the length of wrong doctrines'. They will not be disciples 'in a spirit of humility', so they 'become the masters of falsities' (Moralia VI.57). Life among people 'unveils all' and inflames the passions: anger, love of glory, boasting (Chrysostom, On the Priesthood VI.8). 'Constant cares too have ere now blunted the edge of the understanding' (VI.8). Martha's many things distract the mind (Augustine, Sermon 103 Ben., 5). The life of labour 'must beware of' vice (Augustine, Sermon 104 Ben., 4).
elements.disguise: Busyness passes as duty or compassion. Gregory warns that outward business 'though [it] may sometimes be endured out of compassion, should never be sought after out of affection for the things themselves' (Pastoral Rule II.7). Admiring other people's good works passes for zeal, and it leads to 'changing and shifting about' (Cassian, Conference 14.6). The README records Gregory's list in Book II ch. 9 of vices that pass for virtues, such as haste as promptness and wrath as zeal. That list was not re-read in this task.
elements.counsel: Do not shut yourself up in contemplation beyond your powers (Moralia VI.57). The LF English says 'nor the restless mind stint itself in devotion to contemplation'. It renders the Latin 'nec inquieta ad studium contemplationis angustet', roughly 'nor should the restless mind confine itself to the pursuit of contemplation'. If you are not ready for the heights, 'keep more safely the active life alone', and enter life 'with one eye' (VI.57). 'A weight of fear is an anchor of the heart': fear holds restless souls steady in prayer (VI.58). Test yourself first 'in the field of practice' (VI.59). Do not be 'so immersed in active life as to neglect the contemplation of God' (Augustine, City of God XIX.19). Cassian's bow story: a bow that is never unstrung loses its spring (Conference 24.21).
elements.links: The sources link this side to speculative overreach, pride and error (Moralia VI.57-58). Chrysostom links it to anger, vainglory and cares stirred up among people (On the Priesthood VI.8). Cassian links it to acedia: going out more feels like a cure and makes things worse (Conference 24.5). That is a state anyone can be in. Two possible links that Gregory does not make: the 'unquiet' of Pastoral Rule III.36, and the 'hasty' of III.15 in the existing Book III reading.

elements.name: Stepping forward or holding back when called (Isaiah and Jeremiah)
elements.what_it_is: This is Gregory's own pairing of the two bents, seen in how each answers a call to serve. Isaiah offers himself. Jeremiah pleads that he cannot speak. Gregory praises both and says both come from love: love of neighbour and love of God (Pastoral Rule I.7). He takes the frame from Nazianzen, whom he names in the Book III prologue. Nazianzen lists Aaron and Isaiah as eager, Moses and Jeremiah as holding back, and says neither was blamed (Oration 2.114).
everyday_signs: Isaiah type: he 'offered himself of his own accord' when the Lord asked whom to send (Pastoral Rule I.7).
Jeremiah type: he 'humbly pleads that he should not be sent', 'lest by speaking he should lose the gains of silent contemplation' (Pastoral Rule I.7).
Nazianzen describes wavering 'between two fears': one held him back, the other urged him on (Oration 2.112, paraphrase).
elements.hidden_side: The eager one needs cleansing first. Isaiah 'saw himself previously cleansed by a coal of the altar' (Pastoral Rule I.7). Gregory also says the weak are often the most eager to take a high place (I.7, paraphrase). The one who holds back can harden into disobedience or false humility, because humility is true only when 'not pertinacious' (Pastoral Rule I.6). Nazianzen calls both rashness and disobedience 'undisciplined' (Oration 2.112, paraphrase).
elements.disguise: Refusal presented as humility (Pastoral Rule I.6-7). Eagerness to be chosen presented as zeal: those who 'covet pre-eminence' quote 1 Timothy 3:1 (Pastoral Rule I.8).
elements.counsel: The one holding back should not persist in refusing once the call is clear. The eager one should be cleansed first (Pastoral Rule I.7). In your heart flee, but obey (Pastoral Rule I.6). Nazianzen places himself 'between those who are too bold, or too timid' (Oration 2.112).
elements.links: It links to the quiet and restless make-ups of Moralia VI.57. Gregory ties Jeremiah to the contemplative life and Isaiah to the active life in the same sentence. Pastoral Rule I.5 is about the gifted who flee service.

elements.name: Going in and out: the mixed life (the aim for both, not a type)
elements.what_it_is: This is what both make-ups grow toward. Christ works miracles in the cities by day and prays on the mountain by night (Moralia VI.56; Pastoral Rule II.5). Moses goes in and out of the tabernacle. The angels on Jacob's ladder go up and come down (Pastoral Rule II.5). Augustine calls it the 'composite' life (City of God XIX.19). The order is fixed: 'For the season for action comes first, for contemplation last' (Moralia VI.60). Contemplation is greater in merit, but action comes first in time (Homilies on Ezekiel I.3.9, paraphrase). While we live among neighbours, action is necessary and contemplation is voluntary (Homilies on Ezekiel I.3.10, paraphrase from the Latin). Cassian's Abbot John says perfection in both lives is very rare (Conference 19.8-9). This is a universal ideal, not a temperament.
everyday_signs: Moses 'goes frequently in and out of the tabernacle'. He brings doubts about outward affairs back to prayer before acting (Pastoral Rule II.5).
Real perfection is bearing 'the squalor of the wilderness' and 'the infirmities of the brethren' with equal calm (Cassian, Conference 19.9).
elements.hidden_side: Either life alone is lopsided: 'he is no perfect preacher, who either, from devotion to contemplation, neglects works that ought to be done, or, from urgency in business, puts aside the duties of contemplation' (Moralia VI.56).
elements.counsel: Hold both, in order. First train the mind in action, then 'lay it up in the granary of rest' (Moralia VI.60). After contemplation the mind often usefully returns to action, as Jacob returned to Leah after Rachel (Homilies on Ezekiel II.2.11, paraphrase from the Latin). Augustine: 'holy leisure is longed for by the love of truth; but it is the necessity of love to undertake requisite business' (City of God XIX.19).
elements.links: Rachel and Leah: Rachel is beautiful but barren, Leah weak-eyed but fruitful. The contemplative 'sees more' but bears fewer children to God. The active 'sees less, but it bears more largely' (Moralia VI.61). Homilies on Ezekiel II.2.10 makes the same point and cites Augustine, Contra Faustum XXII.

sources.locus: Book I, Homily 3, sections 9-10 (PL 76 approx. cols. 809-811); Book II, Homily 2, sections 7-11 (PL 76 cols. 952-956)
sources.paraphrase: I.3.9: preachers have two lives. The active comes first in time; the contemplative is greater in merit (Martha and Mary). I.3.10: both lives are gifts of grace, but while we live among neighbours one is of necessity and the other of will. Someone who does the good he can may enter heaven without the contemplative life. No one enters without the active life if he neglects the good he could do. The word 'necessitate' is illegible in the scan; I reconstructed it, so treat it as unsure. II.2.7-8: the measuring reed of six cubits and a palm. The six cubits are the active life, which can be held perfectly: feeding the hungry, teaching the ignorant, correcting the erring, calling the proud back to humility, caring for the sick. The palm is the contemplative life, which we only touch in this life. II.2.10: Rachel is beautiful but barren, because the contemplative life seeks rest in silence and bears no children by preaching. Leah is weak-eyed but fruitful. II.2.11: the good order runs from action to contemplation, but the mind often usefully turns back to action. I found no explicit temperament claim in II.2.7-12; that claim is in Moralia VI.57.

elements.name: Your line in the Body (the many works: hospitality, care of the sick, teaching, intercession, silence)
elements.what_it_is: Cassian's Abba Nesteros says the practical life is divided among many 'professions and interests': the silence of the anchorite, the care of a community, hospitality, the care of the sick, intercession for the oppressed and afflicted, teaching, and almsgiving. Each person keeps 'the line which he has chosen as the grace which he has received'. He grounds this in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12 (Conference 14.4-5). In the Syriac desert collection, Abba Nastir says the same through three figures: Abraham's hospitality, David's humility, Elijah's silence (Budge no. 605). Basil: 'no single man is sufficient to receive all spiritual gifts'. In the common life each person's gift becomes everyone's (Longer Rules 7). Pambo judges a silent brother and a hospitable brother 'of equal merit' when both aim at God (Budge no. 604). I have not settled whether Cassian's Nesteros and the Syriac Nastir are the same man.
everyday_signs: Look at what 'thy soul desireth' among the works that are of God (Abba Nastir, Budge no. 605).
Someone not yet settled in his own line gets excited when others are praised for different virtues, and tries at once to copy them (Cassian, Conference 14.6).
elements.hidden_side: Chasing every good work at once: 'while he pursues them all, he will not thoroughly succeed in any one' (Conference 14.6). Copying a way that suits someone else can be deadly: 'things which turned out well for some, are found to be injurious to others' (Conference 14.7). Cassian's image for this is Saul's armour on David (Conference 24.8). A gift used alone is buried (Basil, Longer Rules 7).
elements.disguise: Admiring and copying other people's holiness looks like zeal, but Cassian calls it light-mindedness (Conference 14.7).
elements.counsel: Keep to your line and admire others without swerving (Conference 14.5). First weigh 'the measure of his powers' (Conference 24.8). 'Whatsoever work is of God, if thy soul desireth it, that do, and God be with thee' (Abba Nastir).
elements.links: This leads straight to the site's spiritual gifts quiz, since Cassian quotes Romans 12:4-8 and 1 Corinthians 12:28 here. It also links to the quiet and restless make-ups: Conference 24.8 says the hermit's life harms many people, and hospitality costs some their patience.

report.orthodox_standing:
- Gregory the Great is St Gregory the Dialogist in the Orthodox Church (feast 12 March). He was a Pope of Rome before the schism. The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts is traditionally ascribed to him. Moralia and Pastoral Rule are pre-schism.
- John Cassian is venerated as a saint (feast 29 February, kept on 28 February in other years). Two of his works are in the Greek Philokalia: On the Eight Vices, and On the Holy Fathers of Sketis and on Discrimination, which is drawn from Conferences 1-2. Conferences 14, 19 and 24 are not in the Philokalia. His Western reputation suffered over Conference 13 on grace. That does not affect how the Orthodox receive him.
- Augustine is commemorated as a saint, often as 'Blessed Augustine' (feast 15 June). He is received with reserve on grace and the Filioque, and he is not a foundation for Orthodox ascetic teaching. Use him as support only.
- John Chrysostom and Gregory Nazianzen (the Theologian) are two of the Three Holy Hierarchs, the highest standing. The 'Basil' in Chrysostom's dialogue is his friend and is not clearly Basil the Great.
- Basil the Great is the third Holy Hierarch. His Rules are the basis of Orthodox monastic life.
- The Desert Fathers named here (Antony, Arsenius, Moses the Ethiopian, Pambo, Nisteros) are all saints in the Orthodox calendar. The Budge text translates the Syriac compilation of Anan-Isho, a 7th-century monk of the Church of the East. The sayings themselves come from the shared Egyptian stock that is also in the Greek collections. The 'old man' answers in Budge's Appendix are the Syriac compiler's glosses, so do not cite them as Orthodox teaching.
- John Climacus (St John of the Ladder) has the Fourth Sunday of Great Lent in his memory, and the Ladder is read in Lent. His standing is very high. I found no public-domain English.
- Isaac the Syrian was a 7th-century bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East. He is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church, and his homilies have circulated in Greek since about the 9th century. His standing is high.
- Aquinas, Scupoli and Loyola were not used.

The standings and feast dates are from general knowledge. I did not check them against a calendar in this task.
report.measurement_notes:
What the sources say could reveal each side in everyday life. These are observations, not quiz items.

1. What free time does to you. For the restless, idleness brings worse thoughts and more turmoil (Moralia VI.57). Quiet 'wearies them all the more', and they 'pant after' business when there is none (Pastoral Rule II.7). The quiet feel relief.

2. What a sudden heavy load does to you. The quiet 'give way at the very beginning' (Moralia VI.57).

3. How you answer when asked to lead, speak or serve. Isaiah offers himself. Jeremiah and Moses plead unfitness first (Pastoral Rule I.7; Nazianzen, Oration 2.114). Gregory counts both as love.

4. How you take interruptions and visitors. Cassian lists concrete signs that a quiet life is hiding faults (Conference 19.12):
- a brother's visit or small delay makes you fretful (impatience, anger);
- lending a book annoys you (avarice);
- comparing your strictness with another's laxity pleases you (pride).
He also describes dread of 'intercourse with men' (19.10).

5. Where the mind goes in study or prayer. The restless 'hunt out more than their wits compass' (Moralia VI.57).

6. The pull toward the other life. Climacus says the enemy tempts the solitary with hospitality and service, and the person under obedience with solitude and extreme fasts (Step 4.118, paraphrase). Cassian says people not settled in their way are excited by praise of other ways and copy them (Conference 14.6).

7. Which work of God your soul desires: hospitality, humility or silence (Abba Nastir, Budge no. 605).

A caution for measurement. When a quiet person reports patience or calm, it may be untested, because nothing provokes them (Chrysostom, On the Priesthood VI.6-7; Basil, Longer Rules 7; Cassian, Conference 19.12). Self-reports of virtue in solitude are the weakest evidence the sources name. Behaviour with people is the test they trust.

The Fathers also expect everyone to live both lives, with action first. So a score can say which make-up a person has. It cannot honestly say someone 'is contemplative' in the sense of having less duty to act (Homilies on Ezekiel I.3.10; Moralia VI.60).
risks: Ranking. The Fathers do not treat Martha and Mary as equals. Cassian says 'yet in praising the one, He implies that the other is inferior' (Conference 1.8). So do Moralia VI.61, Augustine's Sermons 103-104 and Homilies on Ezekiel I.3.9. The site's rule that no pole is 'the good one' holds only for the make-up (quiet or restless), which Gregory treats even-handedly in VI.57. It does not hold for the two lives themselves. Hiding the ranking would misrepresent the sources.

Audience. Most of these texts were written for monks (Cassian, Basil, Climacus, the sayings) or for pastors (Pastoral Rule II, Chrysostom). Applying them to lay people is an extension. Moralia VI.57 speaks generally ('compositions of souls'). Augustine's sermons were preached to lay people, but they do not sort anyone.

Translation. Moralia VI.57 in the LF English says 'infinitely varied'; the Latin says 'valde diversa', which means 'very different'. The phrase 'nor the restless mind stint itself in devotion to contemplation' is ambiguous in English; the Latin 'angustet' means the restless mind should not confine itself to contemplation. The marginal summary in Migne ('Alterutra cuique pro ingenio colenda') is an editor's note. Do not attribute it to Gregory.
Pastoral Rule II.5 and II.7 are addressed to rulers of souls. Their picture of the busy and the quiet matches Moralia VI.57. Saying that Gregory meant II.7 of everyone would be an extension.

OCR-cleaned texts. Basil's Longer Rules 7 (Clarke 1925) and the Budge sayings (1907) were cleaned from OCR, with every step logged in the file header. All quotes match the cleaned files exactly. Five fail a letters-only check against the raw OCR, and I checked each cause. B6 has a stray margin letter 'c'. B8 has a stray margin letter 'E'. In B9 the OCR misreads 'one gift' as 'one sift'. D1 is broken by a page break. D3 has OCR 'Abb£' and 'Abbd' for 'Abba'. Compare against the page images before publishing.

The Appendix answers in Budge (nos. 604-607) come from a Church of the East compilation. The 'old man' explanations there are the compiler's glosses. Cite the sayings of Pambo and Nastir and the two-boats story, not the glosses.

Not public domain, or unsure. Climacus exists here only in Moore's 1959 translation, which is under copyright: paraphrase only. Standard references date Wensinck's Isaac to 1923, but the scan's OCR reads 1933, so its US status is unsure: paraphrase only. I found no public-domain English for the Homilies on Ezekiel. I paraphrased from damaged Latin OCR, and I reconstructed the word 'necessitate' in I.3.10.

Unverified details, all from memory: the Alphabetical Collection numbers (Arsenius 38, Nisteros 2); whether Cassian's Nesteros and the Syriac Nastir are the same person; which Cassian texts are in the Philokalia; the feast dates.

Self-flattery. Someone who avoids people can read 'quiet mind' as permission to keep avoiding them. The sources warn against exactly this: Chrysostom's 'veil', Cassian Conference 19.10, Pastoral Rule I.5 and I.6. Any result on the quiet side needs its hidden danger printed right beside it.
Scope. This topic gives one axis and one vocation layer. On its own it cannot produce a 16-type system or a long list of 'distinctive traits' without invention.

report.framework: Eastern roots and parallels of Gregory's "different medicine for different people" (Pastoral Rule Book III): Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2; John Chrysostom, On the Priesthood; John Cassian, Conferences 2, 5 and 7; John Climacus, the Ladder and To the Shepherd; plus Gregory the Great's own Moralia on Job and Pastoral Rule Book II, mapped onto the README's pairs.
report.verdict_reason: The method behind Book III is older than Gregory, and it comes from the East. Gregory names Nazianzen as his source, and that checks out. Oration 2 has the physician of souls, a list of kinds of people, a list of remedies, and the rule that no remedy suits everyone. Several of the README pairs appear there almost word for word: sanguine and despondent, wrathful and meek, cowardly and courageous, simple and designing, led by doctrine or by example. Chrysostom, Cassian and Climacus add real hidden sides and counsel. Gregory's own Moralia, written before the Pastoral Rule, adds the most: extra hidden sides for nearly every pair, a long list of vices that pass for virtues, and several small typologies he states himself. Two limits. First, the Eastern texts describe conditions a pastor meets, not fixed personality types. Second, five of the README items (envious, givers/takers, at variance, strife/peace, obstinate/fickle) have little or no Eastern support in these texts, only Gregory's. So the tradition strongly grounds and deepens the pairs as leanings. It does not support a 16-type sorter.
report.sorts_people:
Mostly no. The two exceptions are both important.

No: Nazianzen (Oration 2, sections 28-29) and Chrysostom (On the Priesthood II.3-4, VI.4) list kinds of hearers, but they mix temperaments (sanguine/despondent, wrathful/meek, cowardly/courageous, simple/designing) with stations and circumstances (men/women, rich/poor, married/unmarried, sick/whole, prosperous/in reverses). They talk about how to treat people, not about fixed types. Nazianzen does say these classes "differ sometimes more widely from each other in their desires and passion than in their physical characteristics", but he only loosely compares this to "the mixtures and blendings of the elements". Cassian (Conference 5, chapter 13) says the same eight faults attack each person differently, with one fault holding "the chief place". That sorts people by their main fault, which is a state that can change.

Yes, in two places. Gregory's Moralia says outright that "the compositions ['conspersio', dough, paste] of souls are infinitely varied" (Moralia VI.57). It names a settled difference between inactive and restless minds, and says the contemplative life "suited some minds more than the active life". Moralia XXIX.45 says the enemy "first beholds the character ['conspersionem'] of each person", and names four: cheerful, morose, timid, proud. This is the passage behind Book III chapter 3's joyful and sad links. Climacus (Ladder, Step 26, section 28, paraphrase) says some people are inclined by nature to temperance, silence, purity, modesty, meekness or contrition, while others have to force themselves.

Against a type system: Pastoral Rule III.37 (in the README) says one person can carry opposite traits. Every source treats these traits as things that can be healed. The honest reading is tendencies a person has, not boxes.
report.summary:
Gregory's Book III did not start with Gregory. He credits Gregory of Nazianzus by name, and the credit is real. In Oration 2, Nazianzen calls guiding people "the art of arts". He lists the kinds of people who need different care, among them the sanguine and the despondent, the cowardly and the courageous, the wrathful and the meek, and the simple and the designing. He lists the remedies too: teaching or example, spur or curb, praise or blame, rebuke in public or in private. He says no remedy is good for everyone. He pictures the right way as a tightrope, where leaning either way is a fall. That is the root of "neither side is the good one".

Chrysostom's On the Priesthood adds that you judge the person's disposition, not only the size of the fault, and that a shepherd needs "a myriad eyes". Cassian adds that the same vices attack each person differently, so each person should start the fight where he is attacked most. That matches Gregory's "start here". Climacus adds that a natural leaning is a gift, not a virtue, and that meekness, silence and joy each hide their own vice.

The richest source is Gregory's own Moralia on Job, written before the Pastoral Rule. It has a first draft of the Book III list. It says souls are made differently, some inactive and some restless. It names four dispositions (cheerful, morose, timid, proud), each with the temptation that fits it. It also gives four speeds of anger, four kinds of speakers, and a long list of vices that pass for virtues.

So do these sources sort people into types? Mostly no. The Eastern writers list conditions a pastor meets, not personalities. Only the Moralia and Climacus speak of a settled or inborn disposition. The honest shape is a profile of leanings with one thing to start with, plus a few small typologies the sources give themselves. It is not a 16-type system.

elements.name: Joyful / sad (Book III ch 3). Eastern support: YES (Nazianzen lists 'the sanguine and despondent').
elements.what_it_is: Gregory's first temperament pair. Nazianzen's list has the same pair. Gregory's Moralia treats 'cheerful' and 'morose' as a person's settled character (conspersio), not a passing mood.
everyday_signs: Cheerful: mirth comes easily (Moralia XXIX.45).
Sad: gloom that turns into grudges and bitterness, slowness to do what is asked, a wandering mind (Moralia XXXI.88, the 'offspring' of melancholy).
Sad: looking for comfort in owning things once joy inside has gone (Moralia XXXI.89).
elements.hidden_side: Joyful: mirth sits next to pleasure, so lust is the temptation made for the cheerful (Moralia XXIX.45). This is the source of the Book III ch 3 link. Sad: moroseness 'easily slides into anger', so discord is the temptation made for the morose (same passage). New in Moralia XXXI.89: sadness 'runs down into avarice'. A heart with no joy inside looks for comfort outside, in possessions. Climacus (Ladder 26.58, paraphrase): conceit hides inside joy.
elements.disguise: Sadness argues 'as if with reason': why rejoice, when you suffer so many wrongs from other people? (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.counsel: The Eastern texts give nothing new for this pair beyond Nazianzen's general rule: praise, blame, encouragement and rebuke each help some people and harm others, depending on the season (Oration 2.31). Moralia XXIX.45 carries a practical point: watch for the temptation that sits next to your temperament.
elements.links: Gregory's own chain runs vainglory -> envy -> anger -> sadness -> avarice (Moralia XXXI.89). That links this pair to kindly/envious, meek/passionate and givers/takers. Gluttony breeds 'foolish mirth' (XXXI.88), which links joyful to gluttonous.

elements.name: Impudent / bashful (Book III ch 7). Eastern support: YES, strong (Nazianzen on public and private rebuke; Chrysostom on shame).
elements.what_it_is: How a person takes correction. Nazianzen's public/private rule is the exact Eastern root of Gregory's 'rebuke the impudent by many, the bashful gently'.
everyday_signs: Some shrug off a private word but are brought to their senses when several people see the fault (Nazianzen, Oration 2.31).
Some grow reckless if rebuked in public but accept correction in private (same place).
Some are hurt more by harsh words than by hardship; others the reverse (Moralia VII.1).
Some take pride in not feeling correction at all; others feel it so much they lash out with their tongue (Moralia II.28).
elements.hidden_side: New: impudence can be made. Chrysostom (On the Priesthood II.4) says that once shame is forced off a person, the soul 'lapses into a callous condition'. After that, neither kind words nor threats move it. Nazianzen (Oration 2.32) says repeated reproofs can drive people to despair and then to 'utter recklessness' once self-respect is lost. So the bashful, handled roughly, can turn impudent. Moralia II.28 adds two faulty responses to correction: numbness that passes for strength, and over-feeling that bursts into angry words.
elements.disguise: Numbness to correction passes for 'a high degree of philosophical fortitude' (Moralia II.28).
elements.counsel: Impudent: rebuke in public, before 'a number of people' (Nazianzen 2.31). Bashful: rebuke in secret, since they 'yield obedience in return for sympathy' (2.31). Sometimes the pastor should look away, 'seeing not to see' (2.32). Chrysostom II.4: fit the treatment to 'the disposition of the sinner', not only to the size of the fault.
elements.links: Links to forward/faint-hearted (the same danger of despair) and to humble/haughty (Moralia XIII.6: the insolent person 'of such a character as to receive no words of rebuke' is best corrected indirectly, through a general admonition).

elements.name: Forward / faint-hearted (Book III ch 8). Eastern support: YES (Nazianzen: 'cowardly and courageous', spur and curb, close watch vs hope; Chrysostom on pride and despair, and on praise-hunger).
elements.what_it_is: Boldness versus timidity about one's own worth and work. Nazianzen gives both treatments. Chrysostom shows the two poles can live in one person.
everyday_signs: Forward: thinks himself wise when he believes no one is watching (Nazianzen 2.32).
Forward: needs constant praise, and wastes away when it stops or when others are praised (Chrysostom, On the Priesthood V.4).
Faint-hearted: pictures every future setback and so never starts (Moralia XXX.51).
Faint-hearted: calls his fear 'caution' or 'prudence' (Moralia XXXI.59).
elements.hidden_side: New from Chrysostom (II.4): 'many are uplifted to pride, and then sink into despair' when a severe remedy comes. The forward and the faint-hearted can be the same person at two moments. Chrysostom V.4: people used to praise suffer 'as by some famine' when it stops, especially 'if they hear others being praised'. Moralia XXXI.59 names both extremes: 'very precipitate' is the one who always charges at adversity, 'very cowardly' the one who always hides.
elements.disguise: Fear passes for prudence: 'feeble fear is often called, by men, cautious dispensation' (Moralia XXXI.59).
elements.counsel: Faint-hearted: treat 'with condescension and lowliness, aiding them readily to conceive a hope of better things' (Nazianzen 2.32). This matches Gregory's 'praise first'. Forward: keep 'a close watch, even in the minutest details' (2.32). Both: fight fear and rashness inside yourself first, before you act (Moralia XXXI.59).
elements.links: Joins slothful/hasty (spur and curb, Nazianzen 2.30) and humble/haughty (praise-hunger, Moralia XXII.15).

elements.name: Impatient / patient (Book III ch 9). Eastern support: PARTIAL (Chrysostom on wrath and on untested calm; Cassian's three kinds of anger; Climacus Step 8, paraphrase).
elements.what_it_is: How a person bears being wronged. The sources add a speed dimension (how fast anger comes and goes) and a warning that calm may just be untested.
everyday_signs: Anger comes fast and goes fast, or slowly and stays long (Moralia V.80).
Anger that 'lasts for days and long periods' (Cassian, Conference 5.11).
Replaying the insult later, silently composing angry speeches (Moralia V.79).
Arguing with an absent offender, in words and gestures, when alone (Climacus, Ladder 8.13, paraphrase).
Hardship steadies some people and drives others to 'a frenzy of impatience' (Moralia V.16).
elements.hidden_side: Patient: new support for Gregory's 'calm at the time, then recall it and exaggerate it'. Anger held in by silence 'burns the more fiercely, and silently frames clamorous speeches' (Moralia V.79). Climacus (Ladder 8.13, paraphrase) says quarrelling with an absent offender when alone is the mark of a hot temper. Chrysostom (On the Priesthood III.14) says his own calm came 'not by any innate virtue, but by my love of retirement'. Some patience is only a lack of provocation. Impatient: Chrysostom III.14 says the fire of wrath 'is a kind of pleasure'.
elements.disguise: Anger argues 'as if with reason' that 'patiently to endure them is a sin', because wrongs left unanswered will pile up (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.counsel: Moralia V.81 gives two remedies. First, before acting, picture the insults you may meet, so they do not catch you asleep. Second, when others wrong you, remember your own offences. Climacus (Ladder 8.25, paraphrase) sends the sharp-tempered into a strict community rather than solitude.
elements.links: Gregory's own distinction (Book III ch 16): the passionate cause strife, the impatient cannot bear it. The anger-speed grid is a separate element below. Chrysostom's 'athlete at home' (III.14) links to better in public / better in private.

elements.name: Kindly / envious (Book III ch 10). Eastern support: THIN (only Chrysostom's line on grief when others are praised).
elements.what_it_is: How a person takes another's success. Almost all the depth here is Gregory's own (Moralia V.84-86, XXXI.88-90).
everyday_signs: Nothing of one's own gives satisfaction while someone else is doing well (Moralia V.85).
Whispering, running people down, quiet gladness at another's bad luck, grief at their good luck (Moralia XXXI.88).
Being 'wasted in soul' on hearing others praised (Chrysostom, On the Priesthood V.4).
elements.hidden_side: New: we only envy people we think are better than ourselves in some way. So envy quietly admits that we feel smaller (Moralia V.84). Envy also spoils one's own strong deeds: it is 'the rottenness of the bones' (V.85, citing Proverbs 14:30). It grows out of vainglory, the wish for a name that someone else might get (XXXI.89).
elements.disguise: Envy argues 'as if with reason': 'In what art thou inferior to this or that person?' (Moralia XXXI.90).
elements.counsel: Moralia V.86: set your heart on the one inheritance that is not made smaller by sharing, 'which is both one to all and whole to each'. Envy shrinks as that love grows. For the kindly side, the README's 'eager backers, inert spectators' (Book III ch 10) remains the main counsel. Nothing new was found.
elements.links: Vainglory -> envy -> anger (Moralia XXXI.89). This links to humble/haughty and meek/passionate.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For it is impossible for us to envy any but those, whom we think to be better than ourselves in some respect.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job

elements.name: Simple / insincere (Book III ch 11). Eastern support: YES (Nazianzen lists 'the simple and the designing'; Climacus Step 24, paraphrase).
elements.what_it_is: Openness versus calculation. Note: at the same slot, the Oxford Moralia translation of Gregory's first list (XXX.13) reads 'the pure / the unclean'. The translators differ, so do not build on the English label alone. The Latin was not checked here.
everyday_signs: Insincere: covering the heart with inventions, veiling meaning with words (Moralia X.48).
Insincere: admired as sophistication, learnt young (Moralia X.48).
Simple: laughed at as naive for saying what they mean (Moralia X.48, paraphrase).
elements.hidden_side: Simple, new: some are 'so simple as not to know what uprightness is'. Simplicity without judgment is not yet innocence (Moralia I.2). Climacus (Step 24, paraphrase): the simplicity some have by nature is blessed, but less than simplicity gained by effort after repentance. Insincere, new: when it has no power, duplicity dresses itself as 'peaceable good nature' (Moralia X.48).
elements.disguise: Duplicity is glossed over 'so long as frowardness of mind goes by the title of urbanity' (Moralia X.48). Its other mask is 'the guise of peaceable good nature' (same place).
elements.counsel: Moralia I.2 (on Matthew 10:16): the dove's simplicity must be taught by the serpent's prudence, and the serpent's prudence softened by the dove. The README's Book III counsel (the simple must learn to keep silent about some truths) says the same thing from the other side.
elements.links: Moralia I.2 also pairs the dove (simplicity) with fire (zeal). That is the source of Book III ch 16's 'dove and fire' for meek/passionate.

elements.name: Silent / talkative (Book III ch 14). Eastern support: PARTIAL (Climacus, paraphrase). The main new material is Gregory's Moralia VII.57-61, the older passage that Book III ch 14 draws on.
elements.what_it_is: How much a person speaks, and what that hides. The Moralia shows Book III's points ('closed sores', 'a door, not a wall', 'a city without walls') already there. It also adds several new observations.
everyday_signs: Two harmful ways of talking: praising even wrong things, or always carping even at right ones (Moralia VII.57).
Talk that slides from idle words, to other people's business, to running them down, to open insult (VII.57).
Two kinds of starter: those who start talking hastily and never check themselves, and those slow to begin who cannot stop once they start (Moralia III.23, of Job's friends).
Going silent out of bitterness, not calm (Moralia XXXIV.51; V.79).
Talk comes loose at feasts (Moralia I.11).
elements.hidden_side: Silent: over-restraint makes 'much talking in the heart'; 'it keeps the tongue down, but it sets the heart up'; wrongs left unspoken turn into bitterer grief (Moralia VII.60). All of this is in Book III too, and the Moralia shows it is older. New: some talkers go silent only 'from the bitterness of their inward rancour' (XXXIV.51). Angry silence 'in saying nothing, says how he abhors him' (V.79). Climacus (Ladder 26.58, paraphrase): contempt of instruction hides inside silence. Talkative: much talk scatters the mind so 'it has no power to turn back within to the knowledge of itself' (VII.59). New: the two faulty speeches are driven by opposite forces: 'Fear keeps down the one, pride sets up the other' (VII.57).
elements.disguise: Flattery passes for agreeableness and carping for honesty. This is implied in VII.57 and stated for speech in general at Moralia XXXII.45 and XXXIV.51 (fear as humility, pride as rightful freedom).
elements.counsel: The tongue needs 'a door', not 'a bar': held in by self-control and opened when needed (Moralia VII.61). This is the source of Book III's 'a door, not a wall'. For those who keep a needed rebuke to themselves: 'the language of reproof is the key of discovery' (Pastoral Rule II.4).
elements.links: Gluttony -> 'babbling' (Moralia XXXI.88) and talk at feasts (I.11): links to gluttonous. Talk -> detraction -> strife (VII.57): links to sowers of strife. Silence -> private judging and pride (VII.60): links to humble/haughty. See also the 'four sorts of speakers' element.

elements.name: Slothful / hasty (Book III ch 15). Eastern support: YES (Nazianzen 2.30 'sluggish and hard to rouse' vs 'immoderately fervent ... like thoroughbred colts'; Cassian's two kinds of listlessness).
elements.what_it_is: Pace and drive. This is the pair with the strongest claim to be a real temperament. Moralia VI.57 says souls are made differently here.
everyday_signs: Inactive: gives way at the very start when work piles up (Moralia VI.57).
Restless: idle time brings worse inner turmoil, not rest (Moralia VI.57).
Slothful: pictures many dangers ahead and so stays still (Moralia XXX.51).
Hasty: runs 'wide of the turning post' like a thoroughbred colt (Nazianzen 2.30).
Listlessness takes two forms: one sends you to sleep, the other makes you get up and leave (Cassian, Conference 5.11).
elements.hidden_side: New: Moralia VI.57 makes it a matter of make-up, not only habit. 'The compositions [conspersio] of souls are infinitely varied'. The restless have 'only the worse labour' when they stop. Cassian (Conference 5.11) gives the Eastern twin: acedia either 'sends those affected by it to sleep' or 'makes them forsake their cell and flee away'. Slothful: the 'hedge of thorns' of imagined future troubles (Moralia XXX.51) matches Book III's 'would not plough by reason of the cold'.
elements.disguise: Moralia XXXII.45 goes further than Pastoral Rule II.9. Sloth passes for 'a maintenance of peace'. Restlessness passes for 'a watchful solicitude'. Haste passes for 'praiseworthy zeal'. Slowness passes for 'judgment'.
elements.counsel: Nazianzen 2.30: the sluggish 'must be stirred up by being smitten with the word'. The fervent need a word with 'a restraining and checking influence'. Moralia VI.57-58: the tranquil should not overload themselves with works, and the restless should not force themselves into long contemplation. 'Love stimulates inactive souls to work, and fear keeps back restless souls'.
elements.links: Same axis as never begin / never finish, and as the active/contemplative element below. Lust breeds 'inconsiderateness' and 'precipitation'; sadness breeds 'slothfulness in fulfilling the commands' (Moralia XXXI.88).

elements.name: Meek / passionate (Book III ch 16). Eastern support: YES (Nazianzen 'the wrathful and meek'; Chrysostom III.14 on wrath; Cassian's three kinds of anger; Climacus Step 8 and 26.58, paraphrase).
elements.what_it_is: Temper: gentle versus hot. The sources confirm Gregory's own link, meek -> laxity/sloth, from the East. Climacus lists what hides inside meekness.
everyday_signs: Hot temper, in the body: the heart beats quick, the tongue stammers, the face flushes, and familiar people are not recognised (Moralia V.79).
Anger at wrongdoing that is really hot temper, called zeal (Moralia XXXII.45; V.82-83).
Meek: letting things slide and calling it gentleness (Moralia XXXII.45).
Anger comes in three kinds: inward, outward in word and deed, and lasting for days (Cassian, Conference 5.11).
elements.hidden_side: Meek, Eastern support for Gregory's 'meek -> sloth, kindred': Climacus (Ladder 26.58, paraphrase) says meekness can hide duplicity, putting things off, laziness, contrariness, self-will and disobedience. Chrysostom III.14: a calm temper may owe more to 'love of retirement' than to virtue. Climacus (end of Step 8, paraphrase): whoever has freedom from anger by nature has one crown; whoever wins it by sweat has conquered much more. Passionate: 'the fire of wrath is a kind of pleasure' (Chrysostom III.14). That explains why the angry do not want to let it go.
elements.disguise: 'Immoderate anger is believed to be the meritoriousness ['meritum'] of righteous zeal'. 'Negligent remissness is regarded as gentleness and forbearance' (Moralia XXXII.45). Moralia V.82 keeps a real distinction between the anger of hot temper and the anger of zeal.
elements.counsel: Anger of zeal must stay 'like a handmaid ... in the rear of reason' (Moralia V.83). A temper brought under reason becomes 'holy zeal' (Moralia III.70). The Spirit came as a dove and as fire, simplicity and zeal together (Moralia I.2): this is the source of Book III's 'dove and fire'. Temptation is made to fit: the enemy does not try 'to seize the gentle by eagerness for the contest, or the angry by the dread of fear' (Moralia XXIX.45). Each is tempted in his own direction.
elements.links: Vainglory -> envy -> anger -> sadness (Moralia XXXI.89). Anger produces 'strifes' (XXXI.88), which links to sowers of strife. See also the 'four speeds of anger' element.
