elements.name: Humble / haughty (Book III ch 17). Eastern support: YES (Nazianzen 2.32; Climacus, To the Shepherd ch 2, paraphrase). Much new material from Moralia XXXIV.51-52.
elements.what_it_is: Self-regard. Gregory's key Book III point, 'fear passing as humility; pride passing as frankness', appears twice more in the Moralia. The Moralia also gives an outward sketch of the proud.
everyday_signs: The proud, outwardly: 'noisiness in their speech, bitterness in their silence, dissoluteness in their mirth, wrath in their sorrow ... rancour in their reply' (Moralia XXXIV.52).
Quick to hand out contempt, slow to bear it; slow to obey, quick to provoke (XXXIV.52).
Silent in quiet judgment of their leaders, never looking at themselves (XXXIV.51).
Showing oneself lowly, then feeling proud of it (Moralia XXVII.78).
Puffed up by praise: some boast in words, others hide it and never show it (Moralia XXII.17).
elements.hidden_side: Haughty, new: 'it seeks to be compelled to do that which it secretly longs for', afraid of looking cheap by simply wanting it (Moralia XXXIV.52). Gentleness from a teacher can make them angrier, because they feel treated as weak (XXXIV.51). Pride has three doors: understanding, good practice, and praise from others (Moralia XXII.15). Humble, new: two false humilities (Moralia XXVII.78). One thinks lowly of himself but needs to look impressive. The other looks lowly and is proud inside.
elements.disguise: 'Just as many are silent through fear, and yet consider that they are silent from humility, so do some speak from the impatience of pride, and yet think that they are speaking with rightful freedom' (Moralia XXXIV.51). The same point appears at XXXII.45.
elements.counsel: Nazianzen 2.32: keep close watch on the self-wise. 'Some it is often more advantageous to conquer, by others to be overcome' (paraphrase of the same section). Moralia XIII.6: the insolent person 'of such a character as to receive no words of rebuke' is best corrected through a general admonition that he does not know is aimed at him. Pride bowed before the fear of God becomes 'free ... authority in defence of justice' (Moralia III.70). Climacus (To the Shepherd ch 2, paraphrase): obedience works like a sleeping draught, so a person stops seeing his own beauties; 'bands' tighten those puffed up by vainglory and obstinacy.
elements.links: Pride is 'the queen of sins' behind all seven (Moralia XXXI.87). The proud are baited 'by flattering applause' (XXIX.45). Links to forward (praise-hunger) and obstinate (vainglory -> 'obstinacies', XXXI.88).

elements.name: Obstinate / fickle (Book III ch 18). Eastern support: THIN (only Climacus, To the Shepherd ch 2, 'bands' for obstinacy, paraphrase).
elements.what_it_is: Holding a course versus changing it. The Moralia confirms Gregory's roots: obstinacy from pride, inconstancy from lust. It names both disguises exactly.
everyday_signs: Obstinate: will not be turned, and feels this is defending what is right (Moralia XXXII.45).
Fickle: breaks their word to everyone and still feels 'a friend to all' (Moralia XXXII.45).
Keen people who go wrong improve 'but slowly', because they believe they are right (Moralia XXXII.46).
elements.hidden_side: Obstinate: 'obstinacies' and 'discords' are offspring of vainglory (Moralia XXXI.88). This backs Gregory's 'obstinate <- pride'. People who err while seeking holiness change slowly, because they 'consider what they do to be right' (XXXII.46). Fickle: 'inconstancy' is an offspring of lust (XXXI.88), next to 'inconsiderateness' and 'precipitation'.
elements.disguise: 'The pertinacity of the wicked is often termed constancy ... Inconstancy is often regarded as tractability, and because a person does not keep his word to any one, he considers himself on that account a friend to all men' (Moralia XXXII.45).
elements.counsel: Moralia XXXII.45: 'error is corrected with more difficulty, when it is believed to be a virtue'. So the first step is to name the disguise. A fault that is blushed at is easily corrected.
elements.links: Humble/haughty (vainglory as root); slothful/hasty (lust -> precipitation).

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: The pertinacity of the wicked is often termed constancy, and when a mind does not submit to be turned from its wickedness, it glories as if in defending what is right. Inconstancy is often regarded as tractability, and because a person does not keep his word to any one, he considers himself on that account a friend to all men.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Since, therefore, error is corrected with more difficulty, when it is believed to be a virtue

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Hence it is that sometimes those who seek after the way of holiness, when they have fallen into error, are improved but slowly. For they consider what they do to be right

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For from vain glory there arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contentions, obstinacies, discords, and the presumptions of novelties. From envy there spring hatred, whispering, detraction, exultation at the misfortunes of a neighbour, and affliction at his prosperity. From anger are produced strifes, swelling of mind, insults, clamour, indignation, blasphemies. From melancholy there arise malice, rancour, cowardice, despair, slothfulness in fulfilling the commands, and a wandering of the mind on unlawful objects. From avarice there spring treachery, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardnesses of heart against compassion. From gluttony are propagated foolish mirth, scurrility, uncleanness, babbling, dulness of sense in understanding. From lust are generated blindness of mind, inconsiderateness, inconstancy, precipitation, self-love, hatred of God, affection for this present world, but dread or despair of that which is to come.

sources.work: John Climacus, To the Shepherd
sources.paraphrase: Among the physician's remedies, 'bands' are for binding tight those puffed up by vainglory and by obstinacy.
sources.translation: B.P. Otto (2020), not public domain; paraphrase only

elements.name: Gluttonous / abstinent (Book III ch 19). Eastern support: YES (Cassian's three kinds of gluttony; Climacus Step 8, paraphrase, on angry fasters).
elements.what_it_is: The appetite for food and the pride of refusing it. The sources widen gluttony beyond quantity. They also back Gregory's 'abstinent -> impatience and pride' from the East.
everyday_signs: Five ways of gluttony: eating before the time, seeking daintier food, fussing over how it is prepared, eating too much, and eating even plain food with burning eagerness (Moralia XXX.60).
Cassian's three: eating before the set time, gorging, and hunting for delicacies. Asking the host for something extra on your plate is a sign (Conference 5.11).
After a big meal, the tongue comes loose (Moralia I.11).
Irritable people keeping fasts and silence (Climacus 8.21, paraphrase).
elements.hidden_side: Gluttonous, new: 'it is not the food, but the desire that is in fault' (Moralia XXX.60). A picky eater can be the glutton. Offspring: 'foolish mirth, scurrility, uncleanness, babbling, dulness of sense in understanding' (XXXI.88). Abstinent, new Eastern support: Climacus (8.21, paraphrase) says many irritable people practise vigils, fasts and silence, and the demons feed their anger through these under a show of penance. Climacus (8.16, paraphrase): some angry people push food away and so add poison to poison; others overeat to comfort themselves. Gregory: the enemy tempts the abstinent not with food but with 'the pride of abstinence' (Moralia XXIX.45).
elements.disguise: Gluttony argues 'as if with reason': God made all things clean to be eaten (Moralia XXXI.90). For the abstinent: a note in Moore's Ladder (Step 22, footnote to section 31; authorship not established) says being naturally a small eater is no virtue; choosing to abstain is.
elements.counsel: Cassian (Conference 5.27): begin the fight where you are attacked most. No new pair-specific counsel beyond Book III.
elements.links: Gluttony -> babbling (links to talkative) and -> lust (Moralia XXXI.89). Anger -> refusing food or overeating (Climacus 8.16), which links to meek/passionate.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: It should also be known, that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For it is not the food, but the desire that is in fault.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Gluttony is also wont to exhort the conquered heart, as if with reason, when it says, God has created all things clean, in order to be eaten

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: or if he were to assail the greedy by the pride of abstinence, or the abstinent by gluttonousness, or if he were to seek to seize the gentle by eagerness for the contest, or the angry by the dread of fear.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: of gluttony there are three sorts: (1) that which drives a monk to eat before the proper and stated times; (2) that which cares about filling the belly and gorging it with all kinds of food, and (3) that which is on the lookout for dainties and delicacies.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Almost always talkativeness is an attendant upon feasts, and when the belly is replenished, the tongue is unloosed

sources.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
sources.locus: Step 8, sections 16 and 21; Step 22, footnote to section 31 (Moore's edition)
sources.paraphrase: 8.16: some angry people push food away out of bitterness, and others give themselves to gluttony; the sensible mix consolation like good physicians. 8.21: many irritable people practise vigils, fasts and silence, and the demons use these, under a show of penance, to feed the passion. Step 22 footnote: some things that look like virtues are gifts of nature, and being naturally a small eater is no virtue.
sources.translation: Lazarus Moore (1959), not public domain; paraphrase only

elements.name: Givers / takers; keepers / lavish-who-also-take (Book III ch 20-21). Eastern support: THIN (Cassian's three kinds of covetousness; nothing specific in Nazianzen or Chrysostom beyond 'rich and poor').
elements.what_it_is: The money pairs. The new sources explain why someone grasps. There are two roots, and they need different handling.
everyday_signs: Grasping in order to look powerful, or grasping out of fear of running short (Moralia XV.30).
Wanting back what one gave away, or wanting what one never had (Cassian, Conference 5.11).
Seeking comfort in possessions when there is no joy inside (Moralia XXXI.89).
elements.hidden_side: New: 'avarice sometimes steals upon men from pride, and sometimes from apprehension' (Moralia XV.30). The proud grasp to appear greater. The anxious grasp because 'their own may not be enough'. Sadness 'runs down into avarice' (XXXI.89). Avarice's offspring include 'restlessness' and 'hardnesses of heart against compassion' (XXXI.88). Cassian (5.11) adds taking back with eagerness what one had given away. That is close to Gregory's lavish-who-also-take.
elements.disguise: 'Lavishness is sometimes believed to be compassion'. 'Tenacity is sometimes considered frugality' (Moralia XXXII.45, fuller than Pastoral Rule II.9). Avarice's argument: 'thou seekest not to be increased, but art afraid of being in want' (XXXI.90).
elements.counsel: None new beyond Book III. The two roots (pride, fear) suggest the fearful keeper and the status-seeker need different words. That is an inference, not a text.
elements.links: Joyful/sad (sadness -> avarice); humble/haughty (pride as a root).

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: We ought to know, that avarice sometimes steals upon men from pride, and sometimes from apprehension.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Lavishness is sometimes believed to be compassion

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Tenacity is sometimes considered frugality, and since it is a grievous fault not to give, it is considered a virtue to retain what has been received.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Avarice also is wont to exhort the conquered mind, as if with reason, when it says, It is a very blameless thing, that thou desirest some things to possess; because thou seekest not to be increased, but art afraid of being in want

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: (2) that which draws us to resume with excessive eagerness the possession of those things which we have given away and distributed to the poor; (3) that which leads a man to covet and procure what he never previously possessed.

elements.name: At variance / at peace (Book III ch 22). Eastern support: NONE found in these texts.
elements.what_it_is: Living in conflict versus living in harmony. Gregory's Moralia adds one hidden side for 'at peace' and backs his root for 'at variance'.
everyday_signs: Keeping the peace by never standing up for what is right (Moralia XXXII.45).
elements.hidden_side: At peace, new: 'Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace' (Moralia XXXII.45). At variance: 'contentions' and 'discords' are offspring of vainglory (XXXI.88). This backs Gregory's 'at variance <- pride in a gift that sets one apart'.
elements.disguise: Sloth dressed as peace (Moralia XXXII.45).
elements.counsel: No new counsel found. Book III's 'break outward peace ... but guard in your heart's core internal peace' remains the main line.
elements.links: Slothful (the same disguise); humble/haughty (vainglory).

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace, and though it is a grievous fault not to be zealous in doing what is right, it is believed to be a most meritorious virtue, merely to abstain from evil conduct.

elements.name: Sowers of strife / peacemakers (Book III ch 23). Eastern support: NONE found in these texts.
elements.what_it_is: Stirring conflict between others versus making peace between them.
everyday_signs: Strife that begins in idle talk about others and grows into running them down and open insult (Moralia VII.57).
Whispering and detraction, the offspring of envy (Moralia XXXI.88).
elements.hidden_side: New: the route into strife is gradual and runs through talk (Moralia VII.57). Anger produces 'strifes', and envy produces 'whispering, detraction' (XXXI.88). A sower of strife may be an envious or an angry person first.
elements.disguise: Insincerity without power poses as 'peaceable good nature' (Moralia X.48). A false peacemaker is possible.
elements.counsel: No new counsel found beyond Book III (the peacemaker must know between whom to make peace).
elements.links: Talkative, kindly/envious, meek/passionate.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Thus while we neglect to guard against idle words, we are brought to mischievous ones, so that it first gives satisfaction to speak of the concerns of others, and afterwards the tongue by detraction carps at the life of those of whom it speaks, and sometimes even breaks out into open revilings.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: when the opportunity of power is lacking, all whatsoever he cannot accomplish in wickedness to represent in the guise of peaceable good nature.

elements.name: After a mistake: lament but repeat / stop but never lament (Book III ch 29-30). Eastern support: YES (Climacus Step 18 and Step 5, paraphrase).
elements.what_it_is: What a person does after doing wrong. Climacus gives a vivid Eastern portrait of the 'lament but repeat' side.
everyday_signs: Repenting after overeating and soon giving way again; sighing after a passion and yielding again; praising silence with a flood of words (Climacus, Ladder 18.3, paraphrase).
Feeling bad in prayer about something, then doing it again (Moralia X.28).
elements.hidden_side: Lament but repeat: Climacus (18.3, paraphrase) calls this insensibility. The person talks about healing a wound and keeps irritating it, and blames himself before others as a way of fishing for glory. Stop but never lament: 'He who knows not how to lament that which weighs him down, is unable to produce that which raises him up' (Moralia XXXI.93). That supports Book III ch 30 ('a writer who stops writing has not rubbed out what he wrote').
elements.disguise: Self-blame as a bid for praise: Climacus 18.3 (paraphrase).
elements.counsel: 'When thou hast bewailed thy misdoings, never again do any thing for thee to bewail again in prayer' (Moralia X.28, glossing Ecclesiasticus 7:14). Climacus (5.30, paraphrase): do not be surprised that you fall every day, and do not give up. Fresh wounds heal easily. Old, neglected ones need much treatment.
elements.links: Small frequent faults (the same 'fresh versus old wounds' point).

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: When thou hast bewailed thy misdoings, never again do any thing for thee to bewail again in prayer.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: He who knows not how to lament that which weighs him down, is unable to produce that which raises him up.

sources.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
sources.paraphrase: 18.3: the insensible man repents after overeating and soon gives way again, sighs after a passion and yields again, praises silence at length, and blames himself before others to angle for glory. 5.30: do not be surprised at falling daily and do not give up; fresh wounds heal easily, old neglected ones are hard to cure.
sources.translation: Lazarus Moore (1959), not public domain; paraphrase only

elements.name: Small frequent faults / careful in small things but a grave fall (Book III ch 33). Eastern support: PARTIAL (Climacus Step 5.30, paraphrase).
elements.what_it_is: The size and frequency of a person's faults. Gregory's gnat and camel.
everyday_signs: Many small slips that no one counts (Moralia XXXI.87).
A careful life with an occasional big fall (Book III ch 33, in the README).
elements.hidden_side: New: big sins surprise a careless mind, while 'the smaller and the numberless pour themselves upon it in a whole body' (Moralia XXXI.87). Small faults work like an army, not a raid. New: the humble use their small sins to grow, and the proud use their small good deeds to sin more (Moralia XXXIV.45).
elements.disguise: None stated in these texts.
elements.counsel: Climacus (5.30, paraphrase): fresh wounds heal easily; old neglected ones need much treatment.
elements.links: After a mistake (the same healing picture).

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: But while the greater and the few surprise a neglected mind, the smaller and the numberless pour themselves upon it in a whole body.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: when these make use of their slight sins for their advance in virtue, and those avail themselves of their smallest good deeds to add to their sin.

elements.name: Never begin / never finish (Book III ch 34). Eastern support: PARTIAL (Nazianzen 2.30, the sluggish 'hard to rouse').
elements.what_it_is: Starting versus following through.
everyday_signs: Wanting a better life but picturing every setback, and so not starting (Moralia XXX.51).
Giving way 'at the very beginning' when work piles up (Moralia VI.57).
elements.hidden_side: Never begin, new: fear of uncertain future troubles, 'the way of the slothful is as an hedge of thorns' (Moralia XXX.51). Moralia VI.57 ties not beginning to an inactive make-up, not only to laziness.
elements.disguise: Fear as caution (Moralia XXXI.59, see forward/faint-hearted).
elements.counsel: Nazianzen 2.30: the sluggish are 'stirred up by being smitten with the word'. Moralia VI.58: love is what moves inactive souls to work.
elements.links: Slothful/hasty; forward/faint-hearted.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For they place many things before their eyes, on the occurrence of which in their course of life, they are afraid that they can not stand firm.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: often at one and the same time love stimulates inactive souls to work, and fear keeps back restless souls in the exercise of contemplation.

elements.name: Better in public / better in private (Book III ch 35). Eastern support: YES (Chrysostom III.14 and V.4; Nazianzen 2.31; Climacus Step 22, paraphrase).
elements.what_it_is: Whether a person's goodness shows more in public or in private, and how they treat their reputation.
everyday_signs: Doing well in private but never tested (Chrysostom III.14, the athlete at home).
Not caring what people think, even when a false story spreads (Chrysostom V.4).
Living one life outwardly and another in thought (Climacus 22.28, paraphrase).
elements.hidden_side: Better in private, new: seclusion can hide weakness. 'An athlete, as long as he remains at home ... can dissemble his weakness', and it shows only in the contest (Chrysostom III.14). Better in public: vainglory makes a double life (Climacus 22.28, paraphrase). Some hide their delight in praise and never show it (Moralia XXII.17).
elements.disguise: Indifference to reputation can look like humility. Chrysostom says it should not be total.
elements.counsel: Chrysostom V.4 matches Book III ch 35's counsel for those who let evil be thought of them. Do not fear slander too much, but do not 'entirely pass over' it either. Try to put out a false report at once, then stop worrying if people will not be persuaded.
elements.links: Impatient/patient and meek (untested calm). Impudent/bashful (public or private rebuke, Nazianzen 2.31).

sources.work: John Chrysostom, On the Priesthood
sources.quote: So an athlete, as long as he remains at home, and contends with no one, can dissemble his weakness even if it be very great, but when he strips for the contest he is easily detected.

sources.work: John Chrysostom, On the Priesthood
sources.quote: it is well that he should neither fear nor tremble at excessively, nor entirely pass over; but we ought, though it happen to be false, or to be brought against us by the common herd, to try and extinguish it immediately.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: And there are some whom praise so puffs up that it forces them on even to words of self-exalting. But some, as we said before, are ashamed to lay open this same thing, that they are lifted up

sources.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
sources.paraphrase: The one sold to vainglory lives a double life: outwardly among the monks, in mind and thought in the world.
sources.translation: Lazarus Moore (1959), not public domain; paraphrase only

elements.name: What helps you: led by reasons or by example (Book III ch 6, wise / dull). Eastern support: YES, direct (Nazianzen 2.30 and 2.45).
elements.what_it_is: How a person is best moved. The README uses ch 6 for 'what helps you' rather than as a pair. Nazianzen states the same split in plain words, along with the other modes of treatment.
everyday_signs: Moved by argument, or moved by seeing someone live it (Nazianzen 2.30).
Needs simple basics first, or is annoyed by them and needs solid food (Nazianzen 2.45).
Does better with praise or with blame, with encouragement or with rebuke, in public or in private (Nazianzen 2.31).
elements.hidden_side: Nazianzen 2.33: no treatment is simply good. Severity or gentleness 'in some cases ... proves good and useful, in others again it has the contrary effect'. So 'what helps you' is part of the reading, not an extra.
elements.disguise: None.
elements.counsel: The full Eastern menu (Nazianzen 2.30-32): doctrine or example; spur or curb; praise or blame; encouragement or rebuke; public or private correction; close watch or 'seeing not to see'; feigned anger or feigned despair, used for the person's good; condescension and hope; to conquer some and be overcome by others.
elements.links: Each mode maps to a pair: spur/curb to slothful/hasty; public/private to impudent/bashful; close watch/hope to forward/faint-hearted.

sources.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
sources.quote: Some are led by doctrine, others trained by example; some need the spur, others the curb; some are sluggish and hard to rouse to the good, and must be stirred up by being smitten with the word; others are immoderately fervent in spirit, with impulses difficult to restrain, like thoroughbred colts, who run wide of the turning post, and to improve them the word must have a restraining and checking influence.

sources.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
sources.quote: Some are benefited by praise, others by blame, both being applied in season; while if out of season, or unreasonable, they are injurious; some are set right by encouragement, others by rebuke; some, when taken to task in public, others, when privately corrected.

sources.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
sources.quote: In some cases we must even be angry, without feeling angry, or treat them with a disdain we do not feel, or manifest despair, though we do not really despair of them, according to the needs of their nature.

sources.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
sources.quote: For some need to be fed with the milk of the most simple and elementary doctrines

elements.name: EXTRA TYPOLOGY (not one of the pairs): four dispositions and the temptation fitted to each (Moralia XXIX.45)
elements.what_it_is: Gregory's own four-way sorting of 'character' (conspersio): cheerful, morose, timid, proud. The enemy first studies which one you are, then sets the trap next to it. Cassian gives the Eastern parallel: evil spirits read which passion a person is 'especially disposed' to from outward signs (Conference 7.15). This is the one place where the tradition plainly sorts people into a small set of types. It is not the four humours; Gregory does not mention them.
everyday_signs: Cheerful: tempted by pleasure.
Morose: tempted to anger and discord.
Timid: controlled by threats and fear of punishment.
Proud: led anywhere by flattering applause.
elements.hidden_side: The trap always fits the temperament. The greedy are not tempted by the pride of fasting, and the abstinent are not tempted by food. The gentle are not tempted to fight, and the angry are not tempted by fear (XXIX.45).
elements.counsel: Implied, not stated: know your disposition so you know where the trap will be set. Cassian 5.27 says the same about the main fault: begin the fight where you are attacked most.
elements.links: Cheerful and morose = joyful/sad (Book III ch 3). Timid = faint-hearted/bashful. Proud = haughty/forward.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For the ancient enemy first beholds the character [‘conspersionem’] of each person, and then applies the snares of temptations. For one person is of a cheerful, another of a morose, another of a timid, another of a proud disposition.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: even clever men can often discover the state of the inner man from his mien and look and external bearing.

elements.name: EXTRA TYPOLOGY: four speeds of anger (Moralia V.80), with Cassian's three kinds of anger
elements.what_it_is: A two-by-two grid Gregory states himself. Anger catches fast or slow, and lets go fast or slow. 'Kindled reeds' flare and cool; 'harder kinds of wood' are slow to light and slow to go out. Quick to catch and slow to let go is 'the worst'. Slow to catch and quick to let go comes nearest to peace. Cassian (Conference 5.11) gives the Eastern parallel: anger that rages inside, anger that breaks out in word and deed, and anger that lasts for days.
everyday_signs: Crackles loudly, then is over (reeds).
Slow to anger, then holds it a long time (hard wood).
Quick and lasting (worst).
Slow and brief (best).
elements.hidden_side: The slow-to-anger type can look meek while holding a grudge for a long time.
elements.counsel: The two remedies of Moralia V.81 (see impatient/patient).
elements.links: Feeds meek/passionate and impatient/patient.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: But we are to know that there be some, whom anger is somewhat prompt in inflaming, but quickly leaves them; while there are others whom it is slow in exciting, but the longer in retaining possession of.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Others again, and their conduct is the worst, are both quick in catching the flames of anger, and slow in letting them go; and others both catch them slowly, and part with them quickly.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: the third, which is not like those in boiling over and being done with in an hour, but which lasts for days and long periods

elements.name: EXTRA TYPOLOGY: four sorts of speakers (Moralia VIII.58), and the two kinds of starter (Moralia III.23)
elements.what_it_is: A second two-by-two grid Gregory states himself: depth of thought against ease of expression. (1) Full in both: praiseworthy. (2) Meagre in both: deserves pity. (3) Fluent but shallow: the only blameworthy one. (4) Deep but tongue-tied: 'calls for aid'. Moralia III.23 adds a separate split: hasty starters who never check themselves, and slow starters who cannot stop once they begin.
everyday_signs: Says a lot with little behind it.
Thinks deeply but cannot get it out.
Slow to start talking, then cannot stop.
elements.hidden_side: The deep but silent person may look dull and needs help, not blame (VIII.58).
elements.counsel: The fourth sort 'calls for aid'. The third 'ought to be restrained' (VIII.58, same passage).
elements.links: Silent/talkative; what helps you (wise/dull).

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For there be some whom fulness in speaking and thinking combined give width and compass, and there be some whom meagreness both of thought and utterance reduces to small dimensions; and there are some who are furnished with ability in speaking, but not with penetration in thinking; and there are some, who have penetration of thought to support them, but from barrenness of expression are made silent.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For the first is worthy of praise, in that it is powerful and strong in both particulars. The second deserves commiseration, which in its littleness lacks both. The fourth calls for aid, in that it has not power to embody what it thinks.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: For there are some men who both begin to speak with precipitation, and follow out that unchecked beginning with still less check. While there are some who are indeed backward to begin to speak, but having once begun know not how to set limits to their words.

elements.name: EXTRA TYPOLOGY: active or contemplative, inactive or restless souls (Moralia VI.57-58)
elements.what_it_is: Gregory says some minds suit the active life and some the contemplative life, and he ties this to how souls are made. It is the clearest statement in these sources that a person has a lasting make-up, not only habits. It also answers 'where do I serve best?', which bears on 'who you are in the Body'.
everyday_signs: Crushed by too much business (the tranquil or inactive).
Worse off when idle (the restless).
elements.hidden_side: Restless minds that force themselves into deep contemplation can 'launch out even to the length of wrong doctrines' (Moralia VI.57, paraphrase of the same section).
elements.counsel: The tranquil should not overload with works. The restless should not stint their work for contemplation. Love moves the one and fear anchors the other (VI.57-58).
elements.links: Slothful/hasty; never begin.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: Whence it behoves that neither the tranquil mind should open itself wide in the immoderate exercising of works, nor the restless mind stint itself in devotion to contemplation.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
sources.quote: if it were not that the contemplative life suited some minds more than the active life, the Lord would never say by the voice of the Psalmist, Be still, and know that I am God.

elements.name: EXTRA LAYER: natural leaning versus won virtue (Climacus), and the redeemed temperament (Gregory)
elements.what_it_is: An Eastern answer to 'who am I in Christ?'. Climacus says some people are by nature inclined to temperance, silence, purity, modesty, meekness or contrition. Others fight their own nature for these, and those who struggle rank higher, even when they sometimes lose (Ladder 26.28, paraphrase). Gregory adds that a temperament can be turned to God's service: anger under reason becomes holy zeal, and pride under the fear of God becomes bold authority for justice (Moralia III.70). So a leaning is a gift or a battleground, never a verdict.
elements.hidden_side: A natural gift is not yet a virtue. Climacus warns against pride in 'natural advantages' such as cleverness or quick understanding (Ladder 22.31, paraphrase).
elements.counsel: Moralia III.70: 'we turn even those very evil habits to the account of virtue' by bracing against them.
elements.links: Every pair.

sources.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
sources.paraphrase: 26.28: some, he does not know why, are by nature inclined to temperance, silence, purity, modesty, meekness or contrition; others force themselves against their own nature and, though sometimes defeated, are higher. 22.31: do not be proud of gifts received without labour, such as cleverness, ability to learn and quick understanding.

elements.what_it_is: Cassian says the eight faults attack everyone but not in the same way. In one person a single fault 'holds the chief place', so each person should begin the battle where he is attacked most. This is the Eastern support for the README's 'Start here' (Book III ch 38: treat first the fault with 'the more rapid tendency to death').
elements.counsel: Begin the fight where the attack on you is strongest (Conference 5.27).
elements.links: The result's 'Start here' section.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.quote: Although then these eight faults trouble all sorts of men, yet they do not attack them all in the same way. For in one man the spirit of fornication holds the chief place: wrath rides rough shod over another: over another vainglory claims dominion: in an other pride holds the field

key_passages.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus)
key_passages.quote: For the guiding of man, the most variable and manifold of creatures, seems to me in very deed to be the art of arts and science of sciences.
key_passages.paraphrase: Guiding people is the hardest art, because people vary so much. This is the start of the physician-of-souls section (16-34).
key_passages.translation: NPNF 2nd series vol. 7 (1894), tr. C.G. Browne and J.E. Swallow; New Advent, cross-checked against CCEL

key_passages.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
key_passages.quote: For men and women, young and old, rich and poor, the sanguine and despondent, the sick and whole, rulers and ruled, the wise and ignorant, the cowardly and courageous, the wrathful and meek, the successful and failing, do not require the same instruction and encouragement.
key_passages.paraphrase: Section 29 extends the list: married and unmarried, hermits and those in community, the advanced and the barely-holding-on, townsfolk and rustics, the simple and the designing, men of business and men of leisure, those in reverses and the prosperous.

key_passages.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
key_passages.quote: Some are benefited by praise, others by blame, both being applied in season; while if out of season, or unreasonable, they are injurious; some are set right by encouragement, others by rebuke; some, when taken to task in public, others, when privately corrected.
key_passages.paraphrase: With section 30 (doctrine or example, spur or curb) and section 32 (close watch or looking away, feigned anger, condescension and hope), this is the Eastern source of Book III's 'how to speak to each'.

key_passages.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
key_passages.quote: just as it is not safe for those who walk on a lofty tight rope to lean to either side, for even though the inclination seems slight, it has no slight consequences, but their safety depends upon their perfect balance
key_passages.paraphrase: No remedy is good in every case ('our treatment does not correspond with virtue and vice'). The way is the King's highway, turning neither right nor left. This is the Eastern basis for 'neither pole is the good one'. Cassian gives the same picture: discretion walks 'the royal road', avoiding 'excess on either side' (Conference 2.2).

key_passages.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2
key_passages.quote: it is absolutely necessary that its ruler should be at once simple in his uprightness in all respects, and as far as possible manifold and varied in his treatment of individuals, and in dealing with all in an appropriate and suitable manner.
key_passages.paraphrase: The Church is like one animal made of many different animals, each moved differently by the same words or touch. This is useful for 'who you are in the Body'.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule
key_passages.quote: For, as long before us Gregory Nazianzen of reverend memory has taught, one and the same exhortation does not suit all, inasmuch as neither are all bound together by similarity of character.
key_passages.paraphrase: Gregory credits Nazianzen by name. The harp image follows: one quill, many strokes, one tune.
key_passages.translation: NPNF 2nd series vol. 12 (1895), tr. James Barmby; cross-checked against CCEL

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.locus: Book XXX, ch. iii, sections 11-13 (on Job 38:36, the cock given understanding)
key_passages.quote: We ought indeed to mention minutely what course of advice should be observed in each particular case, but are hindered by fear of prolixity in our remarks.
key_passages.paraphrase: Gregory's first draft of the Book III list, with the same prologue images (herbs, hissing, harp strings). He says he hopes to treat each kind 'in another work'. The Oxford translator's brackets identify that work as the Pastoral Rule and cite 'S. Greg. Naz. Or. 2. §. 28'. Those brackets are the translator's, not Gregory's.
key_passages.translation: Morals on the Book of Job, Library of the Fathers, Oxford 1844-1850

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: of souls are infinitely varied one with another, for there are some of such inactivity of mind, that, if the labours of business fall upon them, they give way at the very beginning of their work, and there be some so restless, that if they have cessation from labour, they have only the worse labour, in that they are subject to worse tumults of mind, in proportion as they have more time and liberty for their thoughts.
key_passages.paraphrase: The sentence opens: 'the compositions [conspersio, dough, paste.]', a word for a person's make-up. It is the strongest text that souls differ by constitution.

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: For the ancient enemy first beholds the character [‘conspersionem’] of each person, and then applies the snares of temptations. For one person is of a cheerful, another of a morose, another of a timid, another of a proud disposition.
key_passages.paraphrase: The source of Book III ch 3's joyful -> lust and sad -> anger.

key_passages.work: John Chrysostom, On the Priesthood
key_passages.quote: Therefore the pastor has need of much discretion, and of a myriad eyes to observe on every side the habit of the soul.
key_passages.paraphrase: Fit the treatment to the disposition of the sinner, not only to the size of the offence (same section; New Advent spells it 'offense', the original NPNF 'offence'). Book VI section 4: 'it is not possible to treat all those under one's charge on one plan'.
key_passages.translation: NPNF 1st series vol. 9 (1889), tr. W.R.W. Stephens

key_passages.work: John Cassian, Conferences
key_passages.quote: each one of us ought also to begin the battle with due regard to the character of the attack which is especially made on him
key_passages.paraphrase: Each person is attacked differently, and in each one fault 'holds the chief place'. Start there. This is the Eastern twin of Book III ch 38.
key_passages.translation: NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), tr. Edgar C.S. Gibson

key_passages.work: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
key_passages.quote: Since, therefore, error is corrected with more difficulty, when it is believed to be a virtue
key_passages.paraphrase: The fullest list of vices passing as virtues: cruelty as justice, anger as zeal, remissness as gentleness, lavishness as compassion, tenacity as frugality, pertinacity as constancy, inconstancy as tractability, fear as humility, haughtiness as freedom, sloth as peace, restlessness as watchfulness, haste as zeal, slowness as judgment. It is richer than Pastoral Rule II.9.

key_passages.work: John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent
key_passages.paraphrase: 28: some are by nature inclined to particular virtues; those who fight their nature rank higher. 58: vices come up hidden in virtues, like a frog in well water (meekness can hide procrastination and wilfulness, silence can hide contempt of instruction, joy can hide conceit, quietness can hide despondency and sloth).

report.orthodox_standing:
All the main authors are saints received by the Orthodox Church.
- Gregory of Nazianzus: saint, called 'the Theologian', one of the Three Holy Hierarchs. Oration 2 is the classic Eastern text on pastoral care, and Gregory the Great credits it by name.
- John Chrysostom: saint, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs. The Divine Liturgy most used in the Orthodox Church bears his name.
- Gregory the Great: venerated in the Orthodox Church as St Gregory the Dialogist. He is pre-schism, and the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts is traditionally attributed to him. The Moralia is a Latin work. How widely it was read in the East was not checked. A report that the Pastoral Rule was put into Greek in his lifetime was NOT verified here, so do not state it.
- John Cassian: venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church. The Philokalia includes texts of his on the eight vices and on discernment; which exact chapters was not rechecked here. The Conferences quoted (2, 5, 7) are his, in the NPNF translation.
- John Climacus: saint. The Fourth Sunday of Great Lent is dedicated to him, and the Ladder is standard Lenten reading. 'To the Shepherd' is his short letter to the abbot of Raithu, often attached to the Ladder.
No post-schism Western author was used.
report.measurement_notes:
What the sources say shows a trait in everyday life. These are notes for the main session, not quiz items.
- How correction lands: in public or in private (Nazianzen 2.31); reproach or hardship hurts more (Moralia VII.1); numb or over-feeling under correction (Moralia II.28); severity crushes, or leniency makes careless (Chrysostom II.4).
- Hardship versus success: affliction steadies some and drives others to impatience; prosperity calms some and sets others adrift (Moralia V.16).
- Anger speed: quick or slow to catch, quick or slow to let go (Moralia V.80). Anger held in: silently composing speeches (V.79); arguing with an absent person when alone (Climacus 8.13).
- Idle time versus a full load: which one makes things worse (Moralia VI.57). Listlessness as sleepiness or as the urge to leave (Cassian 5.11).
- Talk: how one starts and stops (Moralia III.23); depth of thought against ease of words (VIII.58); flattering or carping (VII.57); silence from bitterness (XXXIV.51).
- Others' success: reaction to hearing someone else praised (Chrysostom V.4; Moralia V.85).
- Money: grasping to look bigger or out of fear of want (Moralia XV.30); wanting back what one gave (Cassian 5.11).
- Eating: too early, too fussy, too carefully prepared, too much, too eagerly (Moralia XXX.60); asking the host for extras (Cassian 5.11).
- Pride's outward marks: loud speech, bitter silence, anger in sorrow, rancour in reply, wanting to be made to do what one wants (Moralia XXXIV.52).
- After a fall: regret and repeat, or stop without regret (Climacus 18.3; Moralia X.28, XXXI.93).
- Reputation: indifference to a false report (Chrysostom V.4).
Several of these, above all anger speed, idle versus overloaded, speaker type and the root of grasping, are concrete everyday behaviours with a clear source. They are better material than abstract self-ratings. Cassian 7.15 says an inner state shows in 'mien and look and external bearing'; the sources assume behaviour reveals the disposition.
report.report_layer_ideas:
Ideas for what these sources could honestly feed. No copy is written here.
1. 'Your leanings' (the pairs as rails): each pair now has more hidden sides and counsel from the Moralia and the Eastern Fathers (see elements). Mark the pairs with Eastern support.
2. 'Your disposition': Gregory's own four (cheerful, morose, timid, proud), each with the temptation fitted to it (Moralia XXIX.45). This is the one source-given 'type' headline. Present it as a lens, since Pastoral Rule III.37 says traits mix.
3. 'Your fire': the anger-speed grid (Moralia V.80) with Cassian's three kinds (inward, outward, lasting) and the two remedies (V.81).
4. 'Your voice': the speaker grid (Moralia VIII.58), starter type (III.23), and flattering versus carping (VII.57).
5. 'Where you serve best': active or contemplative, restless or tranquil (Moralia VI.57-58). This ties to 'who you are in the Body'.
6. 'How your weakness disguises itself': the disguise list (Moralia XXXII.45, Pastoral Rule II.9) and each vice's 'as if with reason' argument (XXXI.90). This is the 'aha' material.
7. 'What helps you': Nazianzen's menu (2.30-32), each choice keyed to a pair.
8. 'Start here': Cassian 5.13/27 and Pastoral Rule III.38 agree, East and West.
9. 'Gift or battle': Climacus 26.28 (a natural leaning is a gift, not a virtue; the struggle ranks higher) and Moralia III.70 (anger -> holy zeal, pride -> authority for justice). An honest, hopeful 'who you are in Christ' frame.
10. 'In the Body': Nazianzen 2.44 (one creature of many natures) and the harp in the Book III prologue and Moralia XXX.12 (one quill, many strokes, one tune).
11. A Christian counterpart to 'famous people who share your type', using only the figures the sources themselves attach. Envy: Cain, Esau, Joseph's brothers, Saul (Moralia V.84). Zeal versus laxity: Phinehas versus Eli (V.82). Slow starters who could not stop: Job's friends (III.23). Gluttony's five ways: Jonathan, the Israelites, Eli's sons, Sodom, Esau (XXX.60). True humility: David (XXVII.78). Dove and fire: Titus and Timothy (Book III ch 16, README).
risks: The Eastern texts do not sort people into personality types. Their lists mix temperament with rank, health, marriage and fortune. A 16-type system would be invention. Use leanings and the few typologies the sources give themselves.

Five README items have little or no Eastern support in these texts, only Gregory's: kindly/envious, givers/takers, at variance/at peace, sowers of strife/peacemakers, obstinate/fickle. Do not label them 'Eastern'.

Much of the pastoral material is addressed to pastors (the 'ruler'), not hearers. Chrysostom III.14 is about himself, and II.4 is about penance. Turning it into self-knowledge for readers is a reasonable reading but a transfer. Say what the text is about.

Moralia text: an 1844-50 Oxford translation, from an online transcription recovered from the Wayback Machine. Some chapter markers may be missing and there are a few typing slips. Cite by book and section. No quote used contains a slip.
New Advent revises NPNF spelling slightly ('offense' for 'offence' in Chrysostom II.4). Every NPNF quote was cross-checked against the original CCEL text.

Climacus is paraphrase only (Moore 1959 is not public domain). 'To the Shepherd' was seen only in chapters 1-4 of a 2020 amateur translation (PG 88:1165B-1173A). Chapters 5 onward were not read. Do not claim anything else from it.

The footnote at Ladder Step 22.31 in Moore's edition ('many people are naturally meek ... it is no virtue to be naturally a small eater') may be the editor's note or a scholion, not Climacus. Do not attribute it to him without checking.

Gregory's four dispositions (cheerful, morose, timid, proud) invite comparison with the four humours. Gregory does not mention humours. Nazianzen only compares soul-differences loosely to 'mixtures and blendings of the elements'. Do not claim a humoral basis.
The Moralia translator renders the Book III 'simple / insincere' slot as 'the pure / the unclean' (XXX.13). The Latin was not checked. Do not lean on either English label.
Tone: most of this material names vices. The owner wants engaging, not accusing. The disguise lists are powerful but can read as indictments if shown raw.
Dates were not checked beyond what the texts say. The oration's circumstances (ordination 361, return 362) come from the NPNF introduction.
