report.summary: Research only; no questions or result copy. I read the Book III pairs (README), the Book III text, and bible-figure.ts (the site already uses Peter, Moses, David, Elijah, Paul, Barnabas, Martha, Abigail, John the Baptist, Jonathan, Gideon and others). I fetched 33 texts and saved each as plain text. 251 verbatim lines were machine-checked; all pass. Axis labels such as III.16 are Gregory's Pastoral Rule Book III chapters; III.36 is his four-pair shortlist. BSB = Berean Standard Bible (public domain). FINDING 1: Scripture records acts, and seldom names a temperament. Stated outright: Moses humble (Num 12:3), Elijah zealous (his words), Jonah angry, Saul jealous, Nabal harsh, Martha worried and upset, Abigail intelligent, Barnabas Son of Encouragement, Nathanael without deceit, Caleb a different spirit, Diotrephes loves to be first. Everything else is read from events. FINDING 2: Gregory himself ties few Bible people to his pairs. Book III: Titus meeker and Timothy more fervid (16), Nabal and Abigail (16), Asahel's fury (16), Cain's envy (10), Hobab haughty (17), Jehoshaphat at peace with the wicked (22), Balaam (30). Books I and II: Saul humble then proud, Eli soft, David's fall after ease, Isaiah eager and Jeremiah reluctant, Moses both, Peter taking correction. Every other link is ours and is marked 'our match'. FINDING 3: A few Father passages read individuals' tempers directly. These are the best anchors for 'people who share your temperament': Chrysostom on Peter and John ('their several tempers': Peter more fervent, John more lofty), on Peter's temper (not cautious, more vehement), on Thomas (two faults of belief, he the over-curious one), Paul's awe beside Barnabas' kindness, Moses meek beside Elijah zealous; Nazianzen's list of one gift per person (Job patience, Moses and David meekness, Peter and Paul eagerness); Gregory's Titus and Timothy. FINDING 4, for 'who you are in the Body of Christ': the Fathers pair opposite tempers as partners, not as better and worse. Isaiah and Jeremiah answered differently 'from the same fountain of love' (Gregory I.7). Nazianzen says neither the eager nor the reluctant was blamed. Paul and Barnabas contended but the gain came 'to one and the same end' (Chrysostom). John recognised the Lord first, Peter reached Him first. Gregory III.10: what you love in another becomes yours. FINDING 5: the Fathers defend the saints. Chrysostom denies Paul's anger at the high priest, calls the Paul and Barnabas split no enmity, reads Peter at Antioch as staged, and denies Timothy was timid. So saints sit best on their strong poles. The vice poles are shown most clearly by non-saints (Saul, Nabal, Cain, Esau, Eli, Rehoboam), which suit a 'worth watching' line, not a match. Strongest pole coverage: hasty (Peter), meek (Moses, Titus), passionate/zealous (Elijah, Paul, Timothy per Gregory, James and John), bashful/timid (Moses, Jeremiah, Gideon, Saul before his reign), humble then haughty (Saul, per Gregory), envious (Saul, Cain), kindly (John the Baptist, Jonathan, Barnabas), patient (David at Shimei, Job, Stephen), sad with anger (Jonah), sad (Jeremiah), restless (Martha), soft (Eli), peacemaker (Abigail), stingy keeper (Nabal), lavish (Mary of Bethany, the widow), gluttonous (Esau), abstinent (John the Baptist, Daniel), obstinate (Rehoboam, Thomas), careful in small things then a grave fall (David). Is this a kinds-of-people source? Scripture is narrative, not a typology; Gregory supplies the kinds. The figures can illustrate his kinds, with about one to four well-attested people per pole, and several poles have none (see coverage_gaps). The full report is also saved as report-final.json in the sources folder.

figures.name: Peter (Simon Peter)
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint. First among the apostles; the Fathers quoted here are all received in the Orthodox Church.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/figures/peter.jpg (Dore, St Peter at the House of Cornelius; low resolution, 562 px). Also public domain on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gustave_Doré,_St_Peter_Denying_Christ.jpg (750 px).

traits.evidence: When John says it is the Lord, Peter throws on his garment and jumps into the sea.

source.quote: he put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea.

traits.axis: III.15 slothful / hasty; III.14 silent / talkative
traits.evidence: At the Transfiguration he speaks up although, Mark says, he did not know what to say.

source.quote: For they were all so terrified that Peter did not know what else to say.

traits.evidence: He promises he alone will never fall away. That night he denies Jesus three times, then weeps bitterly (Matthew 26:75).

source.quote: Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will.

traits.axis: Gregory III.37 one person with contrary traits (a habit of haste, then a sudden fear)
traits.evidence: He walks on the water, then sees the wind and is afraid. Gregory III.37 describes exactly this mix but names no one; the match to Peter is ours.

source.quote: But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid

traits.axis: III.15 slothful / hasty; III.8 forward / faint-hearted
traits.evidence: Chrysostom calls Peter ardent everywhere and always first forward.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew (tr. Prevost/Riddle, NPNF 1/10 (1888), print wording)
source.quote: What then saith Peter, everywhere ardent, and ever starting forward before the rest?

traits.axis: III.15 slothful / hasty; III.16 meek / passionate
traits.evidence: Chrysostom names it a temper: not cautious, but fervent in love, more vehement than the others and rushing into danger.

source.work: Chrysostom, Commentary on Galatians (tr. Alexander, NPNF 1/13 (1889))
source.locus: on Gal 2:11 (New Advent titles it Homily 2 on Galatians)
source.quote: These words evince, if not a cautious temper, at least a fervent love; and in all instances we find him more vehement than the others, and rushing forward into danger.

traits.evidence: Gregory's example of a ruler who takes correction from one under him (Paul at Antioch).

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book II (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: For hence Peter willingly accepted Paul's rebuke

traits.axis: III.18 obstinate / fickle; III.36 shortlist: proud / timid
traits.evidence: At Antioch he drew back from Gentile believers for fear of the circumcision group. Scripture says fear; see the next line for Chrysostom.

source.quote: he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group.

traits.axis: III.18 obstinate / fickle; III.36 shortlist: proud / timid
traits.evidence: Chrysostom denies that Antioch shows Peter's fear or hypocrisy. He reads it as a scene both apostles staged to teach. Do not build a result on Galatians 2 if the Fathers are the foundation.

source.work: Chrysostom, Commentary on Galatians (tr. Alexander, NPNF 1/13 (1889))
source.quote: Many, on a superficial reading of this part of the Epistle, suppose that Paul accused Peter of hypocrisy. But this is not so

traits.axis: Body of Christ: opposite tempers as partners
traits.evidence: Chrysostom calls these their "several tempers": John sees first, Peter reaches Him first. Both serve.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on John (tr. Marriott, NPNF 1/14 (1889))
source.quote: the disciples Peter and John again exhibited the peculiarities of their several tempers. The one was more fervent, the other more lofty; the one more keen, the other more clear-sighted. On this account John first recognized Jesus, Peter first came to Him.

figures.name: Thomas (Didymus)
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: No Dore plate of Thomas in the two Commons Dore categories. Public domain on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Incredulity_of_Saint_Thomas-Caravaggio_(1601-2).jpg (Caravaggio). It shows a finger in the wound; the site's no-violence rule may exclude it.

traits.axis: Chrysostom, Homily 87 on John: believing too easily / demanding proof beyond measure (nearest Gregory III.18 obstinate / fickle)
traits.pole: demands proof; will not take others' word
traits.evidence: Chrysostom names two opposite faults of belief and puts Thomas on one: too curious, not too easy.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on John (tr. Marriott, NPNF 1/14 (1889))
source.quote: As to believe carelessly and in a random way, comes of an over-easy temper; so to be beyond measure curious and meddlesome, marks a most gross understanding. On this account Thomas is held to blame.

traits.evidence: Told by the other disciples, he refuses to believe without touching the wounds. A week later he says "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28).

source.quote: I will never believe.

traits.evidence: John 11:16 "Let us also go, so that we may die with Him." Many readers hear courage. Chrysostom says it was cowardice and rejects the courage reading.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on John (tr. Marriott, NPNF 1/14 (1889))
source.quote: Some say that he desired himself to die; but it is not so; the expression is rather one of cowardice.

traits.evidence: Chrysostom's arc: weak before the Crucifixion, stronger than all afterwards.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on John (tr. Marriott, NPNF 1/14 (1889))
source.quote: but afterwards he became stronger than all, and invincible.

figures.name: James and John, sons of Zebedee
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint. John is honoured as "the Theologian". Casting him as the angry type will jar Orthodox readers; see the Nazianzen line.
figures.portrait: No Dore plate of the brothers found in the two Commons Dore categories. Not checked further.

traits.evidence: Jesus names them Boanerges, Sons of Thunder. Scripture does not say why.

source.quote: whom He named Boanerges

traits.pole: passionate: anger taken for zeal (Gregory's hidden side, our match)
traits.evidence: A Samaritan village refuses Jesus. They offer to call down fire. Jesus turns and rebukes them (Luke 9:55).

source.quote: Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?

traits.evidence: Chrysostom: Jesus was "training them to forbearance" when they asked for fire.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew (tr. Prevost/Riddle, NPNF 1/10 (1888), print wording)
source.quote: training them to forbearance by the superiority in their gift.

traits.axis: III.8 forward / faint-hearted; III.17 humble / haughty
traits.evidence: They ask for the seats at His right and left. Asked if they can drink His cup, they say "We can" (Mark 10:39).

source.quote: Grant that one of us may sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left in Your glory.

traits.evidence: Gregory Nazianzen reads the name as grandeur of speech, not temper. He lists Bible figures by their one gift.

source.quote: the sons of Zebedee magniloquence, whence also they were entitled Sons of thunder.

traits.axis: Body of Christ: opposite tempers as partners
traits.evidence: Chrysostom: John recognised the Lord first; Peter reached Him first.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on John (tr. Marriott, NPNF 1/14 (1889))
source.quote: the disciples Peter and John again exhibited the peculiarities of their several tempers. The one was more fervent, the other more lofty; the one more keen, the other more clear-sighted. On this account John first recognized Jesus, Peter first came to Him.

figures.name: Martha of Bethany
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint. Honoured with her sister among the Myrrhbearers.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/figures/martha.jpg (Dore, Jesus talks with Mary and Martha in their house; low resolution, 482 px).

traits.evidence: Distracted by the preparations, she asks Jesus to make Mary help (10:40). This is His answer.

source.quote: you are worried and upset about many things.

traits.axis: Chrysostom: which sister was more zealous
traits.evidence: Chrysostom denies Martha was the more zealous. He calls her the weaker in faith (John 11:39). This ranks the sisters.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on John (tr. Marriott, NPNF 1/14 (1889))
source.quote: She was not more zealous, but it was because the other had not yet been informed, since Martha was the weaker.

traits.axis: Cassian: two kinds of work, active / contemplative
traits.evidence: Cassian reads the sisters as two ways of life and says the Lord ranked Mary's higher. The Fathers sort activities here, not kinds of people.

source.quote: she is shown by the Lord to have chosen the better part

figures.name: Mary of Bethany
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint. The Orthodox Church keeps her distinct from Mary Magdalene, who is already a figure on the site.
figures.portrait: Shares Martha's Dore plate on the site (site/public/img/figures/martha.jpg).

traits.axis: III.36 shortlist: restless (unquiet) / listless (the quiet side, not listless)
traits.evidence: She sits at the Lord's feet listening. Gregory's opposite of the unquiet is the listless, which she is not. She does not fit a Gregory pole cleanly.

source.quote: who sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message.

traits.evidence: She pours a pint of expensive nard on Jesus' feet. Some called it waste (Mark 14:4). Jesus defends her. Gregory's lavish pole is a fault; hers is praised.

source.quote: Then Mary took about a pint of expensive perfume, made of pure nard, and she anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped them with her hair.

figures.name: Judas Iscariot
figures.orthodox_standing: Not venerated; the betrayer.
figures.portrait: Not needed as a result figure.

traits.axis: III.20-21 givers / takers; keepers / give-and-take; III.36 shortlist: stingy / lavish
traits.pole: taker; greed dressed as care for the poor
traits.evidence: He objects that the perfume should have gone to the poor. John says he said it because he was a thief. Compare Gregory II.9: vices pass for virtues.

source.quote: Judas did not say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief.

figures.name: Moses
figures.kind: Bible figure (Old Testament), prophet and lawgiver
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint. Called God-seer.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/dore-moses.jpg (Dore, Moses Breaks the Tables of the Law). Note it shows the anger scene.

traits.axis: III.17 humble / haughty; III.16 meek / passionate
traits.evidence: Scripture's one direct description of his character. The BSB says "humble"; older English Bibles say "meek".

source.quote: Now Moses was a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth.

traits.evidence: Chrysostom pairs the two as the models of meekness and of zeal.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew (tr. Prevost/Riddle, NPNF 1/10 (1888))
source.quote: that they should be meek like Moses, and jealous for God like Elias

traits.axis: III.15 slothful / hasty; III.16 meek / passionate
traits.pole: the fire in a meek man
traits.evidence: As a young man he kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew.

source.quote: After looking this way and that and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand.

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate; III.36 shortlist: wrathful / soft-hearted
traits.evidence: Seeing the calf, he burns with anger and shatters the tablets.

source.quote: he burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain.

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate; III.15 slothful / hasty
traits.evidence: At Meribah: "Listen now, you rebels". The Psalm says he spoke rashly (Psalm 106:33).

source.quote: Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?

traits.axis: III.7 impudent / bashful; III.17 humble / haughty (fear passing as humility); III.36 shortlist: proud / timid
traits.evidence: At the bush he asks God to send someone else. God's anger burns against him (Exodus 4:14).

source.quote: Please, Lord, send someone else.

traits.pole: humble, and not blamed for it
traits.evidence: Gregory counts Moses' reluctance true humility, because he obeyed in the end.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book I (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: Moses trembles though God persuades him

traits.evidence: Nazianzen pairs eager and reluctant men God called.

source.quote: Aaron was eager, but Moses resisted

traits.axis: III.8 forward / faint-hearted; III.3 joyful / sad (by temperament)
traits.evidence: Worn out by the people, he asks God to kill him.

source.quote: please kill me right now

traits.evidence: Joshua wants two men stopped from prophesying. Moses wishes all the Lord's people were prophets.

source.quote: Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets

figures.name: Elijah (Elias)
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/figures/elijah.jpg (Dore, Elijah Is Nourished by an Angel). That plate is the broom-tree scene of 1 Kings 19.

traits.evidence: His own words, twice (1 Kings 19:10, 14).

source.quote: I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts

traits.evidence: Cyril of Jerusalem speaks of the prophet's fiery zeal.

source.work: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures (tr. Gifford, NPNF 2/7 (1894), print wording)
source.quote: as if almost He would persuade the fiery zeal of the Prophet to condescend to the penitent.

traits.evidence: Chrysostom's pairing.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew (tr. Prevost/Riddle, NPNF 1/10 (1888))
source.quote: that they should be meek like Moses, and jealous for God like Elias

traits.axis: III.8 forward / faint-hearted; III.3 joyful / sad (by temperament)
traits.evidence: After Carmel, afraid of Jezebel, he flees and asks to die.

source.quote: Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.

traits.axis: Chrysostom: great in the great things, failing in the less
traits.evidence: Chrysostom names Elijah before Jezebel as this pattern.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew (tr. Prevost/Riddle, NPNF 1/10 (1888))
source.quote: For such a thing is human nature; not seldom effecting great things, it exposes itself in the less; as Elias felt toward Jezebel, as Moses toward the Egyptian, as David toward Bathsheba.

figures.name: Jonah
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: Public domain on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:138.Jonah_Preaches_to_the_Ninevites.jpg (Dore, 2313 px).

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate; III.36 shortlist: wrathful / soft-hearted
traits.evidence: God spares Nineveh. Jonah is greatly displeased and angry.

source.quote: Jonah, however, was greatly displeased, and he became angry.

traits.axis: III.3 joyful / sad (by temperament) (Gregory: "the sad have wrath close at hand")
traits.evidence: He asks to die. Sorrow and anger come together, as Gregory III.3 says they do. Gregory does not name Jonah; the match is ours.

source.quote: for it is better for me to die than to live.

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate (anger believed to be righteous)
traits.evidence: God questions whether his anger is right.

source.quote: Have you any right to be angry?

traits.axis: III.15 slothful / hasty; III.34 never begin / never finish
traits.evidence: He says he was quick to flee. The flight is in Jonah 1:3.

source.quote: This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish.

traits.evidence: Gregory Nazianzen defends Jonah: he fled out of sorrow at Israel's fall, not to escape God.

source.quote: and flung himself into the deep of sorrow

figures.name: Jeremiah
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: Public domain on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:123.The_Prophet_Jeremiah.jpg (Dore, 2322 px).

traits.axis: III.7 impudent / bashful; III.8 forward / faint-hearted; III.36 shortlist: proud / timid
traits.evidence: Called, he pleads that he is only a child.

source.quote: I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!

traits.evidence: Gregory: both answers came from the same love. Jeremiah loved quiet contemplation; Isaiah loved active service.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book I (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: Lo, from these two men different voices proceeded outwardly, but they flowed from the same fountain of love.

traits.evidence: He wishes his eyes were a fountain of tears.

source.quote: Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears!

traits.evidence: Gregory names Jeremiah's sorrow as a sorrow of love.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book II (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: the prophet Jeremiah, in the great sorrow of his charity

traits.axis: III.14 silent / talkative (Gregory: held-in words seethe inside)
traits.pole: silent who cannot hold it in (our match)
traits.evidence: He tries to stop speaking; the word burns in his bones. Gregory's over-silent keep grievances in; Jeremiah keeps God's word in. The match is partial.

source.quote: His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones, and I become weary of holding it in, and I cannot prevail.

figures.name: Isaiah
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: Public domain on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:120.The_Prophet_Isaiah.jpg (Dore, 2290 px).

traits.evidence: He volunteers. Gregory I.7 and Nazianzen (Oration 2, 114) set him beside Jeremiah and blame neither.

source.quote: Here am I. Send me!

figures.name: Timothy
figures.kind: Bible figure (New Testament), Paul's disciple, bishop
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: Public domain on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Timothy-and-Lois.jpg (Timothy with his grandmother Lois, 1650s, 1524 px).

traits.evidence: Gregory reads Paul's two letters as care for two tempers: Titus meeker, Timothy more fervid.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book III (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: except that he saw Titus to be of a meeker spirit, and Timothy of one a little more fervid?

traits.evidence: Gregory's image for the two disciples: a spur for one, a bridle for the other.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book III (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: The one he endeavours to push on with a spur, the other to keep back with a bridle.

traits.pole: timid (the modern reading, which the Fathers do not share)
traits.evidence: Paul asks Corinth to make sure Timothy has nothing to fear. Many modern readers call Timothy timid from this and 2 Timothy 1:7.

source.quote: If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you

traits.evidence: Chrysostom says the line was for the hearers' sake, not a sign of fear in Timothy.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on 1 Corinthians (tr. Chambers, NPNF 1/12 (1889))
source.quote: Perhaps some one may think there is something unworthy of Timothy's courage in this piece of advice. But not on Timothy's account is this said, but for the hearers' sake

traits.evidence: Paul remembers his tears (2 Timothy 1:4). Chrysostom: it was natural for him to weep like a weaned child.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on 2 Timothy (tr. Schaff, NPNF 1/13 (1889))
source.quote: It was natural for Timothy, when parting from him, to mourn and weep, more than a child torn away from the milk and from the breast of its mother.

figures.name: Titus
figures.kind: Bible figure (New Testament), Paul's disciple, bishop of Crete
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: None checked.

traits.evidence: Gregory: Titus was of a meeker spirit, so Paul spurs him.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book III (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: except that he saw Titus to be of a meeker spirit, and Timothy of one a little more fervid?

traits.evidence: Titus is told to rebuke with all authority. Gregory takes this as a spur. The inference is Gregory's.

source.quote: Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

traits.evidence: He goes to Corinth eagerly, of his own accord. Gregory warns that the meek lean toward sloth (III.16); Titus shows the meek pole without it.

source.quote: he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition.

figures.name: Barnabas
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: No plate (the site's CREDITS.md already records "No plate ... Barnabas"). None found.

traits.evidence: The apostles named him Son of Encouragement.

source.quote: whom the apostles called Barnabas (meaning Son of Encouragement)

traits.axis: III.20-21 givers / takers; keepers / give-and-take; III.36 shortlist: stingy / lavish
traits.evidence: He sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet.

source.quote: sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

traits.evidence: All were afraid of the converted Saul (Acts 9:26). Barnabas brings him to the apostles.

source.quote: Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles

traits.evidence: At Antioch he sees the grace of God in others and rejoices.

source.quote: he rejoiced and encouraged them all to abide in the Lord with all their hearts.

traits.evidence: He wants Mark on the next journey. Paul will not take a man who deserted them. They part.

source.quote: Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate; Body of Christ: opposite tempers as partners
traits.evidence: Chrysostom: Paul's sternness moved Mark to repent; Barnabas' kindness kept him from being left behind.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts (tr. Walker/Sheppard/Browne, rev. Stevens, NPNF 1/11 (1889))
source.quote: For the awe inspired by Paul converted him, while the kindness of Barnabas caused that he was not left behind

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate; III.22 at variance / at peace
traits.evidence: Chrysostom calls Barnabas the one "who on all occasions gave way".

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts (tr. Walker/Sheppard/Browne, rev. Stevens, NPNF 1/11 (1889))
source.quote: nor that he who on all occasions gave way would not have given way here

figures.name: Paul (Saul of Tarsus)
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/dore-paul.jpg (Dore, St Paul Preaching to the Thessalonians; low resolution).

traits.pole: passionate: "raging fury" in his own words
traits.evidence: His own account to Agrippa.

source.quote: In my raging fury against them, I even went to foreign cities to persecute them.

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate (anger believed to be zeal)
traits.pole: zeal that was persecution (our match to Gregory's hidden side)
traits.evidence: Paul names his old persecution "zeal". Gregory III.16 warns the passionate take anger for zeal. Gregory does not use this verse; the match is ours.

source.quote: as to zeal, persecuting the church

traits.evidence: Chrysostom on Paul going straight into danger at Damascus.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts (tr. Walker/Sheppard/Browne, rev. Stevens, NPNF 1/11 (1889))
source.quote: he leaped into the midst of those who were mad against him. This it is to be on fire, this to be fervent indeed!

traits.evidence: Chrysostom's one-word marks: Stephen's wisdom, Peter's tongue, Paul's vehemence.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on John (tr. Marriott, NPNF 1/14 (1889))
source.quote: the wisdom of Stephen, the tongue of Peter, the vehemence of Paul

traits.evidence: He calls the high priest a whitewashed wall, then says he did not know who he was (Acts 23:5).

source.quote: God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!

traits.evidence: Chrysostom denies this was anger.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts (tr. Walker/Sheppard/Browne, rev. Stevens, NPNF 1/11 (1889))
source.quote: They are the words of boldness, rather than of anger

traits.evidence: Nazianzen gives Peter and Paul eagerness in preaching.

source.quote: Peter and Paul eagerness in preaching

figures.name: David
figures.kind: Bible figure (Old Testament), shepherd, psalmist, king
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint. Honoured as prophet and king.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/figures/david.jpg (Dore, David Mourns the Death of Absalom).

traits.evidence: Shimei curses him and throws stones. David forbids revenge.

source.quote: Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so.

traits.evidence: Ambrose makes David's silence under Shimei the model of bearing abuse.

source.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy (tr. de Romestin/Duckworth, NPNF 2/10 (1896))
source.locus: On the Duties of the Clergy I.6.21
source.quote: For when Shimei the son of Gera reviled him, David was silent

traits.axis: III.9 impatient / patient (the patient's hidden side: recalling the insult later and paying it back)
traits.pole: patient at the time, repaid later (our inference; the Fathers checked do not say this)
traits.evidence: On his deathbed David tells Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless. Gregory III.9 describes the patient who later wishes he had repaid. Ambrose and Cassian read the Shimei story only as patience; the deathbed line is not discussed in the texts checked.

source.quote: Now therefore, do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You know what you ought to do to him to bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood.

traits.axis: III.16 meek / passionate; III.15 slothful / hasty
traits.evidence: Nabal insults him; he swears to kill every male of Nabal's house by morning.

source.quote: if I let one male belonging to Nabal survive until morning.

traits.evidence: Cassian: the oath came from anger and a disturbed mind; the change of mind is the example.

source.quote: his readiness to take a rash oath (which resulted from his anger and disturbance of mind)

traits.axis: III.33 small frequent faults / careful in small things, grave fall
traits.pole: careful in small things, grave fall (our match)
traits.evidence: His conscience strikes him for cutting a corner off Saul's robe. Later he takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed (2 Samuel 11).

source.quote: Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.

traits.axis: III.33 small frequent faults / careful in small things, grave fall; III.36 shortlist: wrathful / soft-hearted
traits.pole: the same contrast, in Gregory's words
traits.evidence: Gregory: he who once spared his enemy later panted for the death of the good. Gregory uses it to warn about power and ease, not as the gnat and camel.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book I (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895), print wording)
source.quote: and he who had before known pitifully how to spare the bad learnt afterwards, without impediment of hesitation, to pant even for the death of the good

traits.axis: III.15 slothful / hasty (Gregory: "the idle man is wholly in desires")
traits.evidence: Kings go to war; David stays home. Gregory I.3 dates the fall to when "the weight of pressure was removed".

source.quote: but David remained in Jerusalem.

traits.axis: III.35 bad in secret / good in secret, careless of repute; III.3 joyful / sad (by temperament)
traits.evidence: He dances with all his might and tells Michal he will be humbled even more (2 Samuel 6:22).

source.quote: danced with all his might before the LORD

traits.axis: III.14 silent / talkative (the over-silent: "closed sores torment the more")
traits.evidence: A psalm of David: he keeps silent, his heart grows hot, then he speaks (Psalm 39:3). Gregory III.14 does not cite this psalm.

source.quote: I was speechless and still; I remained silent, even from speaking good, and my sorrow was stirred.

traits.axis: III.36 shortlist: wrathful / soft-hearted; III.16 meek / passionate (the meek's laxity)
traits.evidence: He never once rebuked his son Adonijah.

source.quote: His father had never once reprimanded him

figures.name: Saul, first king of Israel
figures.orthodox_standing: Not venerated. A warning figure, not a match anyone will want.
figures.portrait: Public domain on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:070A.Samuel_Blesses_Saul.jpg (Dore, 2314 px; calm). Also 074.David Shows Saul How He Spared His Life.jpg (2316 px).

traits.axis: III.7 impudent / bashful; III.36 shortlist: proud / timid
traits.evidence: Chosen king, he is found hiding among the baggage.

source.quote: Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.

traits.pole: humble, then haughty (Gregory names this change)
traits.evidence: Gregory: fled for unworthiness, then puffed up once king.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book I (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: Thus Saul, who had before fled in consideration of his unworthiness, no sooner had assumed the government of the kingdom than he was puffed up

traits.evidence: Samuel is late. Saul offers the sacrifice himself: "I felt compelled."

source.quote: So I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering.

traits.evidence: He blames the troops for the spoil (1 Samuel 15:21), then admits he feared the people. Gregory III.11 describes this rolling-up in excuses; he does not name Saul.

source.quote: because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.

traits.evidence: The women sing David's tens of thousands. From that day Saul keeps a jealous eye on him (18:9).

source.quote: And Saul was furious and resented this song.

traits.evidence: Chrysostom: Saul envied even the one who soothed him.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on 2 Corinthians (tr. Chambers, NPNF 1/12 (1889))
source.quote: So did Saul invite an evil demon against his own soul; and when he had invited, he again envied his physician.

traits.evidence: He throws his spear at his own son.

source.quote: Then Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him.

traits.axis: III.29-30 lament but repeat / stop but never lament
traits.evidence: He weeps and says David is more righteous (24:16-17). Then he hunts him again, and says "I will never harm you again" (26:21).

source.quote: I will never harm you again

figures.name: Nabal
figures.kind: Bible figure (Old Testament), rich herdsman of Carmel
figures.orthodox_standing: Not venerated. His name means Fool (1 Samuel 25:25).
figures.portrait: None of him alone. Abigail's painting (below) shows the story.

traits.axis: III.20-21 givers / takers; keepers / give-and-take (keepers who "commit no wrong"); III.36 shortlist: stingy / lavish
traits.evidence: "My bread and water and the meat". He refuses David's men. Gregory III.21 answers exactly this: keeping one's own is not innocence. Gregory does not name Nabal there.

source.quote: Why should I take my bread and water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, and give them to these men whose origin I do not know?

traits.pole: obstinate: no one can speak to him
traits.evidence: His own servant says so.

source.quote: For he is such a scoundrel that nobody can speak to him!

traits.evidence: Abigail comes home to find him feasting like a king, very drunk.

source.quote: there he was in the house, holding a feast fit for a king, in high spirits and very drunk.

traits.pole: the passionate hear nothing in the heat
traits.evidence: Gregory uses Nabal: Abigail waited until he was sober to tell him.

source.work: Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book III (tr. Barmby, NPNF 2/12 (1895))
source.quote: Whence to Nabal when he was drunk Abigail laudably kept silence about his fault, but, when he had digested his wine, as laudably told him of it

traits.evidence: Chrysostom makes Nabal his example of haughtiness toward men.

source.work: Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans (tr. Walker/Sheppard/Browne, rev. Stevens, NPNF 1/11 (1889))
source.quote: Such was Nabal, if not to Godward, at least toward man, having become senseless from his recklessness.

figures.name: Abigail
figures.kind: Bible figure (Old Testament), wife of Nabal, then of David
figures.orthodox_standing: Unsure whether she has a place in the Orthodox calendar; not checked.
figures.portrait: Public domain dedication (CC0) on Commons, checked: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sir_Peter_Paul_Rubens,_The_Meeting_of_David_and_Abigail,_c._1630,_NGA_99280.jpg (Rubens, National Gallery of Art, 4000 px). The site's CREDITS.md records no Dore plate for her.

traits.evidence: Scripture calls her intelligent and beautiful.

source.quote: She was an intelligent and beautiful woman, but her husband, a Calebite, was harsh and evil in his dealings.

traits.axis: III.15 slothful / hasty; III.20-21 givers / takers; keepers / give-and-take
traits.evidence: She hurries and loads two hundred loaves and more onto donkeys.

source.quote: Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread

traits.evidence: David blesses her discernment: she kept him from bloodshed.

source.quote: Blessed is your discernment, and blessed are you, because today you kept me from bloodshed and from avenging myself by my own hand.

traits.evidence: Ambrose: she restrained David's warriors by her prayers.

source.work: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy (tr. de Romestin/Duckworth, NPNF 2/10 (1896))
source.locus: On the Duties of the Clergy I.21.94
source.quote: The warriors, too, prepared to take vengeance against Nabal, Abigail restrained by her prayers.

traits.axis: III.14 silent / talkative ("a door, not a wall")
traits.pole: knows when to speak (our match to III.14; Gregory praises her timing in III.16)
traits.evidence: She told Nabal nothing until morning.

source.quote: So she told him nothing until morning light.

figures.name: Jonathan, son of Saul
figures.kind: Bible figure (Old Testament), prince and soldier
figures.orthodox_standing: Unsure of his place in the Orthodox calendar; not checked.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/figures/jonathan.jpg (Dore, David and Jonathan).

traits.evidence: Heir to the throne, he tells David: you will be king, I will be second.

source.quote: And you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command.

traits.evidence: He speaks well of David to his father.

source.quote: Then Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul

figures.name: John the Baptist
figures.orthodox_standing: Orthodox saint. Honoured as the Forerunner.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: site/public/img/figures/john-the-baptist.jpg (Dore; low resolution, 564 px).

traits.axis: III.10 kindly / envious; III.17 humble / haughty

coverage_gaps: III.3 joyful by temperament: no figure. David's dancing (2 Sam 6:14) is one joyful act, not a temperament. Gregory's link (joy near lust) has no Bible person attached by him.

III.15 slothful and III.36 listless: no one Scripture calls idle. Nearest: Felix puts Paul off (Acts 24:25, with a bribe in view, 24:26); Chrysostom says Esau sold his birthright 'through his own slothfulness'; David stayed home (2 Sam 11:1), which Gregory reads as ease after pressure, not a lazy temper. The sluggard of Proverbs is a type, not a person.
III.10 the kindly's hidden side ('eager backers, but inert spectators'): no figure.
III.11 simple: one verse only (Nathanael, John 1:47). No story shows the simple man's own fault (saying true things unwisely).
III.7 impudent: Gregory's own examples are a nation and a church (Jer 3:3; Galatians). No individual is called impudent in the texts checked.
III.18 fickle: only Reuben (Gen 49:4, one line about one act) and Antioch (Gal 2:12-13), which Chrysostom reads as staged.
III.19 the abstinent's hidden side (judging the eater): only a group (John's disciples, Matt 9:14) and a parable figure (the Pharisee, Gregory's own example).
III.20-21 the lavish who also seize, and III.36 prodigal as a fault: no individual. The prodigal son is a parable figure. Mary of Bethany and the widow are lavish but praised.
III.29-30 those who stop but never lament: no figure.
III.33 small frequent faults: no figure.
III.35 good in secret and careless of repute: only David's dancing (2 Sam 6:22). Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus are good in secret because they feared repute, the other side of the matter.

III.9 the patient's hidden side (recalling the insult and repaying it later): only David's deathbed charge about Shimei (1 Kgs 2:8-9), and that link is ours; Ambrose and Cassian read David at Shimei only as patience.
III.22 at variance: only Euodia and Syntyche (Phil 4:2, one verse; left out of the figure list) and the Paul and Barnabas parting, which Chrysostom says was not enmity.
III.23 the peacemaker who joins the wrong people: no figure (Gregory's own example is the reverse: Paul dividing his enemies, Acts 23:6).
Gregory's III.36 shortlist, restless/listless: the listless pole is empty (see above); Martha and Peter cover restless.
risks: The Fathers defend the saints from vice readings (Chrysostom on Acts 23:3, Acts 15:39, Gal 2:11, 1 Cor 16:10). A result that puts a saint on a vice pole contradicts the foundation it claims.
Timothy: Gregory calls him 'a little more fervid' and Chrysostom denies he was timid. The popular modern 'timid Timothy' is the opposite. Pick the Fathers' reading or leave him out.
Thomas at John 11:16: Chrysostom hears cowardice and rejects the courage reading most readers hear. Use his arc (weak, then 'stronger than all'), not the one verse.
James and John: Nazianzen reads 'Sons of Thunder' as grand speech, not temper. Luke 9:54 is the temper evidence. St John the Theologian is highly venerated; a wrathful label will jar.

Martha and Mary: Cassian reads them as two ways of life and ranks Mary's; Chrysostom ranks Mary's faith above Martha's; Jesus says Mary chose the good portion. A 'Martha' result is a ranked result. Keep Mary of Bethany distinct from Mary Magdalene (the Orthodox Church distinguishes them; the site already has a Mary Magdalene figure).
Temperament versus circumstance: Gregory III.3 separates them; Scripture mostly shows circumstance. Jeremiah's and Elijah's sorrow come from events. Every 'our match' is the site's claim.

The site's figure quiz (bible-figure.ts, bible-figures.json) already places Peter, Moses, David, Elijah, Paul, Barnabas, Martha, Abigail, John the Baptist, Jonathan and Gideon on six axes. New claims must agree with those cited acts or the two quizzes will contradict each other. (Peter there: acts first, says it; consistent with hasty and talkative here.)

Capitals for God: the BSB lowercases a relative 'who' for God in some verses (2 Cor 7:6, 2 Cor 8:16, 1 Sam 25:32, 2 Sam 6:21, Acts 9:27). Those were avoided or quoted in part. Every lowercase pronoun in the quoted lines was checked and refers to a person, not God.

New Advent's Fathers are 'revised and edited for New Advent' (archaic forms modernised, Scripture references inlined). 71 of the 78 Father lines checked there are word-for-word in the CCEL scan of the printed NPNF volume; the other 7 are given in the printed wording and checked against the CCEL scan. For print on the site, prefer the printed wording.
BSB wording: Numbers 12:3 says 'humble', not 'meek'. 2 Samuel 13:21 in the BSB lacks the Greek clause that David did not punish Amnon because he loved him; do not quote that clause as BSB.
1 Kings 2:8-9 read as the patient man's delayed revenge is our inference and could read as slander of a saint. The Fathers on this verse were not checked.

Basil's homilies on envy (Saul, Joseph's brothers) and on anger (Moses) were seen only in the NPNF editor's summary; not used. A Chrysostom homily in NPNF 1/13 calling Shimei's and Nabal's words 'audacity' was seen in the CCEL volume but not identified or saved; not used.
Gregory's Moralia on Job (Job's simplicity, Elihu's arrogance) was not fetched or checked.
Images: Dore's plates of Absalom, Achan, Stephen and Ananias show deaths, and Caravaggio's Thomas shows a finger in the wound; the site's no-violence rule may exclude them.
Orthodox standing is given without feast dates. Marked unsure: Abigail, Jonathan, Gideon, Aaron, Eli, Jehoshaphat, Caleb; whether John Mark is the Evangelist in Orthodox tradition was not checked.
A match with Saul, Nabal, Cain or Esau will sting. The site's rule of no percentage against a person still applies; these fit 'worth watching' better than 'people like you'.

report.summary:
I checked 25 people for a "saints who share your temperament" layer, all from public-domain texts I fetched and saved. All 123 verbatim quotes pass the substring check.

Main finding: the premise holds up in the sources. The Fathers did name a person's temperament "by nature", not just passing vices. The clearest cases:
- Ephrem was "naturally prone to passion" (Sozomen 3.16).
- Chrysostom was called hot-tempered from his youth, and he says so himself (Socrates 6.3, Sozomen 8.3, On the Priesthood 1.6).
- Ambrose wrote that Theodosius had "a natural vehemence" (Letter 51.4).
- Nazianzen loved quiet "from the first" (Oration 2.6).
- Benedict "from his younger years" had the mind of an old man (Dialogues 2).

The desert tradition also says outright that opposite temperaments can both be holy. In one vision Arsenius sails in silence with the Spirit of God and Moses the Black sails with the angels feeding him honey: "one fleeth from the world for Thy Name's sake, and another receiveth and is gracious" (Budge, Paradise vol. 2, Book 1 ch. 1 no. 21). Antony learned a different virtue from each monk (Life 4).

Framework find (outside my topic, but important): Gregory's Book III openly builds on Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2.28-33. That text is Orthodox and before the schism. It sorts kinds of people: "the sanguine and despondent ... the wrathful and meek", the sluggish versus the "immoderately fervent", and "the mixtures and blendings of the elements of which we are composed". It maps almost exactly onto Gregory's ch 36 shortlist.

Gregory's ch 36 shortlist is well covered, except for "niggardly":
- Timid: Nazianzen.
- Proud: young Basil, plus Basil and Chrysostom as others saw them.
- Listless: Augustine, and Nazianzen as Basil charged him.
- Unquiet: Jerome and John the Dwarf.
- Wrathful: Jerome, Chrysostom, Cassian, Ephrem (by nature) and Theodosius.
- Soft-hearted: Nazianzen, Martin, Macarius and Poemen.
- Prodigal: Benedict, Martin and Antony.
- Niggardly: no saint.

Real friendships give ready-made opposite pairs:
- Basil (driving, a fighter) and Nazianzen (quiet, "unarmed and unwarlike"), in Letters 48-49.
- Arsenius (withdraws) and Moses (welcomes).
- Chrysostom ("the more hot tempered") and his milder friend Basil. This Basil is not Basil the Great.

Two cautions:
1. Several are changed temperaments (Moses the Black, Ephrem, young Basil). The honest line is "was like you, and this is what grace made of it".
2. Much of the desert evidence records holiness won in adult life, not a native disposition. Strength is marked per trait. The "by nature" lines above are the strongest.
