source.quote: I used to sit alone because I was filled with bitterness.

figures.name: John Chrysostom
figures.orthodox_standing: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs; the usual Orthodox Sunday liturgy bears his name.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'chrysostom'; Hagia Sophia mosaic, late 9th century, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Johnchrysostom.jpg

traits.axis: ch 16 meek / passionate (and ch 36 wrathful / soft-hearted)
traits.evidence: Of himself and his friend Basil (not Basil the Great), he says people thought him the hotter-tempered one. The friend was thought the milder. That makes a ready-made pair. Some scholars doubt the story is history.

source.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF1 vol. 9, 1889
source.quote: one who was generally reputed to be the more hot tempered (meaning me)

traits.evidence: Socrates cites an early friend: irritable from his youth. The clergy later shunned him as a passionate man (6.4).

source.quote: in his youth he manifested a proneness to irritability, rather than to modesty

traits.evidence: Sozomen, who admires him, says it was his nature to rebuke wrongdoing. Once he had power, his anger came more readily.

source.quote: He was naturally disposed to reprehend the misconduct of others

traits.evidence: Socrates says he was simple and open, though his frankness offended many.

source.quote: his simplicity of character rendered him open and ingenuous

traits.axis: ch 17 humble / haughty (and ch 36 proud / timid)
traits.evidence: Strangers found him haughty in private conversation. Socrates presents this as how he seemed, not what he was.

source.quote: in private conversation he was frequently thought haughty and assuming by those who did not know him

traits.evidence: As a young hermit he went two years without lying down, and it ruined his stomach and kidneys.

source.work: Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom
source.quote: Two years spent without lying down by night or day deadened his gastric organs

traits.axis: ch 35 bad in secret, good in public / good in secret, careless of bad repute
traits.evidence: He ate alone and refused every dinner invitation, even though his enemies used it against him. Palladius defends the habit (Dialogue ch. 12).

source.quote: the bishop was not willing to eat with any one else, and never accepted an invitation to a feast

figures.name: Basil the Great
figures.orthodox_standing: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'basil'; Palatine Chapel mosaic, Palermo, 12th century, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sanctus_Basilius_Capella_Palatina.jpg

traits.axis: ch 8 forward / faint-hearted (and ch 36 proud / timid)
traits.evidence: His brother says Basil came home from university proud of his speaking and looking down on the local grandees. His sister Macrina turned him round.

source.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
source.quote: He was puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory

traits.pole: forward (his own account of his youth)
traits.evidence: He says himself that he spent his youth on vanity and worldly learning.

source.quote: Much time had I spent in vanity, and had wasted nearly all my youth

traits.evidence: Critics called him proud. His best friend says it was firmness, and that vices sit next door to virtues (the same idea as Pastoral Rule Book II ch 9).

source.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43 (funeral oration on Basil)
source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: Nay, what they term pride is, I fancy, the firmness and steadfastness and stability of his character.

traits.evidence: His smile was praise and his silence a rebuke. He was no chatterer, jester or gossip, and no general favourite. His friend adds that he was kind and witty in person.

source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: His very smile often amounted to praise, his silence to rebuke

traits.evidence: In a famine he opened the stores of those who had grain and fed the starving himself.

source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: For by his word and advice he opened the stores of those who possessed them

traits.evidence: A hurt Nazianzen tells Basil sarcastically to go and win every battle himself. It pictures Basil as the driving one of the pair. The line is sarcastic, so the fit is loose.

source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: Do you then play the man and be strong and draw all parties to your own conclusion

figures.name: Gregory of Nazianzus (the Theologian)
figures.orthodox_standing: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs; called 'the Theologian'. Gregory the Great names him as his source in the Book III prologue.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'nazianzen'; St Sophia, Kyiv, mosaic, 11th century, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Agios_Gregorios_Theologos_Kiev.jpg

traits.axis: ch 36 proud / timid (and ch 8 forward / faint-hearted)
traits.evidence: Resigning Constantinople, he calls himself timid. It is partly the modesty expected in a farewell speech.

source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: What need have you of a timid and unmanly old man

traits.axis: ch 36 wrathful / soft-hearted (and ch 16 meek / passionate)
traits.evidence: He says he is tired of being blamed for his gentleness.

source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: I am weary of being charged with my gentleness.

traits.axis: ch 36 listless / unquiet (and ch 15 slothful / hasty)
traits.evidence: Basil called him lazy. He answered: 'My greatest business always is to keep free from business.' Pastoral Rule Book II ch 9 warns that tardiness can pass for deliberation, so the main session can judge which it was.

source.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 49 (to Basil, 'The Praises of Quiet')
source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: You accuse me of laziness and idleness, because I did not accept your Sasima

traits.evidence: He refuses to fight Basil's church quarrel and calls himself 'unarmed and unwarlike'.

source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: Give me before all things quiet.

traits.axis: ch 14 silent / talkative (love of solitude; closest pair)
traits.evidence: Explaining why he fled ordination, he says he had loved quiet and retirement 'from the first'. That makes it a lifelong disposition.

source.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2 (Defence of his Flight)
source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: an eager longing for the blessings of calm and retirement, of which I had from the first been enamoured

traits.evidence: Long after Basil made him bishop of Sasima, he still writes hurt letters about it. Gregory's ch 9 says the patient are calm at the time and then brood on the wrong. The mapping is mine.

source.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF2 vol. 7, 1894
source.quote: Do leave off speaking of me as an ill-educated and uncouth and unfriendly man, not even worthy to live, because I have ventured to be conscious of the way in which I have been treated.

figures.name: Gregory of Nyssa
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church. Basil's younger brother.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'nyssa'; 11th-century image, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:St._Gregory_of_Nyssa.jpg

traits.evidence: He forged three letters from their uncle, and Basil scolded him. Basil puts it down to simplicity, not guile. Elsewhere Basil calls him inexperienced in church affairs and a stranger to flattery (Letter 215). Letter 58 gives no motive for the forgeries.

source.quote: How can I lay hold of you satisfactorily, with all your simplicity?

traits.evidence: Basil says his brother cannot flatter anyone.

source.quote: a man like my brother, to whom anything like mean servility is unknown

figures.name: Macrina the Younger
figures.kind: saint (ascetic, head of a household community)
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (19 July). She left no writings; everything comes from her brother Gregory of Nyssa.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'macrina'; St Sophia, Kyiv, fresco, 11th century, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Macrina_the_Younger.jpg

traits.evidence: When her brother died and her mother collapsed, she stayed calm and held her mother up. She stayed unbroken through later losses too.

source.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
source.locus: section 'Macrina the one support of her mother'
source.quote: by her own steadfastness and imperturbability taught her mother's soul to be brave

traits.evidence: She refused to let a doctor examine a tumour. This is modesty, a virtue; tying it to Gregory's 'bashful' pole is a stretch.

source.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
source.locus: section 'They find on the body marks of Macrina's sanctity'
source.quote: she judged it worse than the pain, to uncover any part of the body to a stranger's

figures.name: Antony the Great
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in every ancient church (17 January). Almost everything comes from Athanasius's Life.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'antony'; Cretan icon, 15th-17th century, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cretan_Icon_Saint_Anthony_the_Great.jpg

traits.evidence: Athanasius says his face was cheerful because his soul was at peace.

source.quote: he was never downcast, for his mind was joyous

traits.evidence: After twenty years alone he came out unmoved by grief or pleasure, laughter or dejection. The Life holds this balance up as the ideal between the poles.

source.quote: neither contracted as if by grief, nor relaxed by pleasure, nor possessed by laughter or dejection

traits.evidence: He deferred to every cleric and kept asking questions so that he could learn.

source.quote: he was tolerant in disposition and humble in spirit

traits.evidence: He reconciled people who were at odds.

source.quote: set those at variance at one

traits.evidence: As a young man he studied a different virtue in each monk and tried to join them in himself, with no rivalry. This also supports the whole 'saints who share your temperament' idea.

source.quote: He observed the graciousness of one; the unceasing prayer of another

traits.axis: ch 11 simple / insincere (and ch 6 wise / dull)
traits.evidence: As a boy he would not go to school and wanted only to live plainly at home, like Jacob.

source.quote: he could not endure to learn letters, not caring to associate with other boys

traits.axis: ch 20 givers / takers (and ch 36 niggardly / prodigal)
traits.evidence: He heard one Gospel verse and gave away three hundred acres.

source.quote: gave the possessions of his forefathers to the villagers

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.orthodox_standing: Honoured in the Orthodox Church as 'Blessed Augustine' (15 June); many Orthodox writers reject parts of his teaching. Not a foundation-level Orthodox authority.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'augustine'; Lateran fresco, c. 550-600, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rome,_Lateran,_Capella_Sancta_Sanctorum,_Fresco_of_Augustine.jpg

traits.axis: ch 15 slothful / hasty (and ch 36 listless / unquiet; ch 34 never begin / never finish)
traits.evidence: He describes himself as half asleep, putting off change with 'presently' and 'a little while'.

source.quote: Presently, lo, presently; Leave me a little while. But presently, presently, had no present

traits.axis: ch 29-30 lament but repeat / stop but never lament
traits.evidence: As a young man he prayed for chastity, but 'not yet'.

source.quote: Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet.

traits.evidence: He loved talk, jokes, reading and friendly disagreement with friends. Gregory's ch 3 links a joyful temper to lust, which Augustine also confesses (8.7). Gregory's ch 37 says one person can carry contrary traits; see his grief below.

source.quote: to discourse and jest with them; to indulge in an interchange of kindnesses; to read together pleasant books; together to trifle, and together to be earnest

traits.evidence: When a close friend died he was overwhelmed, and his own sadness baffled him.

source.quote: I became a great puzzle to myself, and asked my soul why she was so sad

traits.evidence: He says drunkenness is far from him but that overeating sometimes creeps up on him.

source.quote: But surfeiting sometimes creeps upon Your servant

traits.axis: ch 17 humble / haughty (Gregory: the haughty are moved by praise)
traits.evidence: He admits praise pleases him and blame deflates him. He treats this as a temptation everyone faces daily, so it is weak as a temperament.

source.quote: I am delighted with praise, but more with the truth itself than with praise

figures.name: Gregory the Great (the Dialogist)
figures.kind: Father (pope); author of the Pastoral Rule
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church as St Gregory the Dialogist (12 March).
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'gregory'; Jusepe de Ribera (formerly attributed to Saraceni), c. 1614, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carlo_Saraceni_-_St_Gregory_the_Great_-_WGA20833.jpg

traits.evidence: He opens the Dialogues sitting alone in a place suited to 'a sad and melancholy disposition'. A few scholars doubt he wrote the Dialogues.

source.quote: I retired myself into a solitary place, very fit for a sad and melancholy disposition

traits.evidence: Newly pope, he writes that he can hardly speak for grief.

source.quote: I am stricken with so great sorrow that I can scarcely speak

traits.axis: contemplative / active (his own Rachel and Leah image; not a Book III pair)
traits.evidence: He loved the quiet life and felt the active life had been forced on him.

source.quote: I have loved the beauty of the contemplative life as a Rachel

traits.axis: ch 8 forward / faint-hearted (and ch 36 proud / timid)
traits.evidence: On being made pope he says the emperor has ordered an ape to be made a lion.

source.quote: our most serene Lord the Emperor has ordered an ape to be made a lion

traits.evidence: He ends the Pastoral Rule by calling himself an ugly painter of a handsome man.

source.quote: I have been as an ill-favoured painter pourtraying a handsome man

traits.axis: ch 17 humble / haughty (his rule on fleeing office)
traits.evidence: His own rule for those who flee office: humble only if they then obey God. It applies to the flights of Nazianzen, Ambrose, Ephrem, Chrysostom and Gregory himself. I did not check a public-domain text of his own attempted flight (Gregory of Tours, History 10.1).

source.quote: That those who fly from the burden of rule through humility are then truly humble when they resist not the divine decrees.

figures.name: Martin of Tours
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox and Catholic churches. He wrote nothing; everything comes through his disciple Sulpicius.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'martin'; El Greco, Saint Martin and the Beggar, 1597-99, CC0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:El_Greco_(Domenikos_Theotokopoulos),_Saint_Martin_and_the_Beggar,_1597-1599,_NGA_1164.jpg

traits.evidence: No one ever saw him angry, agitated, grieving or laughing.

source.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
source.quote: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing; he was always one and the same

traits.axis: ch 36 wrathful / soft-hearted (and ch 9 impatient / patient)
traits.evidence: A priest he had raised screamed abuse at him. Martin answered gently and refused for years to remove him. Gregory warns the meek against laxity, and this is the case to test that against.

source.quote: If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio.

traits.axis: ch 20 givers / takers (and ch 36 niggardly / prodigal)
traits.evidence: He had already given away his other clothes before he cut his cloak in half for a beggar.

source.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
source.quote: He had nothing except the cloak in which he was clad, for he had already parted with the rest of his garments for similar purposes.

traits.evidence: Knowing he was near death, he still travelled to reconcile quarrelling clergy at Candes (Condate), and died there.

source.quote: as the clerics of that church were at variance among themselves, Martin, wishing to restore peace

traits.axis: ch 35 bad in secret, good in public / good in secret, careless of bad repute
traits.evidence: Bishops scorned his face, clothes and hair. He went on living like a monk anyway.

source.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
source.quote: a man despicable in countenance, that his clothing was mean, and his hair disgusting

traits.axis: ch 33 small frequent faults / careful in small things but a grave fall
traits.evidence: To save men from execution, he once took communion with the bishops who were hunting heretics. He grieved over it and never attended a synod again. Calling it a grave fall is Martin's own view as Sulpicius reports it.

source.quote: he was filled with mourning and lamentation that he had even for an hour been mixed up with the evil communion

figures.name: Benedict of Nursia
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox and Catholic churches. His Life is Gregory the Great's Dialogues Book 2, so Gregory himself is the narrator.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'benedict'; Hans Memling, 1487, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Memling,_Trittico_di_Benedetto_Portinari,_San_Benedetto.jpg

traits.evidence: Gregory says Benedict had the mind of an old man from youth and scorned pleasure. Gravity is not sadness, so the fit to the pair is mine.

source.quote: from his younger years, carried always the mind of an old man

traits.axis: ch 21 keepers / lavish (and ch 36 niggardly / prodigal)
traits.evidence: In a famine he gave away the abbey's goods. His cellarer held back the last oil, saying there would be none left for the monks. That cellarer is the 'keeper' pole, but he is not a saint.

source.quote: that was resolved to give away all upon earth that he might find all in heaven

traits.axis: ch 16 meek / passionate (Gregory: anger taken for zeal)
traits.evidence: Angry at the disobedient cellarer, he had the oil thrown out of the window. This is one incident.

source.quote: Then in an anger he commanded others to take that glass with the oil, and to throw it out at the window

traits.evidence: A jealous priest tried to poison him. Benedict grieved more for the priest than for himself.

source.quote: was far more sorry for him than grieved for himself

traits.evidence: His sister Scholastica begged him to stay and talk through the night, and he refused because of the rule. Gregory's verdict is that she did more because she loved more. The mapping is mine.

source.quote: by no persuasion would he agree unto that, saying that he might not by any means tarry all night out of his Abbey

figures.name: Ephrem the Syrian
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in every ancient church (Orthodox 28 January). Many writings under his name are not his.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. Nea Moni mosaic, 11th century, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ephrem_the_Syrian_(mosaic_in_Nea_Moni).jpg

traits.pole: passionate by nature, meek after conversion
traits.evidence: Sozomen reports that Ephrem was quick to anger by nature, but never showed anger after he became a monk. It is a clear case of a temperament changed by grace.

source.quote: although he was naturally prone to passion, he never exhibited angry feeling toward any one from the period of his embracing a monastic life

traits.evidence: After days of fasting, his servant dropped the dish. Ephrem comforted the man and ate from the pieces.

source.quote: Take courage; we will go to the food as the food does not come to us

traits.evidence: Sozomen says he especially loved quiet.

source.quote: He was particularly fond of tranquillity.

traits.evidence: To avoid being made a bishop, he acted mad in the market-place.

source.quote: he ran to the market-place, and showed himself as a madman

traits.evidence: In the Edessa famine he ran the relief himself, with about 300 beds.

source.quote: See, on your behalf I appoint myself hospitaller.

figures.name: Arsenius the Great
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (8 May). The court details come from the sayings and later tradition.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. 14th-century image, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Arsenius_the_Great.jpg

traits.evidence: His repeated saying: he often regretted speaking, never keeping silent. A voice had told him to flee people and keep silence (no. 2).

source.work: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers (Syriac collection), vol. 2
source.locus: Book 1, ch. 1, no. 53 (repeated in ch. 10, no. 549)
source.quote: I have many times repented that I spoke, but that I held my peace I have never repented.

traits.axis: withdraws / welcomes (the desert's own contrast; nearest Book III pair is ch 14)
traits.evidence: A visitor was received in silence by Arsenius and warmly by Moses the Black. An old monk asked God which was right. He was shown both men in boats, each with God. This is the strongest early text saying that two opposite temperaments are both holy.

source.quote: one fleeth from the world for Thy Name’s sake, and another receiveth and is gracious for Thy Name’s sake

traits.evidence: He wept so much that he lost his eyelashes, and he was afraid when he came to die (Book 1 ch. 4 no. 151).

source.quote: his eyelashes were destroyed by weeping

traits.evidence: In church he sat behind a pillar so he would neither see nor be seen. The sources frame this as avoiding people, not shame, so the mapping is weak.

source.quote: he used to sit behind a pillar so that no one might see his face, and he might not see the faces of others

figures.name: Moses the Black (Moses the Ethiopian)
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (28 August) and the Coptic Church.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. Novgorod icon fragment, late 15th century, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Преподобный_Моисей_Мурин._Фрагмент_новгородской_иконы_конца_XV_века.jpg ; alternative showing him with Poemen, 15th century, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Saints_Poimen,_Elijah,_and_Moses_the_Black.jpg

traits.axis: ch 16 meek / passionate; ch 20 givers / takers
traits.evidence: He was a violent robber-chief, thrown out by his master. Palladius tells it only to show how far his repentance went.

source.quote: His own master drove him out because of his immorality and brigandage.

traits.evidence: He feasted on stolen rams and wine. After his conversion he lived on twelve ounces of dry bread a day (19.6).

source.quote: having eaten the best of the flesh and sold the skins in exchange for wine, he drank a quart

traits.evidence: He refused his abbot's advice to stop fighting temptation. The abbot then told him he had been kept from winning so that he would not boast.

source.quote: I will never cease until the appearance of the demons ceases.

traits.axis: ch 35 bad in secret, good in public / good in secret
traits.evidence: At night he secretly filled the water jars of the old monks.

source.quote: taking their water-pots secretly would fill them with water

traits.evidence: Insulted in the assembly, he said nothing, though he admitted he felt it.

source.quote: Although I was afraid I uttered not a word.

traits.evidence: Called to judge a brother, he came carrying a leaking basket of sand. The brother was let off.

source.quote: my sins which are running down behind me and I cannot see them

traits.axis: withdraws / welcomes (the desert's own contrast with Arsenius)
traits.evidence: He received the visitor with joy and fed him. The vision puts him in a boat with the angels feeding him honey.

source.quote: the old man received them with joy, and having refreshed them greatly he dismissed them in peace

figures.name: Agathon
figures.orthodox_standing: Venerated as a desert father in the Orthodox Church. I did not check his feast date.
figures.portrait: No public-domain image found on Wikimedia Commons (searched 'Agathon', 'Agathon of Egypt').

traits.evidence: He kept a stone in his mouth for three years to learn silence. The source presents silence as something he trained himself into. Poemen said his speech was what made him an abba (Book 2, Questions and Answers no. 100).

source.quote: for a period of three years he placed a stone in his mouth [and kept it there], until he had learned thoroughly how to hold his peace

traits.axis: ch 22 at variance / at peace (and ch 16 meek / passionate)
traits.evidence: He never slept holding anger, and never let anyone else sleep angry with him.

source.quote: I have never lain down to sleep and kept anger in my heart, or even a thought of enmity against any man

traits.evidence: Visitors called him a fornicator, a boaster and a chatterer, and he agreed with all of it. He denied only being a heretic.

source.quote: The earlier things I accounted as profitable to my soul, but heresy meaneth separation from God

traits.evidence: He rented a room and nursed a sick stranger for four months, paying with his own work.

source.quote: he hired a room in the town and remained therein working with his hands

figures.name: Poemen the Great
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (27 August). Some sayings under his name may belong to other monks.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. Hosios Loukas mosaic, 11th century, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hosios_Loukas_(nave,_vault_over_south-west_bay)_-_S.Poimen.jpg

traits.axis: ch 36 wrathful / soft-hearted (and ch 16 meek / passionate)
traits.evidence: Asked whether monks who doze in church should be hit, he said he would rest the sleeper's head on his own knees.

source.quote: If I see my brother sleeping, I place his head upon my knees, and I give him a place to rest upon

traits.axis: ch 23 sowers of strife / peacemakers (and ch 10 kindly / envious)
traits.evidence: An older monk envied him and cursed his followers. Poemen took him food and wine and waited at his door until he was welcomed. The two became friends.

source.quote: we will eat with him, and perhaps by these means we shall be able to pacify him

figures.name: Macarius the Great (of Egypt)
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (19 January).
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. 16th-century image, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Macarius_the_Great.jpg

traits.axis: ch 36 wrathful / soft-hearted (and ch 16 meek / passionate)
traits.evidence: He covered other people's faults as if he had not seen them. This is exactly Gregory's soft-hearted pole in its virtue form. Gregory's warning about laxity applies.

source.locus: Book 2, 'Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men', no. 244
source.quote: as God overshadoweth the world so also did Abbâ Macarius cover over the shortcomings which he saw as if he did not see them

traits.evidence: He helped a thief load his own belongings onto a camel. The saying says only 'Abbâ Macarius', so which Macarius is meant is uncertain.

source.quote: The camel wisheth to carry off this also, O brother

figures.name: Pambo
figures.orthodox_standing: Venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church. I did not check his feast date.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. Rijksmuseum print, c. 1636-1670, CC0: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Heilige_Pambo_van_Nitria_Kluizenaars_Thebaanse_heiligen_(serietitel)_Pambo_Nitriota_(titel_op_object),_RP-P-BI-1652.jpg ; also an icon marked public domain with a vague date: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pambo_of_Nitria.jpeg

traits.axis: ch 14 silent / talkative (and the opposite of ch 15 'hasty')
traits.evidence: He never answered at once; sometimes he took three months. He was known for exactness of speech.

source.quote: Often he went three months even and gave no answer, saying he had not put his hand on it.

traits.evidence: On his deathbed he said he did not regret a single word he had spoken.

source.quote: I have not had to repent of any word that I have spoken up to the present hour.

traits.evidence: He was wary of money. He gave away a rich woman's silver without even looking up.

source.quote: he was very suspicious of gold and silver

figures.name: Paul the Simple
figures.orthodox_standing: Venerated in the Orthodox Church (he is in the Menologion of Basil II). I did not check his feast date.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. Menologion of Basil II, c. 985, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_the_Simple_of_Egypt_(Menologion_of_Basil_II).jpg

traits.evidence: The whole brotherhood nicknamed him 'Simple'. Antony saw his simplicity as grace at work.

source.quote: This is the marvellous tale of Paul who was surnamed Simple by all the brotherhood.

traits.evidence: Antony made him unpick and reweave his work while hungry. He did not complain.

source.quote: he neither murmured nor was discouraged nor angry

figures.name: John the Dwarf (John the Less, John Kolobos)
figures.orthodox_standing: Venerated as a saint in the Orthodox and Coptic churches. I did not check his feast date.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. Hosios Loukas mosaic, 11th century, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hosios_Loukas_(nave,_vault_over_south-west_bay)_-_John_Kolobos.jpg

traits.axis: ch 15 slothful / hasty (and ch 36 listless / unquiet)
traits.evidence: Wanting to live like the angels, he stripped off his clothes and walked into the desert. He was back in a week, and his brother made him wait outside all night.

source.locus: Book 2, 'Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men', no. 70
source.quote: I wanted to be without any care whatsoever, and to be like the angels of God, who do nothing except sing and pray to Him.

traits.evidence: The same story: a bold start, abandoned after a week. It is a single youthful episode; he became a great elder.

source.locus: Book 2, 'Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life', no. 70
source.quote: and when he had passed one week there, he returned to his brother

traits.evidence: He dropped his load and fled when something began to make him angry. Budge's text says a camel was speaking, which may be a translation oddity.

source.quote: he was about to make me angry, but I straightway left the palm leaves and fled

figures.name: Amma Syncletica
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (4 or 5 January). Everything comes from one Greek Life of disputed date and authorship. Budge's Syriac collection does not include her. No public-domain translation of her Life exists; only Baring-Gould's Victorian retelling.
figures.portrait: Not on the site yet. Menologion of Basil II, c. 985, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Righteous_Syncletica_of_Alexandria_(Menologion_of_Basil_II).jpg

traits.axis: ch 35 bad in secret, good in public / good in secret
traits.evidence: Baring-Gould says she hid her good deeds and did not want to be known. This is a 19th-century retelling, not a primary source, so it is marked inferred.

source.work: S. Baring-Gould, The Lives of the Saints, vol. 1 (January), retelling the Greek Life
source.quote: she sought to avoid notice in all that she did, and to conceal her good deeds and self-sacrifices

traits.evidence: Same retelling: she dreaded becoming a teacher but did not refuse the young women who came to her.

source.work: S. Baring-Gould, The Lives of the Saints, vol. 1
source.quote: She was reluctant to be forced thus into a position which she dreaded

figures.name: Ambrose of Milan
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (7 December).
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'ambrose'; San Vittore in Ciel d'Oro mosaic, late 5th century, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:San_Vittore_in_Ciel_d%27oro._Ambrosius_Mediolanensis.jpg

traits.axis: ch 17 humble / haughty (fleeing office; Pastoral Rule Book 1 ch 6)
traits.evidence: Chosen bishop by the crowd, he fled Milan at midnight. Before that he had tried to make himself look unworthy.

source.work: Paulinus of Milan, Life of St Ambrose
source.translation: Mary Simplicia Kaniecka, 1928 (public domain in the US since 2024)
source.quote: he prepared himself for flight, leaving the city at midnight

traits.evidence: Augustine saw him read silently. Visitors sat in silence and left rather than interrupt him. This describes a habit of reading, not clearly a temperament.

source.quote: his eyes glanced over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were silent

traits.axis: how he corrects (Gregory's method; Nazianzen Oration 2.31 on private rebuke; not a temperament)
traits.evidence: After the Thessalonica massacre he rebuked the emperor in a private letter in his own hand. He also read the emperor's temperament first (see Theodosius). It is Gregory's method in action.

source.translation: H. de Romestin et al., NPNF2 vol. 10, 1896
source.quote: Lastly, I am writing with my own hand that which you alone may read.

figures.name: Theodosius I (the Great)
figures.orthodox_standing: I believe the Orthodox calendar commemorates him as St Theodosius the Great (17 January), but I did not verify that here. Not a saint in the West. He ordered the massacre at Thessalonica (390) and then did public penance.
figures.portrait: Not on the site. Missorium of Theodosius I (detail), 388, public domain: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Missorium_of_Theodosius_I_(detail).png

traits.axis: ch 16 meek / passionate (and ch 36 wrathful / soft-hearted)
traits.evidence: Ambrose names the emperor's natural vehemence: gentleness turns it to mercy, provocation makes it hard to hold back. This is a Father reading a temperament, in Gregory's own manner.

source.translation: H. de Romestin et al., NPNF2 vol. 10, 1896
source.quote: But you have a natural vehemence, which, if any one endeavours to soothe, you quickly turn to mercy; if any one stirs it up, you rouse it so much more that you can scarcely restrain it.

figures.name: John Cassian
figures.orthodox_standing: Saint in the Orthodox Church (29 February, kept on 28 February in other years). His writings are in the Philokalia.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'cassian'; Sacra Parallela miniature, 9th century, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Saint_Jean_Cassien_-_Grec_923.jpg

traits.axis: ch 9 impatient / patient (and ch 36 wrathful / soft-hearted)
traits.evidence: He remembers being angry at his pen, his penknife and his flint while living alone. His lesson: solitude does not cure a temper. He writes 'we', meaning himself and his companion.

source.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF2 vol. 11, 1894
source.quote: we recollect that when we were living in solitude a feeling of irritation would creep over us against our pen because it was too large or too small

figures.name: Tertullian
figures.orthodox_standing: Not a saint. He later joined the New Prophecy movement. The site already carries him with a status note.
figures.portrait: Already on the site: people.json key 'tertullian'; Thevet imaginary portrait, 1584, public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tertullian2.png

traits.evidence: He opens his book On Patience by admitting that he has none.

source.quote: So I, most miserable, ever sick with the heats of impatience

coverage_gaps: Gregory's ch 36 'niggardly' pole and ch 21 'keepers' (neither take nor give): no saint. The only figure is the unnamed cellarer in Dialogues 2.28, who is not a saint.
ch 7 'impudent': no saint. The 'bashful' pole is only inferred (Arsenius behind the pillar, Macrina's modesty).
ch 11 'insincere': no saint. Do not use Chrysostom's defended trick on his friend (On the Priesthood 1) or Nyssa's forged letters as a type; Basil reads Nyssa as simple, not guileful.
ch 14 'talkative': no saint. Agathon and John Climacus were only accused of it, falsely.
ch 18 'fickle': no saint. John the Dwarf's one-week desert venture is the nearest, and it is weak.
ch 23 'sowers of strife': no saint.
ch 35 'bad in secret, good in public': no saint, rightly.
ch 29-30 'stops but never laments': no saint. 'Laments but repeats' has only Augustine.
ch 33 both poles: weak. Only Martin at Trier, inferred, for 'one grave fall'.
ch 34 'never finishes': only John the Dwarf, inferred. 'Never begins' has only Augustine.
ch 10 'envious': only Jerome, and only through a hostile witness (Palladius). No friendly source.
ch 20 'takers' and ch 19 'gluttonous': only Moses the Black before his conversion, plus Augustine's mild self-report on overeating.
ch 8 'forward' and ch 36 'proud': only young Basil. Basil and Chrysostom as bishops were only 'seen as' proud, and their defenders deny it.
Isaac the Syrian: no temperament recorded in any early public-domain source. The only fact is his resignation after five months (Isho'dnah, via the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia; secondary).
Amma Syncletica: no primary source in public-domain English. Only Baring-Gould's retelling.
Agathon: no public-domain portrait found on Commons.
Ambrose: little on his temperament beyond fleeing office and reading silently.
Gregory the Great's own attempt to flee the papacy (Gregory of Tours, History 10.1) was not checked against a public-domain text here. The Fordham Brehaut selection does not contain it.
risks: Changed temperaments. Moses the Black, Ephrem and young Basil were changed by grace. A match should say 'was like you, and this is what grace made of it', never that the saint stayed that way.

Most desert evidence records holiness won in adult life (Martin never angry, Pambo slow to speak, Macarius covering faults), not a native disposition. The strongest 'by nature' lines are Ephrem (Sozomen 3.16), Chrysostom (Socrates 6.3; Sozomen 8.3; On the Priesthood 1.6), Theodosius (Ambrose, Letter 51.4), Nazianzen 'from the first' (Oration 2.6) and Benedict 'from his younger years' (Dialogues 2 prologue).

Hostile witnesses. Palladius on Jerome's temper and envy comes from the opposing camp in the Origenist quarrel. Socrates mixes praise and blame of Chrysostom and says his seeming haughtiness was misread.

Racially charged lines. Moses the Black's sayings include a test in which he is expelled with 'Get outside, O Ethiopian', followed by self-talk about his skin (Budge, Book 1 ch. 10 no. 477). Jerome likens his sunburnt skin to an Ethiopian's (Letter 22.7). Do not quote either.
Pairing a reader with a saint's weakness ('you share Jerome's temper', 'Augustine's overeating') needs care in tone. The owner's rule still holds: never a percentage against a person.

Standing. Augustine is 'Blessed Augustine' in the Orthodox Church, and his teaching is disputed there. Tertullian is not a saint. Theodosius's Orthodox commemoration was not verified here, and he ordered a massacre. Isaac the Syrian was a bishop of the Church of the East.

Doubtful attributions. A few scholars doubt Gregory wrote the Dialogues (the source for Benedict and Gregory's own melancholy). Sayings under 'Poemen' may belong to several monks. Budge Book 1 ch. 6 no. 189 says only 'Abbâ Macarius', so which Macarius is uncertain. Some scholars doubt the historicity of Chrysostom's story about his friend Basil.
Budge's Syriac collection restarts its numbering in each section. Always cite book, chapter and number together.
Kaniecka's 1928 translation of Paulinus is public domain in the US (since 2024). Check the rule if the site is judged elsewhere.

Several mappings to Gregory's poles are mine, not the sources'. They are marked 'inferred'. Examples: Jerome's industry as 'unquiet', Benedict's gravity as 'sad', Benedict and Scholastica as 'obstinate', Nazianzen's brooding as the 'patient' pole.

Framework note for the main session: Gregory's Book III openly builds on Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2.28-33 (NPNF2 vol. 7, public domain). That text sorts kinds of people ('the sanguine and despondent', 'the cowardly and courageous, the wrathful and meek', 'the simple and the designing'). It sets the 'sluggish and hard to rouse' against the 'immoderately fervent in spirit ... like thoroughbred colts', and grounds the differences in 'the mixtures and blendings of the elements of which we are composed'. Oration 43.64 adds that 'the vices are settled close to the virtues'. These are Orthodox and pre-schism, and all were checked in the quote run (FW1-FW5).
