report.summary:
Research only. I wrote no questions and no result copy. Every source I relied on is saved as plain text under C:/Users/Light/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-Light-Desktop-claude-theology-compass/8320fd9e-53fe-4117-91cb-ee92de243e5b/scratchpad/gregory/sources/benchmarks/ (root: test pages and sample reports; studies/: abstracts and two full texts; patristic/: public-domain Fathers; shots/: crops of the owner's seven Clearer Thinking captures, described in ct-owner-report-screenshots.txt). Two scripts check the work. verify_quotes.py confirms 21 of 21 verbatim quotes are exact substrings of the saved texts. It normalises whitespace only, and it drops the stray space New Advent's link markup leaves before punctuation. verify_facts.py finds 64 of 64 key phrases behind the paraphrased facts.

What the best secular reports do. They stack layers, not just items. Each layer answers a different question:
- One memorable name, with a portrait and a share image.
- A motive layer: fear, desire, antidote, growth path, and best/average/worst stages.
- Continuous bars, with both poles explained.
- A ranked list of adjectives, strongest and weakest.
- Life-domain chapters: relationships, work, communication.
- A friend comparison.
Clearer Thinking's own study makes the key point. Type labels make people feel good and are easy to remember. Continuous scores predict better. Their answer is to give both. In their randomised test of report sections (236 people), the only significant difference was that the positively framed Jungian section made people feel better. 10% disagreed that it did, against 19% for the Big Five. So flattery is what wins on first read. The research on feedback points the other way for lasting value. Unfavourable feedback is judged less accurate (Ditto and Boardman 1995). Yet negative moral feedback was found helpful when it surprised people and came with explanations (Casali et al. 2024, N=17). Feedback is best taken when it moves from what people already believe to what is new (Finn; Tharinger et al. 2008). Personalised, collaborative feedback has measurable benefit (Poston and Hanson 2010, d=0.42).

Scale points. The evidence says five against seven matters little for validity. For agree/disagree statements, 5 beat 7 (Revilla, Saris and Krosnick 2014). The bigger levers are two-sided, item-specific wording and more items per trait. The site's two-sided statement format is well supported. Seven points on a two-sided item is defensible but will not by itself add depth.

The Fathers. Several layers have an honest counterpart.
- Gregory's pairs as rails. He sorts kinds of people and says so: "some are not made joyful or sad by circumstances, but are so by temperament" (Pastoral Rule III.3).
- Communication tips from Gregory's modes of admonition and Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 2.30-32 ("some need the spur, others the curb").
- A vocation layer from Gregory, Moralia VI.57. It is a true temperament sort: tranquil against restless minds decide the balance of action and contemplation, with Martha and Mary in VI.61.
- A "chief struggle" layer from Cassian, Conferences V.13-14 and 27. This one is vices, not temperament: all eight attack everyone, but one "holds the chief place" in each person.
- A "what moves you" layer from Cassian, Conferences XI.6-7 (fear, hope, love; slave, hireling, son). This is a ladder of stages anyone climbs, not a type. Scoring it risks counting devotion.
- "People like you" from saints only where a Father names the trait: Titus and Timothy (Gregory III.16); Moses and Hobab (III.17); Martha and Mary, Leah and Rachel (Moralia VI.61); Arsenius and Moses the Ethiopian (Apophthegmata, modern translation only, so paraphrase).
- The "anti-personality" turned into "the member you need" (Chrysostom, Homily 31 on 1 Corinthians; Nazianzen, Oration 2.44).

Standing in the Orthodox Church:
- Gregory the Great is St Gregory the Dialogist.
- Gregory Nazianzen (St Gregory the Theologian) and John Chrysostom are among the Three Holy Hierarchs.
- John Cassian is a saint, and texts drawn from his works are in the Philokalia, vol. 1.
- Arsenius the Great and Moses the Ethiopian are saints.
- Evagrius is not a saint. His speculative teaching was condemned with Origen's in the sixth-century controversies, as later councils report. His ascetic works were kept, some under St Nilus's name, and some are in the Philokalia. His eight thoughts reached the tradition through Cassian. The Enneagram's claimed descent from him is debated.

Limits. Trustpilot showed a bot check and Reddit refused scripted access. I did not bypass either, so forum and review evidence is thin. I relied on Clearer Thinking's randomised data and the published feedback research instead. 16Personalities' "AI Reference" page contains instructions addressed to AI systems. I used it only as a source of facts.

report_sections.what_it_shows: One shareable image. It holds the cluster name ('NONCONFORMIST') with an illustrated portrait, the five Big Five traits as five-dot ratings, the Jungian type (INTP), the Enneagram type (5) and the site URL. It sits under an 8-page table of contents, a request to share and a $9 PDF offer. Seen in the owner's own captures.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Their 2.0 announcement sells it as an infographic for sharing on social media. It puts every layer in one glance. Their own data says type labels are the part people find simple and memorable (ct-2-0.txt). Why it spreads is my inference; they did not measure it.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: This is layout, not a source. The honest move is to name the card with Gregory's own words for the kinds of hearer, such as 'the silent' or 'the hasty' (Pastoral Rule III.1 list). Put the one 'Start here' item on the card too (III.38: begin with the fault that has 'the more rapid tendency to death'). The site's existing share-card standard already carries the rest.

report_sections.section: Personality Cluster (page 2): name, description, strengths, weaknesses, communication tips
report_sections.what_it_shows: One of 16 types. They were found by cluster analysis of 560 people's answers to 120 questions. The names and descriptions were then written by the team, which they say 'involved making some subjective choices' (ct-clusters.txt). The page gives three strengths, three weaknesses and three communication tips.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Clearer Thinking argues that types are easier to understand, remember and discuss, even though they predict less than continuous scores (ct-2-0.txt).
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: No Father offers sixteen clusters, and inventing named clusters would be our own work. Honest options: (1) make the headline the person's strongest Gregory pair-side, in his words. (2) Allow a combined reading only where Gregory himself links two traits, per the personality README. Examples: meek with sloth, 'kindred' (III.16); silent with private judging and pride (III.14); abstinent with impatience and pride (III.19). Strengths and weaknesses map onto Gregory's visible side and hidden side. His principle is 'what worse thing presses on him in connection with it' (III.3).

report_sections.what_it_shows: '4% of people share your cluster', from a sample of about 63,000 users (owner's capture).
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Rarity makes a result feel special. That is my inference; it was not measured.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: None is possible today. It needs a real sample of takers. After launch it could show how many people share the strongest leaning, only from real data with N printed. The owner should rule first on whether this breaks 'never a percentage against a person'.

report_sections.section: Famous people who share your cluster
report_sections.what_it_shows: Four illustrated public figures: Steve Jobs, Rosa Parks, Katniss Everdeen and Galileo. A note says the placements are the site's interpretation of public information.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: People like to identify with admired figures. Inference; not measured.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea:
Use saints and biblical figures only where a Father describes the temperament:
- Titus and Timothy. Paul spoke differently to each because 'he saw Titus to be of a meeker spirit, and Timothy of one a little more fervid' (Gregory, Pastoral Rule III.16).
- Moses and Hobab (III.17, per the README).
- Martha and Mary, and Leah and Rachel, as the active and contemplative lives (Gregory, Moralia VI.61).
- Arsenius, who fled people, and Moses the Ethiopian, who welcomed them. A Father was shown both in two boats, one with the Spirit of God in silence, one with angels eating honey cakes (Apophthegmata, alphabetical collection, Arsenius/Moses). The only English checked is modern (saved: patristic/sanidopoulos-moses-sayings.txt), so paraphrase. The saying number needs checking against Ward.
Never assign a saint by guesswork.

report_sections.what_it_shows: The cluster (LONER) and the Enneagram type (Type 2) the reader scored least like, each with a description.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Contrast sharpens a self-image. On this site, quiz #4's 'which would argue with you' already works this way. Inference for the secular test.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Show the opposite pole of the person's strongest Gregory pair. Reframe it as the member the Body needs, not an 'anti'. Chrysostom: 'let all be eye or all head: will not the body perish?' The body is made 'by their being many and diverse' (Homily 31 on 1 Corinthians). Nazianzen: 'the common body of the church is composed of many different characters and minds' (Oration 2.44).

report_sections.what_it_shows: Five bars, each 'higher than N% of users' against about 63,000 users, with a two-sentence meaning. There is a note that different frameworks can conflict.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Numbers feel scientific. Clearer Thinking found continuous scores predict life outcomes better than types (average R 0.23 for the Big Five; ct-study.txt).
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory's pairs as two-pole rails, placed from the person's own answers. The site already builds these. No percentile until a real norm exists; the 'names no position' middle band stands in for 'average'.

report_sections.section: Enneagram core: fundamental fear, mental habit, core aspiration, antidote (page 4)
report_sections.what_it_shows: The type description, then the fear, the habit that grows from it, the aspiration and the 'antidote'.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: It speaks to motive, why you do what you do. In a systematic review, several studies found the Enneagram helpful for personal and spiritual growth (Hook et al. 2021).
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Cassian's chief fault. The eight faults attack everyone, 'yet the difficulties come to each of us in very different ways and manners' (Conferences V.13). So 'every one should discover his besetting sin, and direct his main attack against it' (V.14). This sorts people by which fault holds the chief place, but it is a vice profile, not a temperament. Frame it as 'your chief struggle'. The antidote would be the virtue Cassian sets against each fault (Institutes V-XII); not checked here fault by fault. It overlaps the site's seven deadly sins draft.

report_sections.section: Stages of Progression: Optimal / Average / Negative
report_sections.what_it_shows: Three cards showing how the type looks at its best, typically and at its worst.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: It turns a label into a range you can move along. Inference.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory, Pastoral Rule II.9 (per the README): vices pass as virtues. Niggardliness passes as frugality, wrath as zeal, haste as promptness, tardiness as deliberation. That gives 'the same trait at its best and as its counterfeit'. Do not use Cassian's fear/hope/love ladder here as a ranking of the person. It is a ladder of spiritual stages (Conferences XI.7), and scoring it would count devotion.

report_sections.what_it_shows: Five short, bolded tips.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Something to do next. Hook et al. 2021 report growth use as the Enneagram's main reported benefit.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: ONE starting point, as the README plan already has. Gregory: when several faults press, first help 'that through which there is the more rapid tendency to death' (III.38). Cassian: the order differs by person, so 'one man will have to fight his first battle against the fault which stands third on the list, another against that which is fourth or fifth' (Conferences V.27).

report_sections.section: Scores for all nine types, with a close-call note
report_sections.what_it_shows: A bar chart of percentiles for all nine types. When the top two are within 13 points, a warning says you likely share traits of both, with a link to the second type.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: It is honest about ambiguity and invites exploring. Inference.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Show all 18 pairs. Flag close leanings. Gregory says one person can carry contrary traits (III.37, per the README). Add 'browse all results', which the owner asked for on the Psalm quiz.

report_sections.what_it_shows: A four-letter type, then four percentile bars. Each explanation names the opposite pole.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: In Clearer Thinking's randomised test it made readers feel best. 10% disagreed that it made them feel good, against 19% for the Big Five. In a Nov 2024 sample it was also rated most accurate (1.7 against 1.6 for the Big Five and 1.3 for the Enneagram).
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory's pairs already name both poles. Nazianzen gives the Cappadocian root of the principle: 'Some are led by doctrine, others trained by example; some need the spur, others the curb' (Oration 2.30). Gregory credits Nazianzen for 'one and the same exhortation does not suit all' (Pastoral Rule III, Prologue).

report_sections.what_it_shows: 24 adjectives as percentile bars, grouped Top / Middle / Bottom. A chart of the top three and bottom two, and a tip to 'describe yourself in three words'.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Concrete adjectives are easy to repeat about yourself. Inference.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Rank within the person, as VIA does, so no norm sample is needed. Show the three pair-sides the person leans to most and the two least, labelled in Gregory's words.

report_sections.what_it_shows: Three tips 'to improve your relationships with others'.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Practical and social. Inference.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: The strongest honest match in this whole list. Gregory gives, for each side of each pair, how that person is best spoken to. Nazianzen adds: 'some, when taken to task in public, others, when privately corrected', and some by praise, others by blame (Oration 2.31). This can become 'How to help someone like me', a card to hand to a friend or priest.

report_sections.what_it_shows: Page 7 gives predictions of career, relationships and life satisfaction from regression on their users. Page 8 gives AI-written advice. Both are listed in the owner's contents page but were not captured.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Not measured. Their predictive R is modest: average R 0.23 for the Big Five.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: There is no honest statistical counterpart without outcome data. Gregory's own chains can be told as his warnings, not as predictions: much talk leads to detraction, then quarrels (III.14); over-giving leads to want, then grumbling, then grasping (III.20-21). AI insights are ruled out by the site's no-AI-over-theology rule.

report_sections.what_it_shows: A link. The friend gets a side-by-side comparison after finishing.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Their 2.0 post lists 'Compare with a friend' as a headline feature.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: The site's pair overlay, with no percentage between two people. Research adds a second use. Friends judge some traits better than the self does (Vazire 2010). Johnson's public-domain IPIP-NEO report advises: 'Questions about the accuracy of your results are best resolved by showing your report to people who know you well.' Informant feedback on moral traits was found helpful (Casali et al. 2024). So add 'Ask someone who knows you' to answer a few pairs about you.

report_sections.section: Type, Assertive/Turbulent identity, and percentages on five scales
report_sections.what_it_shows: A four-letter type plus -A or -T. Percentages on Energy, Mind, Nature, Tactics and Identity, with poles named. Types are grouped into four Roles (Analysts, Diplomats, Sentinels, Explorers) and into Strategies.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: The vendor claims 1.5 billion tests taken. The type name is simple, and a fifth, neuroticism-like scale was added. Clearer Thinking found that missing neuroticism cost MBTI-style tests accuracy.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory's joyful/sad pair and impatient/patient pair touch the same emotional ground (III.3, III.9). He ties sadness by temperament to anger and joy to lust (III.3).

report_sections.section: Free chapters: Introduction, Strengths & Weaknesses, Romantic Relationships, Friendships, Parenthood, Career Paths, Workplace Habits, Conclusion; then Premium
report_sections.what_it_shows: Long type essays applied to each life domain. The premium tier is a career suite.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Life-domain application ('what this means for my marriage or job'). Inference; no usage data found.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory's Book III also has station pairs the README left out as temperaments: subjects and prelates (ch 4), servants and masters (5), married and single (27), prosperity and adversity (26). They could supply honest 'at home', 'under authority' and 'leading others' sections. For vocation, Moralia VI.57: 'of souls are infinitely varied one with another'. So 'neither the tranquil mind should open itself wide in the immoderate exercising of works, nor the restless mind stint itself in devotion to contemplation'. VI.61 gives Martha and Mary: 'Now Martha's concern is not reproved, but that of Mary is even commended.'

report_sections.test: Truity Enneagram Personality Test (19-page paid sample report)
report_sections.section: Scores for all nine types by centre; Your Type in Depth; Spectrum of Health; Wings and Arrows; A Path Forward with mantra; Top 3 Superpowers and Blindspots
report_sections.what_it_shows: A 'match' percentage for all nine types, grouped as Body, Head and Heart types, each with a core emotion (anger, fear, sadness). Then: in a nutshell, strengths, challenges, core weakness, belief, fear, desire and traits, emotional life, childhood origins, relationships (the good and the bad), and at work. Then stressed, average and thriving versions; wings and arrows; growth tasks and a mantra; and three superpowers and three blindspots. The free brief report shows only the scores.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Depth and a motive story. Hook et al. 2021 report growth use.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Cassian's eight (Conferences V.2: 'There are eight principal faults which attack mankind'), with the chief one per person (V.13-14). Gregory's hidden side is the 'blindspot'. A single short line from Gregory can play the mantra's role (already planned). Do NOT borrow wings or arrows: the review found little research support for them.

report_sections.section: Facets as named bipolar pairs; the four temperaments; values, motivators, how others see you, communication, relationships, leadership, teamwork, careers; strengths, opportunities, pitfalls
report_sections.what_it_shows: Each of the four preferences splits into 5-6 facets, each a pair with both names and split percentages (e.g. PLACID 59% / ENERGETIC 41%). There is a four-temperaments chart and a 16-type chart, then application sections and a career list.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: The facets make a type feel precise. The application sections make it usable. Inference.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: This is the secular precedent closest to Gregory's rails: named two-pole facets. 'How others see you' maps onto Gregory's visible side, with the hidden side as its complement.

report_sections.test: IPIP-NEO (J. A. Johnson; public-domain items and report text)
report_sections.section: Narrative report with domain and facet percentiles
report_sections.what_it_shows: Five domains and 30 facets as percentile estimates against people of the same sex and roughly the same age. Low, average and high mean the bottom 30%, middle 40% and top 30%. Each has a narrative. It says traits are neither good nor bad. The report was a temporary web page that readers had to save themselves.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Detail and credibility. Not measured.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory corrects both sides of every pair, so no pole is the good one; the site already keeps that rule. The 'names no position' middle band plays the role of 'average'. No percentiles without a norm.

report_sections.what_it_shows: Percentiles against a norm of 10,000 people of mixed sex and age. The FAQ says the reports are written to lay out strengths and weaknesses fully, not so that everyone wins. It can be taken once only. A partner who also takes it unlocks a relationship report (paid vouchers).
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Seriousness and a couples use. Not measured.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory's even-handedness: both sides are corrected. The site's pair overlay covers the couple use, with no percentage between two people.

report_sections.section: Ranked 24 strengths; top five 'signature strengths'; 'lesser strengths'
report_sections.what_it_shows: A free rank order of 24 strengths from 96 items, ranked within the person by mean score, grouped under six virtues. The FAQ says lesser strengths 'are not viewed as weaknesses'.
report_sections.why_people_like_it: Entirely positive, and a ranking needs no norm sample. The virtue language is close to Christian ethics.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Borrow the method, not the flattery. Rank Gregory's pair-sides within the person, and keep his hidden side so it is not a Barnum list of virtues.

report_sections.what_it_shows: A sixth factor. High scorers avoid manipulating others, feel little pull to break rules, do not want luxury and feel no special entitlement to status (hexaco.org scale descriptions).
report_sections.why_people_like_it: It measures moral character, which the Big Five blurs. Not measured as user preference.
report_sections.christian_counterpart_idea: Gregory's humble/haughty pair (III.17) and giver/taker pairs (III.20-21) cover similar ground. He adds that fear can pass as humility and pride as frankness (per the README).

report.formats:
Clearer Thinking Ultimate Personality Test:
- Format: agree/disagree statements on a 7-point scale, 'totally disagree' to 'totally agree'.
- Items: v1.0 had 120 questions (60 Big Five, 60 Jungian, 45 Enneagram; some items count for two frameworks). The v2.0 analysis used 116. The owner recalls about 70; I could not confirm that for any version. One report URL from the web carries a 130-character answer string, version unknown.
- Time: '12 minutes' stated.
- Report: 8 pages (sections above).
- Sharing and comparison: a shareable Snapshot image, invite-a-friend side-by-side comparison, and a $9 PDF.
- Norms: about 63,000 users in the owner's report. The study used attention checks.

16Personalities:
- Items: 60 statements, 6 per screen.
- Scale: 7 points, labelled for screen readers 'I strongly agree', 'I moderately agree', 'I agree', 'I am not sure', 'I disagree', 'I moderately disagree', 'I strongly disagree'. Only 'Agree' and 'Disagree' show on screen. Checked on the live page.
- Time: about 10 minutes.
- Result: type with -A/-T and percentages on 5 scales, then 8 free chapters and a premium career suite.
- Friend comparison: not verified.

Truity TypeFinder:
- Items: 130, as paired phrases ('From each pair, choose the phrase that describes you best').
- Scale: 5 points between the two phrases, 15 pairs per page (checked live).
- Time: 10-15 minutes.
- Report: free brief report; paid full report (18-page sample).

Truity Enneagram:
- Items: about 105 single statements, 10 per page.
- Scale: 5 points from Inaccurate through Neutral to Accurate (checked live).
- Time: 10-15 minutes.
- Report: free scores; paid 19-page report.

Truity Big Five:
- Items: 60, 5-point Inaccurate to Accurate.
- Time: 5-10 minutes.

IPIP-NEO-120 (Johnson 2014):
- Items: 120, four per facet.
- Scale: the standard IPIP 5-point labels, 'Very Inaccurate' to 'Very Accurate' (ipip.ori.org).
- Report: narrative with percentiles by sex and age. Free.

Understand Myself:
- Items: 100 phrases (Big Five Aspect Scales, DeYoung, Quilty and Peterson 2007).
- Time: '10 to 20 minutes' on one page, '15-20 minutes' on another.
- Report: percentiles against 10,000 people, one take only, partner relationship report.
- Price: paid. Vouchers sell in bundles, e.g. 5 for $44.95.

VIA Survey:
- Items: 96, scored as means from 1 to 5.
- Time: 10-15 minutes.
- Report: free ranked 24 strengths; paid reports. They suggest retaking every couple of years.

HEXACO:
- Items: the HEXACO-60 has 10 items per scale (Ashton and Lee 2009).
- The online version and its scale points were not verified.

The site's first-look design, for comparison: about 36 two-sided items over 18 Gregory pairs, a five-point slide between two real ways of being, about six minutes.
report.scale_points_evidence:
1. Number of points, general.
- Preston and Colman (2000, Acta Psychologica 104:1-15; N=149, ratings of a store or restaurant, not personality): 2-4 points did poorly. Reliability, validity and discrimination rose with more categories 'up to about 7'. Test-retest reliability fell beyond 10. Respondents preferred 10, then 7 and 9.
- Lozano, Garcia-Cueto and Muniz (2008, Methodology 4:73-79; Monte Carlo simulation): the optimum is 4 to 7.
- Maitland (2009, Survey Practice 2(5), summarising Krosnick and Fabrigar 1997 and Alwin and Krosnick 1991): 5-7 points were more reliable than fewer or more. Differences among bipolar scale lengths were smaller than among unipolar ones.

2. Personality items specifically.
- Simms, Zelazny, Williams and Bernstein (2019, Psychological Assessment 31:557-566; N=1,358 randomly assigned to 2 to 11 options or a visual slider): precision was weaker with 2-5 options, and there was no gain beyond 6 options, including sliders. But criterion validity did not follow this pattern.
- Maydeu-Olivares et al. (2009, Behavior Research Methods 41:295-308; within-person, two personality questionnaires): more options raised internal consistency. They had no effect on convergent validity, and model fit got worse.

3. Agree/disagree against two-sided wording. This matters more for this site than 5 against 7.
- Revilla, Saris and Krosnick (2014, Sociological Methods and Research 43:73-97; European Social Survey experiments): agree/disagree scales suffer acquiescence. If you use them, offer 5 categories, not 7 or 11, which gave lower-quality data.
- Saris, Revilla, Krosnick and Shaeffer (2010, Survey Research Methods 4:61-79): agree/disagree items had much lower quality than items with item-specific response options.
- Krosnick (1999, Annual Review of Psychology 50:537-567): scale labels and satisficing shape answers.
- Zhang and Savalei (2016, Educational and Psychological Measurement 76:357-386): replacing each Likert option with a full sentence (the 'Expanded format') kept reliability the same and gave a cleaner factor structure than reverse-worded Likert items.
- Truity's TypeFinder already uses two named phrases with 5 points between them.
- Reading (mine): the site's two-sided statements are item-specific, not agree/disagree. So Revilla's 5-over-7 result for agree/disagree does not transfer directly, and the literature favours the two-sided format itself.

4. Forced choice. This is a different thing from the site's two-sided slider.
- Multidimensional forced choice means picking between statements that measure different traits.
- It gives similar or slightly higher validity than single statements (Salgado and Tauriz 2014, European Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology 23:3-30).
- It resists faking: a score-inflation effect of 0.06 (Cao and Drasgow 2019, Journal of Applied Psychology 104:1347-1368). Rating scales were faked more (Wetzel, Frick and Brown 2021, Psychological Assessment 33:156-170).
- Scored the traditional way it produces ipsative data, where every profile has the same total, which distorts it (Brown and Maydeu-Olivares 2013, Psychological Methods 18:36-52).
- The site's slider is one bipolar dimension per item, so it is not ipsative. Faking pressure is low in a self-discovery quiz.

5. Length of scales.
- Very short scales (1-2 items per trait) underestimate what traits predict. Slightly longer measures help a lot (Crede et al. 2012, JPSP 102:874-888).

Bottom line for the owner's question:
- Seven points is a common choice (Clearer Thinking, 16Personalities). It is defensible on a two-sided item, and it adds no questions.
- The evidence does not show it will make results more accurate in any way a reader would notice. Validity gains past 5-6 points are nil in the best personality study.
- More items per pair and two-sided wording matter more than more points.
- Keep a true middle so the 'names no position' band stays meaningful.
cautions: Barnum/Forer effect. In 1949 Forer's students rated one identical sketch, taken from an astrology book, as fitting them at 4.30 out of 5 (saved Wikipedia summary). Acceptance depends on the relevance and favourability of the profile (Dickson and Kelly 1985, Psychological Reports 57:367-382). A report full of pleasant generalities will be believed whether or not it is true. Tie every sentence to the person's own answers ('You said... you also said...'), which the README plan already does.

Flattery wins on first read. Clearer Thinking's randomised test found the positively framed Jungian section was the only one that made people feel significantly better. Unfavourable feedback is rated less accurate (Ditto and Boardman 1995, Basic and Applied Social Psychology 16:137). But negative moral feedback was found helpful when it surprised and was explained (Casali, Metselaar and Thielmann 2024, Identity 25:428-438; N=17, small). Order feedback from familiar to new (Tharinger et al. 2008, citing Schroeder, Hahn, Finn and Swann 1993). People with negative self-views seek confirming feedback (Swann et al. 1992). Gregory corrects both sides of every pair, and that is the built-in guard against flattering types.

Percentiles without a real norm. Every percentile seen here rests on a named sample: IPIP-NEO by sex and age; Understand Myself 10,000; Clearer Thinking about 63,000; Truity 'a large, international sample'. The site has none. Use rails placed from the person's own answers, and rankings within the person (as VIA does). Add percentiles or rarity only from real takers with N shown, and only after the owner rules whether that counts as 'a percentage against a person'.

Types lose information and flip near the middle. Clearer Thinking found traits form bell curves, and continuous scores beat binary types. MBTI score distributions are centre-weighted, not bimodal (Bess and Harvey 2002). There are published critiques of MBTI (Pittenger 2005; Stein and Swan 2019). A 'type' headline must keep the middle band and show close leanings.

Cluster types are disputed and their names are subjective. Gerlach et al. (2018, Nature Human Behaviour 2:735-742) found four types in 1.5 million people. A reply argues the types may be neither robust nor exhaustive (Freudenstein et al. 2019). Clearer Thinking says its cluster names 'involved making some subjective choices'. Any named cluster the site makes would be its own invention and must say so.

Famous-people lists are interpretation, not data (Clearer Thinking's own note). Pair a saint with a result only where a Father describes that temperament. Never assign a modern or ancient person by guesswork.

Enneagram machinery is weak and its Christian lineage is contested. A review of 104 samples found mixed reliability and validity. Factor analyses typically find fewer than nine factors, and there is little support for wings and arrows (Hook et al. 2021, Journal of Clinical Psychology 77:865-883). Its origins 'remain a subject of debate'; the link to Evagrius is only claimed. Catholic cautions exist: a USCCB doctrine committee draft and a 2003 Vatican document (per saved Wikipedia text). I found no Orthodox statement and am unsure of one. Go to Cassian's own text instead of borrowing Enneagram structure.

Vices are not temperaments. Cassian says all eight faults attack everyone (Conferences V.13). A 'chief struggle' layer is a vice profile anyone could have. Frame it gently, name it once, and mind the overlap with the seven deadly sins draft.

Stages are not types, and must not become devotion scores. Cassian's fear, hope and love (Conferences XI.6-7: slave, hireling, son) is a ladder to climb. Scoring someone's rung would break 'count knowledge, never devotion' and could wound or flatter.

Gregory ranks the two lives. Moralia VI.61 says the merits of the active life are great 'but of the contemplative, far better'. A 'Martha' result could feel lesser. VI.57 balances this: restless minds are harmed by too much contemplation, and 'Martha's concern is not reproved'. Print both.

Self-report blind spots. Friends judge evaluative traits such as intellect better than the self (Vazire 2010). A self-report cannot see everything, which is a reason for an 'ask someone who knows you' option. It is not a reason to claim more than the answers show.

Predictions and AI insights. Clearer Thinking's predictions come from regression on outcome data (Big Five average R 0.23). The site has no outcome data. AI insights are banned by the site's rules. Gregory's causal chains may be given as his warnings, never as statistics.

Gathering limits. Trustpilot put up a bot check and Reddit refused scripted access. I did not bypass either, so 'what users value' rests on Clearer Thinking's randomised study and published feedback research, not on reviews. 16Personalities' '1.5 billion' figure is the vendor's own claim. Their AI reference page contains instructions addressed to AI systems; I used it only for facts.
engagement_hooks: One name you can say out loud, plus a portrait. Clearer Thinking, 16Personalities and Truity all lead with it. Clearer Thinking's data: types are memorable, and factors are accurate; give both.
A single share image with all layers on it (Clearer Thinking Snapshot).
A 'you vs your opposite' contrast (Anti-Personality, Farthest Type). The honest version is 'the member you most need' (Chrysostom, Homily 31 on 1 Corinthians).
A motive layer: fear, desire, antidote and growth path (Enneagram sections). The honest version is Cassian's chief fault with one 'Start here' (Conferences V.14, 27; Pastoral Rule III.38).
Best / typical / worst version of the same trait (Truity 'Spectrum of Health'; Clearer Thinking 'Stages'). The honest version is Gregory's vices that pass as virtues (Pastoral Rule II.9).
A ranked list of adjectives with a 'describe yourself in three words' prompt (Clearer Thinking Distinctive Traits; VIA signature strengths).
Named two-pole facets under each headline (Truity TypeFinder), close to Gregory's rails.
Communication tips someone else can use. The honest version is Gregory's modes of admonition plus Nazianzen, Oration 2.30-31, which could become a 'How to help someone like me' card.
Life-domain chapters: relationships, friendships, parenting, work (16Personalities). Gregory's station pairs (Book III ch 4, 5, 26, 27) can honestly supply some of these.
A close-call note when two results are near, with a link to the second (Clearer Thinking).
Browse all results (Clearer Thinking 'Explore All Types'; the owner asked for this on the Psalm quiz).

Invite a friend for a side-by-side view (Clearer Thinking; Understand Myself partner report). The site's pair overlay covers it; add an 'ask someone who knows you' informant option (Vazire 2010; Casali et al. 2024).
Saints and biblical figures 'like you', only where a Father names the temperament: Titus and Timothy; Moses and Hobab; Martha and Mary; Leah and Rachel; Arsenius and Moses the Ethiopian.

Honest method notes that build trust (Clearer Thinking's 'How accurate are personality tests?' panel and its published study). For this site, that means the how-it-works page naming Gregory, Cassian and Nazianzen.
report.length_and_dropoff:
Market norm:
- Serious free tests run 60-130 items and 10-15 minutes: 16Personalities 60 items in about 10 minutes; Truity 60-130 items in 5-15 minutes; VIA 96 items in 10-15 minutes; IPIP-NEO-120; Understand Myself 100 phrases in 10-20 minutes; Clearer Thinking 116-120 items in 12 minutes.
- The first-look Gregory design (about 36 items, about 6 minutes) is about half that.

Evidence on drop-off:
- Hoerger (2010, Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking 13:697-700; 1,963 undergraduates in six web studies): about 10% drop out almost at once, then about 2% more per 100 items. By that estimate, going from 36 to about 70 items costs under 1 extra point of drop-off. The sample was students, not self-selected quiz takers, so it is only a rough guide.
- Galesic and Bosnjak (2009, Public Opinion Quarterly 73:349-360): the longer the stated length (10, 20 or 30 minutes), the fewer people start and finish. Later answers are faster, shorter and more uniform. So state an honest, modest time. Spread each layer's items through the quiz rather than putting one layer last. Put the most important pairs early.
- Villar, Callegaro and Yang (2013, Social Science Computer Review 31:744-762; 32 experiments): a steady progress bar does not reduce drop-off. Fast-then-slow bars reduce it; slow-then-fast bars increase it.
- Crede et al. (2012): one or two items per trait badly understate what traits predict, and a few more items help a lot. That argues for three to four items on the pairs that drive the headline, not one.
- Kosinski et al. (2015, American Psychologist 70:543-556): Facebook-based psychology studies with personal feedback drew over 10 million participants. That is evidence that personal feedback motivates people, not a length figure.

Efficiency:
- Clearer Thinking lets one item score for two frameworks, which adds layers without adding length.
- For this site, that is honest only where a Father links the two things. Examples: Gregory ties meekness to sloth (III.16) and silence to private judging (III.14).

Practical reading: a multi-layer Christian report at about 60-75 items and 10-12 minutes sits inside the norm set by the tests the owner admires.
